candidate: This paper presents a study evaluating the use of nanopore sequencing combined with adaptive sampling and a novel tool called NanoExpansion to accurately characterize repeat expansion disorders. The objective was to improve the diagnostic accuracy and efficiency of identifying these disorders, which are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). The study included 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), DM2, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and other neurodegenerative conditions, as well as healthy controls. Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling on Oxford Nanopore platforms, and NanoExpansion was developed to analyze the data, identifying expanded alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. The results showed that nanopore sequencing with NanoExpansion accurately characterized all cases of DM1, DM2, ALS, Friedreich ataxia, Huntington’s disease, and Kennedy disease, and identified several cases of spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs) and cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS). Compared to long PCR, nanopore sequencing provided more accurate results for larger expansions, and detected repeat interruptions in a significant proportion of DM1 cases. However, the study noted limitations, including the potential for sequencing errors and the need for further validation on larger datasets. The findings suggest that the integration of nanopore sequencing and NanoExpansion offers a promising approach for the comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders, with the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

Abstract
Expansion repeat disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). We evaluated targeted long-read nanopore
sequencing for comprehensive characterization of STR expansions in 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1,
n = 51) and DM2 (n = 3) already characterized by Southern blot, C9orf72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS n = 11) evaluated by
repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RP-PCR; validation group), suspected spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA, n = 46), cerebellar ataxia with
neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS; n = 13), Huntington’s disease (1), Kennedy disease (1), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, 2), and
4 healthy controls (test group). Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling (AS) on Oxford Nanopore GridION or PromethION-2Solo
platforms. Long-PCR sequencing was performed for comparison. We also developed NanoExpansion, a Python-based tool for sizing expanded
alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. We correctly characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, and Kennedy disease
cases, and identified eight SCA27B, two SCA37, three SCA31, one SCA3, and nine CANVAS cases. Compared with the AS approach, longPCR underestimated alleles exceeding 800 repeats. Repeat interruptions were detected in 27/51 (52.9%) DM1 cases and 1/10 (10%) ALS, but
not in CANVAS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, Kennedy disease, or SCA cases. This integrated sequencing analysis pipeline provides accurate,
comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders and has the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

Introduction
Short tandem repeats (STRs), also known as microsatellites,
are repeating tracts of DNA, usually 2–12 bp long, that can
be found in both coding and noncoding regions of the genome
[1]. They are characterized by high length polymorphism and
instability which results in >50 different diseases [2], that
are called repeat expansion disorders (REDs) [3], as listed in
STRchive (https://strchive.org) [4].
Among those, myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is the
most common muscular dystrophy in adults, with an estimated prevalence of about 1/8000 worldwide [5]. It is an autosomal dominant disorder and can involve multiple organs
and systems [6]. DM1 is caused by the expansion of the unstable CTG trinucleotide repeat in the 3 untranslated region
of the DMPK gene, located on chromosome 19q13.32 [7].
The size of the expansion can greatly vary with healthy people showing a range between 5 and 35 CTG repeats. Patients

with a CTG expansion from 36 and 49 are asymptomatic,
and do not meet diagnostic criteria for DM1. However, these
alleles are unstable during transmission, particularly through
meiosis, and can expand into the pathogenic range in the next
generation (premutation or mutable normal alleles). Affected
patients have a CTG expansion >50. Expansion size is associated with age of onset and severity: mild late-onset, classic and congenital DM1 are associated with expansions ≤150
CTGs (E1), ≤1000 CTGs (E2), and ≥1000 CTGs (E3), respectively [8]. Clinical features in DM1 patients vary according
to severity group. Most common symptoms are distal muscle weakness and myotonia [7]. However, the high individual
variability in DM1 patients of the same subtype makes the
genotype–phenotype correlation not completely understood.
The great instability of CTG expansion in both somatic and
germline cells, which persists during patient’s lifetime, is called
somatic mosaicism phenomenon [9]. Another crucial aspect

that makes the genotype–phenotype correlation more complex is the presence of interruptions within the CTG expansion. Several variant expansions, such as CCG, CGG, CTC,
TTG, GGC, CAG, have been observed, especially at the 3 and
5 ends of the DMPK gene [10, 11]. These interruption motifs
have a stabilizing effect of the expansion on germline transmission. However, the great heterogeneity in terms of motif,
length and location of the interruption patterns along the CTG
expansion leads to a huge phenotypic variability, which deserves to be further investigated [12].
Other REDs are spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs), which are
a heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative autosomal dominant diseases (prevalence of about 3/100 000 [13, 14]. Despite
their complex genotype–phenotype spectrum, common clinical features among SCAs are progressive cerebellar ataxia,
with oculomotor abnormalities, visual problems, pyramidal
and extrapyramidal signs, dysarthria and cognitive dysfunction [13, 15].
Cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia
syndrome (CANVAS) has recently been included among the
REDs [16]. It is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative
balance disorder, caused by biallelic repeat expansion mutations in the RFC1 gene, characterized by the peculiar clinical phenotype including cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy), bilateral vestibular hypofunction, and
chronic cough. Huntington’s disease and Kennedy disease are
two other well-known REDs.
The current diagnosis of REDs is mainly based on two wellknown and standardized techniques: Southern blot (SB) assay and triplet-repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RPPCR), often coupled. SB is considered the gold-standard, but it
is labor-intensive and time-consuming, it requires large quantities (≥10 μg) of high-quality DNA to produce valuable results [17], it is inaccurate in repeat expansion estimates, and
suffers from low resolution and sensitivity in detecting short
expansions. SB also lacks in providing a sequence context on
the evaluated STRs [18].
RP-PCR is relatively inexpensive, easy to implement and
more efficient in detecting short expansions with respect to
SB. However, it cannot reveal long repeated regions and mosaicisms. Furthermore, it cannot determine the size of the expansion and is prone to errors due to amplification artifacts
[19]. The high concentration of GC in some repeat and interruption motifs causes the allelic drop out polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) bias, leading to further sequencing errors.
The recent third generation long-read sequencing (LRS)
technologies, such as Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT,
Oxford Science Park, UK) or PacBio (Menlo Park, CA), allow
to obtain long DNA fragments and to accurately characterize the size of expansions, mosaicisms and interruption patterns [20–22]. Long reads enable robust structural variation
and tandem repeats detection. In addition, nanopore sequencing provides an in-silico target sequencing technique, named
adaptive sampling (AS) [23]. During a sequencing experiment,
if the basecalled sequence does not fall within the region of
interest provided to the machine beforehand, the sequencing
process stops and the DNA fragment is ejected from the pore.
A new fragment then begins to be sequenced. This application avoids using PCR for target sequencing, that can introduce artefacts, biases and may generate false negative results
[23–25].
Several computational tools, including Straglr [26],
LongTR [27], STRdust [28], and STRkit [29], have been

developed to estimate repeat lengths and genotype expanded
alleles from LRS data. Although these tools provide reliable
repeat sizing and, in some cases, allele phasing or motif annotation, their primary objective remains repeat genotyping.
However, the repeat pattern architecture of expanded regions,
such as motif interruptions, internal sequence organization,
and DNA methylation, can significantly influence disease
characterization and clinical severity. Therefore, to address
the need of a more comprehensive analysis of repeated regions, we developed NanoExpansion, a prototype software
designed to reconstruct and characterize the complete architecture of expanded alleles from long read sequencing
data.
In addition to repeat sizing, NanoExpansion identifies motif interruptions, performs allele clustering, and extracts locusspecific DNA methylation profiles directly from the sequencing reads, providing an integrated genetic and epigenetic characterization of repeat expansion loci. Moreover, NanoExpansion also provide a complete and detailed report to guide
and support medical doctors in the diagnosis of patients with
REDs. This comprehensive framework enables a more detailed investigation of genotype–phenotype relationships than
currently available repeat genotyping software.
This study aimed to demonstrate the potential diagnostic
power of nanopore sequencing by characterizing repeat expansion regions in two cohorts. The first cohort comprised patients with DM1, DM2, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
carrying a C9orf72 expansion for whom a genetic diagnosis
had already been made. The second cohort comprised subjects with suspected SCA, CANVAS, HD, or Kennedy disease.
A comprehensive bioinformatics pipeline has been developed.
The present work would reinforce the findings of previous research studies using the latest human genome reference (hs1),
which was provided by the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium [23, 24, 30, 31].

Materials and methods
Patient consent
The study has been approved by the AUSL Bologna Ethical Committee (BITRO N◦ 599–2022-SPER-AUSLBO). This
study was conducted in agreement with either the most updated Declaration of Helsinki and all the international and
local laws applied to clinical studies and patient protection.

Study setting and data collection
The dataset included 132 participants enrolled at the IRCCS
Istituto delle Scienze Neurologiche di Bologna, Bellaria Hospital, Italy. The cohort included 51 individuals with genetically
confirmed diagnoses of DM1, three DM2, 11 ALS cases, of
which 10 already identified for expansion in C9orf72 with RPPCR (validation group). Additionally, the cohort comprises
patients with clinical diagnoses (suspected cases, test group)
of SCA (46), CANVAS (13), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, two),
Huntington’s disease (HD, one), and Kennedy disorder (one).
Four healthy controls (mean age: 71) were also included.

DNA purification
DNA was purified from whole blood samples, using the
Maxwell® 16 Blood DNA Purification Kit (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA). DNA concentration was measured using
Quantus Fluorometer (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA).

NanoExpansion enables accurate characterization of repeat expansion disorders

Library preparation for ONT platform
Two different types of libraries were processed: one from
native DNA and one for long PCR product. For native
DNA, the Ligation Sequencing Kit V14 (SQK-LSK114, Oxford Nanopore, Oxford Science Park, UK) was used starting with 2 μg of total DNA following the protocol of the
provider. In brief, DNA was incubated with DNA-repair and
end-repair enzymes in thermal cycler at 20◦ C for 10 min and
65◦ C for 5 min. It followed AMPure XP bead purification
(Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) and 20 min incubation
with Quick T4 DNA Ligase (NEB, Ipswich, MA) and the
Ligation Adapter. After AMPure XP purification with Long
Fragment Buffer (LFB), the concentration was measured by
Quantus™ Fluorometer (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA),
Fragment Analyzer 5200 (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA) and NEB
Bio Calculator (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA) or
Promega Biocalculator (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA).
Then, 200–800 ng of DNA were loaded onto the R10.4.1 flow
cell (FLO-MIN114) using the ONT GridION platform (ONT,
Oxford UK). Twenty-one cases were loaded onto PromethION 2 Solo (ONT, Oxford UK) to increase the coverage
depth. To reduce the costs, the P2Solo setup was optimized by
reusing the same flow cell with a running time of 16 h. After DNase treatment, libraries were loaded with no barcoding
step to maximise the coverage depth.
For long PCR product, the Native Barcoding Kit 24 V14
(SQK- NBD114.24) was used including 24 different samples.
Primers used for all loci and PCR conditions are described in
Supplementary File 1. In brief, 400 ng of purified amplicon
pools were treated with NEBNext FFPE DNA repair and Ultra II End-Prep enzyme mix (NEB, Ipswich, MA), at 20◦ C and
at 65◦ C for 10 min each, purified with AMPure XP beads and
barcoded with NEB Blunt/TA Ligase Master Mix (NEB, Ipswich, MA), for 20 min at room temperature. After pooling
and repurification with AMPure XP beads, DNA was ligated
with Native Adapter (NA) using Quick T4 DNA ligase (NEB,
Ipswich, MA) for 20 min at room temperature. After the final bead purification using LFB to enrich DNA >3 kb, the library was evaluated with Quantus™ Fluorometer (Promega,
Madison, WI 53711 USA). Depending on the fragment size,
200–800 ng of DNA were loaded onto washed and reused
R10.4.1 flow cell (FLO-MIN114) coming from AS experiments using the ONT GridION platform (ONT, Oxford UK).

Native nanopore sequencing downstream analysis
During nanopore sequencing, the MinKnow software (version 6.2.14, ONT) stored the raw current signal into POD5
files. Real-time basecalling was set up to HAC algorithm
to avoid overloading the GridION computing unit. MinKnow also performed AS enriching for 37 loci of interests
(see Supplementary Tables S1 and S2). Those loci involved
classical expansion repeat regions, as well as a list of 13
genes in which (CAG)>5 polyQ repeats were detected using
blat tool (https://genome.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgBlat) in the human genome. The latter have not yet been associated with
any disease. Each sequencing run usually lasted 16–24 h.
New MinION flow cells were used for native DNA processing, while used and washed flow cells were used for long
amplicons. After sequencing, the raw signal was transferred
to a high-performance computing station (equipped with a
single AMD EPYC 9654 processor (96 cores, 192 threads,
base clock 1.5 GHz, boost up to 3.7 GHz) and two NVIDIA

3

L40 GPUs (45 GiB memory each, CUDA 12.2); the system
ran Debian GNU/Linux 6.1.0–29-amd64) and basecalled with
Dorado, version 1.3.0, models v5.2.0. Samples were basecalled with both high accurate (hac, a part of them) and super accurate (sup) Dorado models. The q score filter was set
to 10. The basecalled sequences were aligned to the reference genome (GRCh38 and T2T CHM13v2/hs1) using minimap2 (version 2.26) [32]. All native samples were aligned
to the GRCh38 reference (hg38), and seven subjects with
DM1 were also mapped to hs1 (T2T). Samples sequenced
with long PCR were aligned to T2T CHM13v2/hs1. Aligned
reads were stored in BAM files and indexed. The aligned
data were visually inspected with IGV [33]. Single nucleotide
variants were called using Clair3 (version 1.0.10) [34]. SNP
information was used to perform haplotyping with Whatshap (version 2.4) [35]. Structural variants were called with
Sniffles (version 2.2) [36], CuteSV (version 2.1.0) [37, 38],
while STRs were detected using several tools, such as Sniffles (version 2.2), CuteSV(version 2.1.0), Nanorepeat [39],
Straglr (version 1.4.1)(26), STRdust (version 0.20.0) [28],
STRkit (version 0.24.2) [29], and LongTR (version 638942f)
[27]. The VCF output files were annotated with Stranger (version 0.9.5, doi:10.5281/zenodo.4548873). Finally, NanoExpansion, which is a prototype software developed within our
research group, was used to characterize repeat expansion patterns, detecting the main motifs and the interruptions. The
whole pipeline was integrated into a Snakemake [40] workflow.

NanoExpansion
NanoExpansion is a Python-based software package designed
to reconstruct the internal architecture of pathogenic repeat
expansions from LRS data. By providing an aligned BAMfile and the genomic coordinates of a target repeat locus, the
software extracts spanning reads and iteratively identifies repeat and interruption motifs within each expanded allele. Unlike repeat genotyping tools that primarily estimate repeat expansion size, NanoExpansion reconstructs the sequential pattern of repeat blocks, filtering spurious nucleotides, and generated a compact representation of the expanded allele [e.g.
(CTG)n(CCG)m(CTG)k]. In addition, NanoExpansion computes allele-specific summary statistics, extracts DNA methylation profiles across the target locus, and produces a detailed
report to support medical doctors in the diagnostic decision
process. Users provide genomic coordinates of the target locus, together with canonical repeat motif and a group of interruption motifs to be investigated (if not specified, NanoExpansion can also automatically detect interruption motifs), allowing the tool to characterize a broad range of REDs. Additional
filtering parameters could be provided by the user. NanoExpansion is designed to work with hg38 and T2T genome references. The software has been benchmarked on a set of artificially expanded reads (see Supplementary Material) to prove
its accuracy in detecting expansion patterns.

Library preparation for short read exome
sequencing
To rule out possible false calls coming from ONT, we performed a separate test on five samples already evaluated with
exome sequencing using NovaSEQ6000 for all loci listed in
Supplementary Table S1. The sample library for exome sequencing was prepared using xGen™ DNA EZ Library Prep

4

Kit (IDT, Coralville, Iowa, USA), enriched with xGen Exome
Research Panel v2 probes, and then sequenced with 2 × 150
bp paired end reads on a NovaSeq 6000 instrument (Illumina).
Bioinformatic analysis followed the GATK v.4.2.0.0 workflow
for germline variant discovery, aligning to reference genome
GRCh38/hg38. BAM files were visualized on IGV.

Triplet-RP-PCR for C9orf72
C9orf72 repeat was typed using the AmplideXPCR/CE
C9orf72 Kit (Asuragen, Austin Texas, USA) amplifying the
target using a three-primer G4C2-RP-PCR configuration [41]
followed by fragment sizing on a capillary electrophoresis instrument. The sizing of amplicons was performed by GeneMapper software according to the manufacturer’s protocols.

SB for DMPK expansion repeats
SB data analysis was performed as previously described [42].

Statistical analysis
The comparison between using Dorado hac and sup models
have been assessed by computing the following metrics: mismatch, insertion, deletion, and homopolymer error rate (homopolymers ≥ 4 bp, that is known to be an ONT-specific
bias). Statistically significant differences have been verified
using the Wilcoxon test (α = 0.05, one-tailed). Agreement
at read level (i.e. comparing both BAM files) was assessed
by computing mean and 95% confidence interval of the difference inedit distance (NM, global measure of error per
read), mapping quality (MAPQ, which measures mapping
efficiency), and in the number of clipped bases, that indicates
partial or problematic alignments. Same statistical procedure
has been used for comparing alignment to hg38 and T2T/hs1
reference genome.
Effectiveness of AS was measured by computing enrichment
ratio (ER) and fold-enrichment (FE, using a control samples,
sequenced both with and without AS); mean ER and FE have
been provided, together with 95% confidence interval (ER ≥
5×, FE ≥ 4× can be considered good efficacy). All these metrics have been computed using Python 3.6.13 (Pysam 0.21.0
and Pybedtools 0.9.0 packages).
The agreement between native ONT and SB has been measured considering that SB only provided intervals of expansion size. First, considering only genomic classification (E1,
E2, and E3), ordinal metrics such as quadratic weighted Cohen’s Kappa (κw ), ordinal accuracy, and mean absolute error
(MAE) have been used. These metrics evaluate ordinal classification, considering that a misclassification E1–E2 or E2–E3,
is less severe than E1–E3. Genomic classes have been assigned
to native nanopore sequencing according to the mean of the
distribution of repeat sizes. In addition, metrics evaluating the
overlapping between nanopore and SB results have been used:
coverage rate of native ONT within the SB intervals, distance
of the median of native ONT from SB intervals, and probabilistic overlap between a uniform distribution defined by SB
intervals and a kernel density estimate of native ONT.
Native and long PCR ONT were compared by drawing
scatter plots, fitting a linear model (R2 is reported), and computing both the Pearson correlation coefficient (ρ) and the
Lin’s Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC, that measures the degree to which observations are close to the 45◦
line) by disease. Native ONT results have been obtained from
IGV, while for long PCR, most frequent reads covering both

repeated loci and flanking regions were considered. Comparison between long PCR and native ONT has been conducted
using R 4.3.1.
Metrics used to compare the different variant caller software tools against the IGV ground truth spanned accuracy,
completeness, and agreement measures. Accuracy and error
dispersion were quantified using MAE, root mean squared error (RMSE), bias, standard deviation of errors (Std Error),
interquartile range error (IQR), and coefficient of variation
of errors. Completeness was assessed via the hit rate (HR)
relative to ground truth (number of calls over the calls of
the ground truth). To penalize tools with low call rates, HRadjusted metrics were computed, including weighted MAE,
weighted RMSE, and a combined score.
To estimate reliability and concordance between tools and
ground truth, Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, and CCC
have been used, respectively. To estimate parameter uncertainty, 95% confidence intervals were derived using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (2000 iterations). In addition,
Bland–Altman plots have been drawn for visual evaluation.
All these metrics have been computed using Python 3.6.13.
All the listed metrics are mathematically defined in the Supplementary Material.

Results
A summary of nanopore sequencing quality by comparing
basecalling models, reference genomes, coverage, enrichment,
and motif detection is reported in Fig. 1. Samples were basecalled using both hac (version 5.0.0) and sup (version 5.0.0)
Dorado models. These two models differ significantly in terms
of time to return the basecalled reads (sup model takes at
least 2–3 additional hours with respect to hac model) and
of quality of basecalled reads. Distributions of the computed
metrics for hac and sup models are shown in Fig. 1A and
listed in Supplementary Table S3. Basecalling with super accurate Dorado model clearly reduced the total amount of error (Wilcoxon test, P <.05 for each metric). Mean values and
95% confidence intervals of NM, MAPQ, and difference
in number of clipped bases are −6.305 [−6.322, −6.289],
0.626 [0.623, 0.629], and −58.42 [−58.53, −58.31], respectively, confirming that sup model is more reliable and stable.
Similarly, mapping reads to T2T reference resulted in a general
decreasing of mismatch, insertion, deletion, and homopolymer
error rates (P <.05 for all metrics, Wilcoxon test). Violin plots
are shown in Fig. 1B (see also Supplementary Table S4).
An example of a DM1 case comparing hac and sup model is
shown in Supplementary Fig. S1. The IGV display shows more
point mutations in the hac model (bottom), which is due to the
lower accuracy with respect to the sup model (top). Moreover,
the sizes of STRs are slightly different (hac model usually tends
to overestimate the inserted repeats).
The regions of interest had a median coverage of 10×, indicating that AS enrichment worked effectively. Distributions of
the coverage for each target region are shown in Fig. 1C (see
also Supplementary Table S5). Relatively low coverage was
associated with a lower quantity of DNA available for preparing the library (i.e <2 μg). The AS effectiveness resulted in an
ER of 5.79× [5.12, 6.47] and in an FE of 5.24× [4.63, 5.85]
(mean and 95% confidence interval). The distribution of FE
according to each disease is shown in Fig. 1D, while ER distribution is reported in Supplementary Fig. S2 (values are listed
in Supplementary Table S6).

After super accurate basecalling, only CTC motif in 17
cases and CCG motif in two cases survived. Long PCR products were also inspected for interruptions, finding CTC interruptions in 15 cases, and confirming the CCG interruptions in
two individuals.

Discussion
The use of ONT sequencing coupled with AS is crucial in designing an advanced diagnostic tool for REDs. New genomic
regions associated with these diseases can be easily included
in the workflow, by simply adding the new coordinates to the
BED file used for the enrichment. It is essential to include the

Dorado sup model in the bioinformatic workflow to achieve
more robust, high-quality results (Fig. 1A), even though basecalling takes longer than with the hac model. In addition, the
use of AS is another crucial aspect of pipeline design, since
it enables consistent enrichment of the region of interest, as
confirmed by ER and FE. An FE >4× (and ER above 5×)
demonstrated the efficacy of AS. The relatively high internal
variability could be explained by the fact that some samples
underwent AS with a minor number of target regions, resulting in underestimated enrichment metrics. Moreover, the different amounts of starting DNA could have also affected the
AS enrichment efficacy. Exploiting T2T reference improved
the mapping quality of samples (see Fig. 1B). Moreover, since
it has been constructed using long read techniques, it would
allow to better estimate the expansion detection and sizes.
Currently, with our High-Performance Computing (HPC)
infrastructure, each sample required ∼10 h of computational
time to perform super accurate basecalling with base modifications (5mCG–5hmCG). However, it is important to notice
that the computational time is affected by the amount of starting DNA. A run with a mean coverage of 10–15× requires
about 10 h. Our HPC setup enables the concurrent processing of two samples in parallel. The GridION platform, which
is GPU enabled, can run an additional super accurate basecalling (in ∼20 h). The downstream integrative analysis of each
sample is then completed in ∼2 h. The possibility to use hac or
fast basecalling and selecting only part of downstream analysis (according to the need of the user) can significantly drop
the run time and computational overhead (especially selecting
fast basecalling, which however does not allow for base modification detection). Also running sup basecalling without base
modification would halve the total computational time.
Focusing on the DM1 cohort, all individuals were correctly
found to be expanded (detecting >50 CTG expansion), confirming the SB diagnosis and clinical data. Considering the
assigned genomic class, ONT correctly classified 28 subjects,
while six were misclassified. The agreement between SB and
ONT increases when considering the statistical metrics. In particular, the median of coverage ratio and distance to confidence interval, which estimates the overlapping of ONT and
SB, were optimal, proving the reliability of ONT in quantifying the repeat expansion size. The relatively high widths of

uncertainties estimates are due to the high skewness of the
distribution (majority of cases in agreement, a few that are
discordant).
The benefits of exploiting ONT sequencing for the characterization of expanded ALS samples for C9orf72 are shown in
Supplementary Fig. S5. The large GGGGCC hexanucleotide
expansion (up to 3084 and 1421 repeats, for case als_1 and
als_2, respectively) requires ultra long reads to be fully captured, since RP-PCR cannot completely characterize it. The
use of sup basecalling allowed to correctly characterize repeat
expansions in all investigated ALS cases, minimizing false repeat interruption calls. In this small cohort, no repeated expansions were found in the gene LRP12, which has been reported only in Japanese patients [45, 46]. We detected >30
expansion repeats in all cases except one revealing 26 repeats,
confirming data from RP-PCR. Since RP-PCR provided only
a lower limit for the expansion size, we did not compute any
agreement metrics between ONT and RP-PCR estimates.
The implementation of ONT LRS in the diagnostic process
for detecting STRs in neurological disorders represents a valuable tool for achieving accurate diagnosis more quickly and
efficiently [3]. For example, >40 known dominant SCA syndromes present with cerebellar ataxia with overlapping features, makes clinical differentiation almost impossible without genetic testing. Traditional approaches require sequential
testing of individual genes, which can take months and may
still miss rare variants. The ability to make an accurate differential diagnosis through a single laboratory test can facilitate
the early provision of genetic counselling with an accurate description of disease severity and prognosis. This could avoid
the slow, labor-intensive, and resource-intensive methods traditionally required for STR detection across multiple genes,
such as SB or RP-PCR. Early recognition of similar genetic
diseases will become particularly valuable for patient enrolment in clinical trials and with the emergence of new diseasemodifying treatments, where early administration is typically
associated with better outcomes.
The entire cohort of suspected SCA patients was composed
of 46 individuals, of which only 12 showed repeat expansions
in the known regions of interest (two in two loci). All these
cases were also evaluated for exome sequencing, finding mutations in 5 non expanded cases in SCN4A or CLCN1 genes.
The remaining 29 cases did not show any expansion in the list
of investigated loci using AS. This may depend on the fact that
not all the forms of SCA are characterized by an STRs, even
though symptoms are similar among different forms.
Long PCR validated results obtained with native ONT,
however, while the estimates for shorter expansions are very
accurate, it underestimated expansions larger than 800 repeats. This is expected, since PCR failed to amplify very
large reads especially with GC-rich regions. Moreover, long
PCR provides reads with expansions varying in size (see
Supplementary Fig. S3), since it generated a high number of
reads derived from many cells which may be affected by mosaicisms. For this reason, it is important to note that long PCR
can be adopted as a valid alternative to native ONT, providing an orthogonal method of assessing native ONT results
at limited additional cost. One limitation of this approach is
the generation of incomplete reads due to partial polymerization of the region of interest by polymerase enzyme during
the PCR process. However, these artefacts can be easily detected and excluded from the analysis. We considered only
reads that cover the repeats and the flanking regions including

primers. Correlation plots confirmed the agreement between
native and long PCR ONT estimates, highlighting the problem
of large expansions. Long PCR resulted to be very accurate
in detecting expansions for SCAs, reaching a CCC of 0.975
(see Fig. 3B). However, considering samples with CANVAS,
the agreement resulted to be very poor, probably due to the
length of expansions in RFC1 in GC-rich region.
In terms of identifying repeat expansions, IGV was used
to inspect the repeat patterns and validate results from other
tools. In our hands, LongTR resulted to be the most performant software with respect to Straglr, Sniffles, CuteSV,
NanoRepeat, STRdust, and STRkit. Nevertheless, none of
these tools provided a comprehensive description of the composition of the repeat patterns. Although IGV allowed direct
visualization of repeat composition in both native and longPCR datasets, this process required manual inspection and
interpretation, making it impractical for routine analyses or
large-scale studies. NanoExpansion was developed to specifically address this limitation by generating a compact representation of repeat patterns, while simultaneously extracting methylation information. Although LongTR had a lower
MAE in repeat size estimation, NanoExpansion demonstrated
superior overall performance when the HR was considered,
demonstrating greater robustness in scenarios resembling routine diagnostic sequencing (reduced coverage).
Across all evaluated software, some repeat expansions were
missed in individual patients. This might be due to technical
challenges, including partially aligned reads, incomplete reads
terminating within the expanded repeat tract, or sequencing
errors that complicate repeat boundary identification, which
can alter the performance of the variant detection tools. NanoExpansion consistently reconstruct the repeat patterns in a
larger portion of samples, outperforming all the other evaluated tools (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. S6), additionally
providing information on interruption motifs and methylation patterns. Moreover, the algorithm is relatively simple and
operates on a restricted subset of reads spanning the locus
of interest, avoiding computationally expensive analyses. The
analysis of a single sample can be completed in <1 min on a
standard desktop computer, making NanoExpansion suitable
for both research applications and routine laboratory workflows.
As shown in Fig. 2, the CTG repeat size is variable in cells
belonging to the same specimen. This phenomenon is called
mosaicism and is known to characterize several REDs [44].
CTG instability in DM1 patients can be present in both somatic and germline cells and can change over time [44]. The
mosaicism condition is known to be associated with patient
prognosis. A decrease in the somatic mosaicism is often associated with a less severe clinical phenotype [12], confirming the importance of characterizing repeat expansion patterns. Mosaicism forms, when found in native DNA, were also
confirmed in long-PCR data analysis. In addition, given the
high stability of expansion estimates for patients with SCA,
HD, and Kennedy disease (see Table 2), it is highly likely that
the variability observed in some patients of the DM1 cohort
(Supplementary Table S7) raised from mosaicism, rather than
artefactual errors.
The inspection of interruption insertions is another crucial
aspect of this diagnostic pipeline. It is known that CTG expansions in DMPK gene can be characterized by the presence of alternate motifs. The effects of these interruption patterns are not yet fully understood. For instance, Swinkels H

et al. [47] reported that intermediate repeats of size 37–43
with CCGCTG interruptions are not prone to further expansion, and therefore they do not act as pre-mutations. An accurate characterization of them is crucial for prognostic purposes. Since ONT is prone to sequencing errors, we observed
how an interruption motif changed according to the basecalling model. In particular, the TTG motif, the most frequently inserted interruption, always disappeared after rebasecalling with the sup model. CCG appeared to be more
accurate as it was consistently identified by both basecalling
models. Moreover, the presence of CCG motif in two individuals (dm_6 and dm_10) is observed also using long PCR,
confirming what was found with native nanopore sequencing.
When a CTC interruption is detected, other expanded reads
from the same samples showed only noninterrupted CTG motifs (Supplementary Table S7). This fact could indicate that
these CTC interruptions could be mosaicisms due to the high
coverage depth potential to detect variants, or alternatively
possible artefacts, due to the inherent inaccuracies of the sequencing techniques. The fact that the interruption pattern
was only detected in DM1-expanded cases and not in the
other loci investigated (with one exception for one C9orf72
expanded case), suggests the high accuracy of nanopore sequencing in limiting the generation of artefactual results.
Some limitations need consideration for the present study.
First, the patient cohort is relatively small, since REDs are rare
diseases. However, due to the continuous patient enrolling at
our center, the size of the cohort is expected to increase. Indeed, this diagnostic workflow should be further validated on
a larger dataset, and we are currently planning a multicentre
study to test its robustness and scalability. Furthermore, the
use of high throughput PromethION platform (ONT) will increase the coverage depth, related accuracy and precision.
In summary, the diagnostic pipeline based on both native
DNA and long PCR sequencing allows to correctly detect
and characterize STRs. Although NanoExpansion proved to
be a valuable component of the analysis pipeline, the current
implementation still has some limitations, which will be addressed in further development. First, its performance should
be validated on additional datasets, possibly generated in different experimental conditions, to assess the robustness and
generalizability of the algorithm. This step is crucial before integrating NanoExpansion into routine clinical bioinformatic
workflows. Additional developments also include improved
handling of highly fragmented reads, and a more efficient automatic motif detection module, to enable the reveal of previously unreported interruption patterns. Despite these limitations, NanoExpansion provides a comprehensive framework
for the analysis and characterization of pathogenic repeat expansions and represents a promising foundation for future
methodological developments.
Finally, the patients belonging to this research cohort were
undergoing clinical examinations, magnetic resonance imaging, and neuropsychological evaluation. This is a crucial aspect, since collecting these different sources of information
would allow to correlate them with the genomic data. Integrating multi-modal data and exploiting statistical methods
and machine learning algorithms would help to shed light on
the genotype–phenotype correlation, which remains an open
question with regard to these REDs.
This study considered a relatively large cohort of repeat expansion patients, which proved the robustness of the proposed
diagnostic pipeline. This could be further strengthened by ap-

11

plying the pipeline to other STR datasets. The pipeline could
potentially become standard practice for diagnosing patients
at the IRCCS Istituto delle Scienze Neurologiche di Bologna
and other healthcare institutions.

The researchers analyzed native DNA and long-PCR products from 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2), C9orf72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and various spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs), alongside healthy controls. Abstract
Expansion repeat disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). We evaluated targeted long-read nanopore
sequencing for comprehensive characterization of STR expansions in 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1,
n = 51) and DM2 (n = 3) already characterized by Southern blot, C9orf72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS n = 11) evaluated by
repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RP-PCR; validation group), suspected spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA, n = 46), cerebellar ataxia with
neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS; n = 13), Huntington’s disease (1), Kennedy disease (1), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, 2), and
4 healthy controls (test group). Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling (AS) on Oxford Nanopore GridION or PromethION-2Solo
platforms. Long-PCR sequencing was performed for comparison. We also developed NanoExpansion, a Python-based tool for sizing expanded
alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. We correctly characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, and Kennedy disease
cases, and identified eight SCA27B, two SCA37, three SCA31, one SCA3, and nine CANVAS cases. Compared with the AS approach, longPCR underestimated alleles exceeding 800 repeats. Repeat interruptions were detected in 27/51 (52.9%) DM1 cases and 1/10 (10%) ALS, but
not in CANVAS, FRDA, Huntington’s disease, Kennedy disease, or SCA cases. This integrated sequencing analysis pipeline provides accurate,
comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders and has the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

Introduction
Short tandem repeats (STRs), also known as microsatellites,
are repeating tracts of DNA, usually 2–12 bp long, that can
be found in both coding and noncoding regions of the genome
[1]. They are characterized by high length polymorphism and
instability which results in >50 different diseases [2], that
are called repeat expansion disorders (REDs) [3], as listed in
STRchive (https://strchive.org) [4].
Among those, myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is the
most common muscular dystrophy in adults, with an estimated prevalence of about 1/8000 worldwide [5]. It is an autosomal dominant disorder and can involve multiple organs
and systems [6]. DM1 is caused by the expansion of the unstable CTG trinucleotide repeat in the 3 untranslated region
of the DMPK gene, located on chromosome 19q13.32 [7].
The size of the expansion can greatly vary with healthy people showing a range between 5 and 35 CTG repeats. Patients

with a CTG expansion from 36 and 49 are asymptomatic,
and do not meet diagnostic criteria for DM1. However, these
alleles are unstable during transmission, particularly through
meiosis, and can expand into the pathogenic range in the next
generation (premutation or mutable normal alleles). Affected
patients have a CTG expansion >50. Expansion size is associated with age of onset and severity: mild late-onset, classic and congenital DM1 are associated with expansions ≤150
CTGs (E1), ≤1000 CTGs (E2), and ≥1000 CTGs (E3), respectively [8]. Clinical features in DM1 patients vary according
to severity group. Most common symptoms are distal muscle weakness and myotonia [7]. However, the high individual
variability in DM1 patients of the same subtype makes the
genotype–phenotype correlation not completely understood.
The great instability of CTG expansion in both somatic and
germline cells, which persists during patient’s lifetime, is called
somatic mosaicism phenomenon [9]. Another crucial aspect

that makes the genotype–phenotype correlation more complex is the presence of interruptions within the CTG expansion. Several variant expansions, such as CCG, CGG, CTC,
TTG, GGC, CAG, have been observed, especially at the 3 and
5 ends of the DMPK gene [10, 11]. These interruption motifs
have a stabilizing effect of the expansion on germline transmission. However, the great heterogeneity in terms of motif,
length and location of the interruption patterns along the CTG
expansion leads to a huge phenotypic variability, which deserves to be further investigated [12].
Other REDs are spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs), which are
a heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative autosomal dominant diseases (prevalence of about 3/100 000 [13, 14]. Despite
their complex genotype–phenotype spectrum, common clinical features among SCAs are progressive cerebellar ataxia,
with oculomotor abnormalities, visual problems, pyramidal
and extrapyramidal signs, dysarthria and cognitive dysfunction [13, 15].
Cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia
syndrome (CANVAS) has recently been included among the
REDs [16]. It is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative
balance disorder, caused by biallelic repeat expansion mutations in the RFC1 gene, characterized by the peculiar clinical phenotype including cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy), bilateral vestibular hypofunction, and
chronic cough. Huntington’s disease and Kennedy disease are
two other well-known REDs.
The current diagnosis of REDs is mainly based on two wellknown and standardized techniques: Southern blot (SB) assay and triplet-repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RPPCR), often coupled. SB is considered the gold-standard, but it
is labor-intensive and time-consuming, it requires large quantities (≥10 μg) of high-quality DNA to produce valuable results [17], it is inaccurate in repeat expansion estimates, and
suffers from low resolution and sensitivity in detecting short
expansions. SB also lacks in providing a sequence context on
the evaluated STRs [18].
RP-PCR is relatively inexpensive, easy to implement and
more efficient in detecting short expansions with respect to
SB. However, it cannot reveal long repeated regions and mosaicisms. Furthermore, it cannot determine the size of the expansion and is prone to errors due to amplification artifacts
[19]. The high concentration of GC in some repeat and interruption motifs causes the allelic drop out polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) bias, leading to further sequencing errors.
The recent third generation long-read sequencing (LRS)
technologies, such as Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT,
Oxford Science Park, UK) or PacBio (Menlo Park, CA), allow
to obtain long DNA fragments and to accurately characterize the size of expansions, mosaicisms and interruption patterns [20–22]. Long reads enable robust structural variation
and tandem repeats detection. In addition, nanopore sequencing provides an in-silico target sequencing technique, named
adaptive sampling (AS) [23]. During a sequencing experiment,
if the basecalled sequence does not fall within the region of
interest provided to the machine beforehand, the sequencing
process stops and the DNA fragment is ejected from the pore.
A new fragment then begins to be sequenced. This application avoids using PCR for target sequencing, that can introduce artefacts, biases and may generate false negative results
[23–25].
Several computational tools, including Straglr [26],
LongTR [27], STRdust [28], and STRkit [29], have been

developed to estimate repeat lengths and genotype expanded
alleles from LRS data. Although these tools provide reliable
repeat sizing and, in some cases, allele phasing or motif annotation, their primary objective remains repeat genotyping.
However, the repeat pattern architecture of expanded regions,
such as motif interruptions, internal sequence organization,
and DNA methylation, can significantly influence disease
characterization and clinical severity. Therefore, to address
the need of a more comprehensive analysis of repeated regions, we developed NanoExpansion, a prototype software
designed to reconstruct and characterize the complete architecture of expanded alleles from long read sequencing
data.
In addition to repeat sizing, NanoExpansion identifies motif interruptions, performs allele clustering, and extracts locusspecific DNA methylation profiles directly from the sequencing reads, providing an integrated genetic and epigenetic characterization of repeat expansion loci. Moreover, NanoExpansion also provide a complete and detailed report to guide
and support medical doctors in the diagnosis of patients with
REDs. This comprehensive framework enables a more detailed investigation of genotype–phenotype relationships than
currently available repeat genotyping software.
This study aimed to demonstrate the potential diagnostic
power of nanopore sequencing by characterizing repeat expansion regions in two cohorts. The first cohort comprised patients with DM1, DM2, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
carrying a C9orf72 expansion for whom a genetic diagnosis
had already been made. The second cohort comprised subjects with suspected SCA, CANVAS, HD, or Kennedy disease.
A comprehensive bioinformatics pipeline has been developed.
The present work would reinforce the findings of previous research studies using the latest human genome reference (hs1),
which was provided by the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium [23, 24, 30, 31].

Materials and methods
Patient consent
The study has been approved by the AUSL Bologna Ethical Committee (BITRO N◦ 599–2022-SPER-AUSLBO). This
study was conducted in agreement with either the most updated Declaration of Helsinki and all the international and
local laws applied to clinical studies and patient protection.

Study setting and data collection
The dataset included 132 participants enrolled at the IRCCS
Istituto delle Scienze Neurologiche di Bologna, Bellaria Hospital, Italy. The cohort included 51 individuals with genetically
confirmed diagnoses of DM1, three DM2, 11 ALS cases, of
which 10 already identified for expansion in C9orf72 with RPPCR (validation group). Additionally, the cohort comprises
patients with clinical diagnoses (suspected cases, test group)
of SCA (46), CANVAS (13), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, two),
Huntington’s disease (HD, one), and Kennedy disorder (one).
Four healthy controls (mean age: 71) were also included.

DNA purification
DNA was purified from whole blood samples, using the
Maxwell® 16 Blood DNA Purification Kit (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA). DNA concentration was measured using
Quantus Fluorometer (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA).

NanoExpansion enables accurate characterization of repeat expansion disorders

Library preparation for ONT platform
Two different types of libraries were processed: one from
native DNA and one for long PCR product. For native
DNA, the Ligation Sequencing Kit V14 (SQK-LSK114, Oxford Nanopore, Oxford Science Park, UK) was used starting with 2 μg of total DNA following the protocol of the
provider. In brief, DNA was incubated with DNA-repair and
end-repair enzymes in thermal cycler at 20◦ C for 10 min and
65◦ C for 5 min. It followed AMPure XP bead purification
(Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) and 20 min incubation
with Quick T4 DNA Ligase (NEB, Ipswich, MA) and the
Ligation Adapter. After AMPure XP purification with Long
Fragment Buffer (LFB), the concentration was measured by
Quantus™ Fluorometer (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA),
Fragment Analyzer 5200 (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA) and NEB
Bio Calculator (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA) or
Promega Biocalculator (Promega, Madison, WI 53711 USA).
Then, 200–800 ng of DNA were loaded onto the R10.4.1 flow
cell (FLO-MIN114) using the ONT GridION platform (ONT,
Oxford UK). Twenty-one cases were loaded onto PromethION 2 Solo (ONT, Oxford UK) to increase the coverage
depth. To reduce the costs, the P2Solo setup was optimized by
reusing the same flow cell with a running time of 16 h. After DNase treatment, libraries were loaded with no barcoding
step to maximise the coverage depth.
For long PCR product, the Native Barcoding Kit 24 V14
(SQK- NBD114.24) was used including 24 different samples.
Primers used for all loci and PCR conditions are described in
Supplementary File 1. In brief, 400 ng of purified amplicon
pools were treated with NEBNext FFPE DNA repair and Ultra II End-Prep enzyme mix (NEB, Ipswich, MA), at 20◦ C and
at 65◦ C for 10 min each, purified with AMPure XP beads and
barcoded with NEB Blunt/TA Ligase Master Mix (NEB, Ipswich, MA), for 20 min at room temperature. After pooling
and repurification with AMPure XP beads, DNA was ligated
with Native Adapter (NA) using Quick T4 DNA ligase (NEB,
Ipswich, MA) for 20 min at room temperature. After the final bead purification using LFB to enrich DNA >3 kb, the library was evaluated with Quantus™ Fluorometer (Promega,
Madison, WI 53711 USA). Depending on the fragment size,
200–800 ng of DNA were loaded onto washed and reused
R10.4.1 flow cell (FLO-MIN114) coming from AS experiments using the ONT GridION platform (ONT, Oxford UK).

Native nanopore sequencing downstream analysis
During nanopore sequencing, the MinKnow software (version 6.2.14, ONT) stored the raw current signal into POD5
files. Real-time basecalling was set up to HAC algorithm
to avoid overloading the GridION computing unit. MinKnow also performed AS enriching for 37 loci of interests
(see Supplementary Tables S1 and S2). Those loci involved
classical expansion repeat regions, as well as a list of 13
genes in which (CAG)>5 polyQ repeats were detected using
blat tool (https://genome.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgBlat) in the human genome. The latter have not yet been associated with
any disease. Each sequencing run usually lasted 16–24 h.
New MinION flow cells were used for native DNA processing, while used and washed flow cells were used for long
amplicons. After sequencing, the raw signal was transferred
to a high-performance computing station (equipped with a
single AMD EPYC 9654 processor (96 cores, 192 threads,
base clock 1.5 GHz, boost up to 3.7 GHz) and two NVIDIA

3

L40 GPUs (45 GiB memory each, CUDA 12.2); the system
ran Debian GNU/Linux 6.1.0–29-amd64) and basecalled with
Dorado, version 1.3.0, models v5.2.0. Samples were basecalled with both high accurate (hac, a part of them) and super accurate (sup) Dorado models. The q score filter was set
to 10. The basecalled sequences were aligned to the reference genome (GRCh38 and T2T CHM13v2/hs1) using minimap2 (version 2.26) [32]. All native samples were aligned
to the GRCh38 reference (hg38), and seven subjects with
DM1 were also mapped to hs1 (T2T). Samples sequenced
with long PCR were aligned to T2T CHM13v2/hs1. Aligned
reads were stored in BAM files and indexed. The aligned
data were visually inspected with IGV [33]. Single nucleotide
variants were called using Clair3 (version 1.0.10) [34]. SNP
information was used to perform haplotyping with Whatshap (version 2.4) [35]. Structural variants were called with
Sniffles (version 2.2) [36], CuteSV (version 2.1.0) [37, 38],
while STRs were detected using several tools, such as Sniffles (version 2.2), CuteSV(version 2.1.0), Nanorepeat [39],
Straglr (version 1.4.1)(26), STRdust (version 0.20.0) [28],
STRkit (version 0.24.2) [29], and LongTR (version 638942f)
[27]. The VCF output files were annotated with Stranger (version 0.9.5, doi:10.5281/zenodo.4548873). Finally, NanoExpansion, which is a prototype software developed within our
research group, was used to characterize repeat expansion patterns, detecting the main motifs and the interruptions. The
whole pipeline was integrated into a Snakemake [40] workflow.

NanoExpansion
NanoExpansion is a Python-based software package designed
to reconstruct the internal architecture of pathogenic repeat
expansions from LRS data. By providing an aligned BAMfile and the genomic coordinates of a target repeat locus, the
software extracts spanning reads and iteratively identifies repeat and interruption motifs within each expanded allele. Unlike repeat genotyping tools that primarily estimate repeat expansion size, NanoExpansion reconstructs the sequential pattern of repeat blocks, filtering spurious nucleotides, and generated a compact representation of the expanded allele [e.g.
(CTG)n(CCG)m(CTG)k]. In addition, NanoExpansion computes allele-specific summary statistics, extracts DNA methylation profiles across the target locus, and produces a detailed
report to support medical doctors in the diagnostic decision
process. Users provide genomic coordinates of the target locus, together with canonical repeat motif and a group of interruption motifs to be investigated (if not specified, NanoExpansion can also automatically detect interruption motifs), allowing the tool to characterize a broad range of REDs. Additional
filtering parameters could be provided by the user. NanoExpansion is designed to work with hg38 and T2T genome references. The software has been benchmarked on a set of artificially expanded reads (see Supplementary Material) to prove
its accuracy in detecting expansion patterns.

Library preparation for short read exome
sequencing
To rule out possible false calls coming from ONT, we performed a separate test on five samples already evaluated with
exome sequencing using NovaSEQ6000 for all loci listed in
Supplementary Table S1. The sample library for exome sequencing was prepared using xGen™ DNA EZ Library Prep

Statistical analysis
The comparison between using Dorado hac and sup models
have been assessed by computing the following metrics: mismatch, insertion, deletion, and homopolymer error rate (homopolymers ≥ 4 bp, that is known to be an ONT-specific
bias). Statistically significant differences have been verified
using the Wilcoxon test (α = 0.05, one-tailed). Agreement
at read level (i.e. comparing both BAM files) was assessed
by computing mean and 95% confidence interval of the difference inedit distance (NM, global measure of error per
read), mapping quality (MAPQ, which measures mapping
efficiency), and in the number of clipped bases, that indicates
partial or problematic alignments. Same statistical procedure
has been used for comparing alignment to hg38 and T2T/hs1
reference genome.
Effectiveness of AS was measured by computing enrichment
ratio (ER) and fold-enrichment (FE, using a control samples,
sequenced both with and without AS); mean ER and FE have
been provided, together with 95% confidence interval (ER ≥
5×, FE ≥ 4× can be considered good efficacy). All these metrics have been computed using Python 3.6.13 (Pysam 0.21.0
and Pybedtools 0.9.0 packages).
The agreement between native ONT and SB has been measured considering that SB only provided intervals of expansion size. First, considering only genomic classification (E1,
E2, and E3), ordinal metrics such as quadratic weighted Cohen’s Kappa (κw ), ordinal accuracy, and mean absolute error
(MAE) have been used. These metrics evaluate ordinal classification, considering that a misclassification E1–E2 or E2–E3,
is less severe than E1–E3. Genomic classes have been assigned
to native nanopore sequencing according to the mean of the
distribution of repeat sizes. In addition, metrics evaluating the
overlapping between nanopore and SB results have been used:
coverage rate of native ONT within the SB intervals, distance
of the median of native ONT from SB intervals, and probabilistic overlap between a uniform distribution defined by SB
intervals and a kernel density estimate of native ONT.
Native and long PCR ONT were compared by drawing
scatter plots, fitting a linear model (R2 is reported), and computing both the Pearson correlation coefficient (ρ) and the
Lin’s Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC, that measures the degree to which observations are close to the 45◦
line) by disease. Native ONT results have been obtained from
IGV, while for long PCR, most frequent reads covering both

repeated loci and flanking regions were considered. Comparison between long PCR and native ONT has been conducted
using R 4.3.1.
Metrics used to compare the different variant caller software tools against the IGV ground truth spanned accuracy,
completeness, and agreement measures. Accuracy and error
dispersion were quantified using MAE, root mean squared error (RMSE), bias, standard deviation of errors (Std Error),
interquartile range error (IQR), and coefficient of variation
of errors. Completeness was assessed via the hit rate (HR)
relative to ground truth (number of calls over the calls of
the ground truth). To penalize tools with low call rates, HRadjusted metrics were computed, including weighted MAE,
weighted RMSE, and a combined score.
To estimate reliability and concordance between tools and
ground truth, Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, and CCC
have been used, respectively. To estimate parameter uncertainty, 95% confidence intervals were derived using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (2000 iterations). In addition,
Bland–Altman plots have been drawn for visual evaluation.
All these metrics have been computed using Python 3.6.13.
All the listed metrics are mathematically defined in the Supplementary Material.

Results
A summary of nanopore sequencing quality by comparing
basecalling models, reference genomes, coverage, enrichment,
and motif detection is reported in Fig. 1. Samples were basecalled using both hac (version 5.0.0) and sup (version 5.0.0)
Dorado models. These two models differ significantly in terms
of time to return the basecalled reads (sup model takes at
least 2–3 additional hours with respect to hac model) and
of quality of basecalled reads. Distributions of the computed
metrics for hac and sup models are shown in Fig. 1A and
listed in Supplementary Table S3. Basecalling with super accurate Dorado model clearly reduced the total amount of error (Wilcoxon test, P <.05 for each metric). Mean values and
95% confidence intervals of NM, MAPQ, and difference
in number of clipped bases are −6.305 [−6.322, −6.289],
0.626 [0.623, 0.629], and −58.42 [−58.53, −58.31], respectively, confirming that sup model is more reliable and stable.
Similarly, mapping reads to T2T reference resulted in a general
decreasing of mismatch, insertion, deletion, and homopolymer
error rates (P <.05 for all metrics, Wilcoxon test). Violin plots
are shown in Fig. 1B (see also Supplementary Table S4).
An example of a DM1 case comparing hac and sup model is
shown in Supplementary Fig. S1. The IGV display shows more
point mutations in the hac model (bottom), which is due to the
lower accuracy with respect to the sup model (top). Moreover,
the sizes of STRs are slightly different (hac model usually tends
to overestimate the inserted repeats).
The regions of interest had a median coverage of 10×, indicating that AS enrichment worked effectively. Distributions of
the coverage for each target region are shown in Fig. 1C (see
also Supplementary Table S5). Relatively low coverage was
associated with a lower quantity of DNA available for preparing the library (i.e <2 μg). The AS effectiveness resulted in an
ER of 5.79× [5.12, 6.47] and in an FE of 5.24× [4.63, 5.85]
(mean and 95% confidence interval). The distribution of FE
according to each disease is shown in Fig. 1D, while ER distribution is reported in Supplementary Fig. S2 (values are listed
in Supplementary Table S6).

A total of 12 out of 46 cases suspected for SCA were detected with at least one STR out of the normal range by native ONT. They showed a median age at disease onset of 64
years (IQR 41–64.9). Cases sc_2 and sc_12 showed unexpectedly an insertion of 120 and 363 ATTCC repeats respectively
in DAB1 (SCA37), since the previously described pathogenic
motif was ATTTC. This repeat motif was confirmed by both
algorithms (HAC and SUP), and also from long PCR sequencing data. Sample sc_4 had 69 CAG repeats in ATXN3 (SCA3).
A very rare expansion in Caucasian population for BEAN1
(SCA31) was found in case sc_3 with 431 TGGAA repeats;
this case was tested three times both using native and long
PCR due to the rarity of this disease in the European population [43] to check possible artefactual results. Case sc_9

showed an expansion in BEAN1 with 143–161 repeats with
mixed TAAAA/TGGAA motifs as well.

with pathogenic expansion: BEAN1(SCA31) and FGF14

sc_7_cnv_1) was also found to have both alleles of RFC1 out

for being incorporated in the LRS based diagnostic pipeline.
Supplementary Tables S9–S12 report all the estimated size obtained through the different variant callers, for DM1 (hg38
and T2T), ALS, and test group, respectively. A graphical comparison between results from different tools and IGV (taken as
ground truth) are shown in Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. S6.
From both Bland–Altman plots (Supplementary Fig. S6A–H)
and violin plots (Fig. 4), Straglr and NanoExpansion (where
available) consistently outperformed the other software tools.
All the computed metrics shown in Supplementary Table S13
confirmed this result. Benchmarking of NanoExpansion is detailed in Supplementary material.
Supplementary Table S14 summarize the comparison between the number of repeats recognized by short read
sequencing (exome sequencing with NovaSEQ6000) and
ONT. A perfect agreement between the two approaches was
achieved for wild type alleles, when short read sequencing was
able to characterize expansion numbers covering the whole locus with repeat motifs. However, when the number of repeats
exceeded 150 bp, NovaSEQ6000 gave no informative data
due to short sequencing reads. Expansion size estimates were
done through visual inspection using IGV, consistently with
the approach used for long reads. Underestimated expansion
size or inferior limits were obtained.

Discussion
The use of ONT sequencing coupled with AS is crucial in designing an advanced diagnostic tool for REDs. New genomic
regions associated with these diseases can be easily included
in the workflow, by simply adding the new coordinates to the
BED file used for the enrichment. It is essential to include the

Dorado sup model in the bioinformatic workflow to achieve
more robust, high-quality results (Fig. 1A), even though basecalling takes longer than with the hac model. In addition, the
use of AS is another crucial aspect of pipeline design, since
it enables consistent enrichment of the region of interest, as
confirmed by ER and FE. An FE >4× (and ER above 5×)
demonstrated the efficacy of AS. The relatively high internal
variability could be explained by the fact that some samples
underwent AS with a minor number of target regions, resulting in underestimated enrichment metrics. Moreover, the different amounts of starting DNA could have also affected the
AS enrichment efficacy. Exploiting T2T reference improved
the mapping quality of samples (see Fig. 1B). Moreover, since
it has been constructed using long read techniques, it would
allow to better estimate the expansion detection and sizes.
Currently, with our High-Performance Computing (HPC)
infrastructure, each sample required ∼10 h of computational
time to perform super accurate basecalling with base modifications (5mCG–5hmCG). However, it is important to notice
that the computational time is affected by the amount of starting DNA. A run with a mean coverage of 10–15× requires
about 10 h. Our HPC setup enables the concurrent processing of two samples in parallel. The GridION platform, which
is GPU enabled, can run an additional super accurate basecalling (in ∼20 h). The downstream integrative analysis of each
sample is then completed in ∼2 h. The possibility to use hac or
fast basecalling and selecting only part of downstream analysis (according to the need of the user) can significantly drop
the run time and computational overhead (especially selecting
fast basecalling, which however does not allow for base modification detection). Also running sup basecalling without base
modification would halve the total computational time.
Focusing on the DM1 cohort, all individuals were correctly
found to be expanded (detecting >50 CTG expansion), confirming the SB diagnosis and clinical data. Considering the
assigned genomic class, ONT correctly classified 28 subjects,
while six were misclassified. The agreement between SB and
ONT increases when considering the statistical metrics. In particular, the median of coverage ratio and distance to confidence interval, which estimates the overlapping of ONT and
SB, were optimal, proving the reliability of ONT in quantifying the repeat expansion size. The relatively high widths of

Morandi et al.

uncertainties estimates are due to the high skewness of the
distribution (majority of cases in agreement, a few that are
discordant).
The benefits of exploiting ONT sequencing for the characterization of expanded ALS samples for C9orf72 are shown in
Supplementary Fig. S5. The large GGGGCC hexanucleotide
expansion (up to 3084 and 1421 repeats, for case als_1 and
als_2, respectively) requires ultra long reads to be fully captured, since RP-PCR cannot completely characterize it. The
use of sup basecalling allowed to correctly characterize repeat
expansions in all investigated ALS cases, minimizing false repeat interruption calls. In this small cohort, no repeated expansions were found in the gene LRP12, which has been reported only in Japanese patients [45, 46]. We detected >30
expansion repeats in all cases except one revealing 26 repeats,
confirming data from RP-PCR. Since RP-PCR provided only
a lower limit for the expansion size, we did not compute any
agreement metrics between ONT and RP-PCR estimates.
The implementation of ONT LRS in the diagnostic process
for detecting STRs in neurological disorders represents a valuable tool for achieving accurate diagnosis more quickly and
efficiently [3]. For example, >40 known dominant SCA syndromes present with cerebellar ataxia with overlapping features, makes clinical differentiation almost impossible without genetic testing. Traditional approaches require sequential
testing of individual genes, which can take months and may
still miss rare variants. The ability to make an accurate differential diagnosis through a single laboratory test can facilitate
the early provision of genetic counselling with an accurate description of disease severity and prognosis. This could avoid
the slow, labor-intensive, and resource-intensive methods traditionally required for STR detection across multiple genes,
such as SB or RP-PCR. Early recognition of similar genetic
diseases will become particularly valuable for patient enrolment in clinical trials and with the emergence of new diseasemodifying treatments, where early administration is typically
associated with better outcomes.
The entire cohort of suspected SCA patients was composed
of 46 individuals, of which only 12 showed repeat expansions
in the known regions of interest (two in two loci). All these
cases were also evaluated for exome sequencing, finding mutations in 5 non expanded cases in SCN4A or CLCN1 genes.
The remaining 29 cases did not show any expansion in the list
of investigated loci using AS. This may depend on the fact that
not all the forms of SCA are characterized by an STRs, even
though symptoms are similar among different forms.
Long PCR validated results obtained with native ONT,
however, while the estimates for shorter expansions are very
accurate, it underestimated expansions larger than 800 repeats. This is expected, since PCR failed to amplify very
large reads especially with GC-rich regions. Moreover, long
PCR provides reads with expansions varying in size (see
Supplementary Fig. S3), since it generated a high number of
reads derived from many cells which may be affected by mosaicisms. For this reason, it is important to note that long PCR
can be adopted as a valid alternative to native ONT, providing an orthogonal method of assessing native ONT results
at limited additional cost. One limitation of this approach is
the generation of incomplete reads due to partial polymerization of the region of interest by polymerase enzyme during
the PCR process. However, these artefacts can be easily detected and excluded from the analysis. We considered only
reads that cover the repeats and the flanking regions including

primers. Correlation plots confirmed the agreement between
native and long PCR ONT estimates, highlighting the problem
of large expansions. Long PCR resulted to be very accurate
in detecting expansions for SCAs, reaching a CCC of 0.975
(see Fig. 3B). However, considering samples with CANVAS,
the agreement resulted to be very poor, probably due to the
length of expansions in RFC1 in GC-rich region.
In terms of identifying repeat expansions, IGV was used
to inspect the repeat patterns and validate results from other
tools. In our hands, LongTR resulted to be the most performant software with respect to Straglr, Sniffles, CuteSV,
NanoRepeat, STRdust, and STRkit. Nevertheless, none of
these tools provided a comprehensive description of the composition of the repeat patterns. Although IGV allowed direct
visualization of repeat composition in both native and longPCR datasets, this process required manual inspection and
interpretation, making it impractical for routine analyses or
large-scale studies. NanoExpansion was developed to specifically address this limitation by generating a compact representation of repeat patterns, while simultaneously extracting methylation information. Although LongTR had a lower
MAE in repeat size estimation, NanoExpansion demonstrated
superior overall performance when the HR was considered,
demonstrating greater robustness in scenarios resembling routine diagnostic sequencing (reduced coverage).
Across all evaluated software, some repeat expansions were
missed in individual patients. This might be due to technical
challenges, including partially aligned reads, incomplete reads
terminating within the expanded repeat tract, or sequencing
errors that complicate repeat boundary identification, which
can alter the performance of the variant detection tools. NanoExpansion consistently reconstruct the repeat patterns in a
larger portion of samples, outperforming all the other evaluated tools (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. S6), additionally
providing information on interruption motifs and methylation patterns. Moreover, the algorithm is relatively simple and
operates on a restricted subset of reads spanning the locus
of interest, avoiding computationally expensive analyses. The
analysis of a single sample can be completed in <1 min on a
standard desktop computer, making NanoExpansion suitable
for both research applications and routine laboratory workflows.
As shown in Fig. 2, the CTG repeat size is variable in cells
belonging to the same specimen. This phenomenon is called
mosaicism and is known to characterize several REDs [44].
CTG instability in DM1 patients can be present in both somatic and germline cells and can change over time [44]. The
mosaicism condition is known to be associated with patient
prognosis. A decrease in the somatic mosaicism is often associated with a less severe clinical phenotype [12], confirming the importance of characterizing repeat expansion patterns. Mosaicism forms, when found in native DNA, were also
confirmed in long-PCR data analysis. In addition, given the
high stability of expansion estimates for patients with SCA,
HD, and Kennedy disease (see Table 2), it is highly likely that
the variability observed in some patients of the DM1 cohort
(Supplementary Table S7) raised from mosaicism, rather than
artefactual errors.
The inspection of interruption insertions is another crucial
aspect of this diagnostic pipeline. It is known that CTG expansions in DMPK gene can be characterized by the presence of alternate motifs. The effects of these interruption patterns are not yet fully understood. For instance, Swinkels H

NanoExpansion enables accurate characterization of repeat expansion disorders

et al. [47] reported that intermediate repeats of size 37–43
with CCGCTG interruptions are not prone to further expansion, and therefore they do not act as pre-mutations. An accurate characterization of them is crucial for prognostic purposes. Since ONT is prone to sequencing errors, we observed
how an interruption motif changed according to the basecalling model. In particular, the TTG motif, the most frequently inserted interruption, always disappeared after rebasecalling with the sup model. CCG appeared to be more
accurate as it was consistently identified by both basecalling
models. Moreover, the presence of CCG motif in two individuals (dm_6 and dm_10) is observed also using long PCR,
confirming what was found with native nanopore sequencing.
When a CTC interruption is detected, other expanded reads
from the same samples showed only noninterrupted CTG motifs (Supplementary Table S7). This fact could indicate that
these CTC interruptions could be mosaicisms due to the high
coverage depth potential to detect variants, or alternatively
possible artefacts, due to the inherent inaccuracies of the sequencing techniques. The fact that the interruption pattern
was only detected in DM1-expanded cases and not in the
other loci investigated (with one exception for one C9orf72
expanded case), suggests the high accuracy of nanopore sequencing in limiting the generation of artefactual results.
Some limitations need consideration for the present study.
First, the patient cohort is relatively small, since REDs are rare
diseases. However, due to the continuous patient enrolling at
our center, the size of the cohort is expected to increase. Indeed, this diagnostic workflow should be further validated on
a larger dataset, and we are currently planning a multicentre
study to test its robustness and scalability. Furthermore, the
use of high throughput PromethION platform (ONT) will increase the coverage depth, related accuracy and precision.
In summary, the diagnostic pipeline based on both native
DNA and long PCR sequencing allows to correctly detect
and characterize STRs. Although NanoExpansion proved to
be a valuable component of the analysis pipeline, the current
implementation still has some limitations, which will be addressed in further development. First, its performance should
be validated on additional datasets, possibly generated in different experimental conditions, to assess the robustness and
generalizability of the algorithm. This step is crucial before integrating NanoExpansion into routine clinical bioinformatic
workflows. Additional developments also include improved
handling of highly fragmented reads, and a more efficient automatic motif detection module, to enable the reveal of previously unreported interruption patterns. Despite these limitations, NanoExpansion provides a comprehensive framework
for the analysis and characterization of pathogenic repeat expansions and represents a promising foundation for future
methodological developments.
Finally, the patients belonging to this research cohort were
undergoing clinical examinations, magnetic resonance imaging, and neuropsychological evaluation. This is a crucial aspect, since collecting these different sources of information
would allow to correlate them with the genomic data. Integrating multi-modal data and exploiting statistical methods
and machine learning algorithms would help to shed light on
the genotype–phenotype correlation, which remains an open
question with regard to these REDs.
This study considered a relatively large cohort of repeat expansion patients, which proved the robustness of the proposed
diagnostic pipeline. This could be further strengthened by ap-

plying the pipeline to other STR datasets. The pipeline could
potentially become standard practice for diagnosing patients
at the IRCCS Istituto delle Scienze Neurologiche di Bologna
and other healthcare institutions.

The objective was to examine whether aversive well-being comparisons—such as social, temporal, counterfactual, and expectation-based comparisons—predicted higher psychopathology, including prolonged grief disorder (PGD), posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, somatic symptoms, and loneliness.
