contribute to the persistence of grief reactions and
associated symptoms.
5.2. Incremental contribution of aversive wellbeing comparisons
Our results revealed a nuanced role of comparative
thinking in mental health outcomes following
bereavement. This role remained evident even
when controlling for worry, rumination, avoidance,
and childhood adversity. Comparison frequency consistently emerged as an important predictor of distress across models, particularly in relation to
anxiety, depression, somatic symptoms, and loneliness both cross-sectionally and longitudinally.
These symptoms encompass cognitive and emotional
patterns and may, therefore, be influenced by the
repetitive and evaluative nature of comparison frequency. Comparison affective impact also emerged
as predictor in correlational analyses. In addition,
in regression models (Models 3 & 4) affective impact
at T2 was related to depression, anxiety, and somatic
symptoms at T2. Affective impact directly reflects the
psychological consequences of frequent comparisons
(Morina, 2021). Comparison affective impact may
have immediate and cumulative effects on mental
health, as it informs how individuals perceive their
current well-being and shapes subsequent emotional
and behavioural responses. Our findings are
especially significant because comparative thinking
accounted for unique variance to mental health outcomes beyond established risk factors such as worry,
rumination, avoidance, and childhood adversity
(McEvoy et al., 2013; McLaughlin et al., 2012; Morina, 2011). Importantly, associations remained significant when we accounted for autoregressive
effects. This underscores the important role of aversive well-being comparisons in shaping distress following bereavement.
5.3. Comparative thinking and rumination
In models with all predictors, comparison frequency
over the last three weeks as assessed at T1 did not
significantly predict grief reactions longitudinally,

11

whereas rumination emerged as the most important
factor across models. However, comparative frequency at T2 emerged as the only significant variable
when accounting for autoregressive effects. This may
be attributable to the time frame. The retrospective
window at T1 may not capture the cumulative
effects of comparative thinking over time, as the
bereavement process is still in its early stages, and
comparative thinking in the last three weeks may
not be predictive of grief symptoms six months
later. Rumination was assessed at a more trait-like,
habitual level and may, thus, have exerted longerterm effects. Yet, in the concurrent models at T2,
specific comparisons in the last three weeks may
become more representative of the individual’s cognitive processes. This was also reflected in findings
concerning comparison affective impact. The
finding that it was negatively associated with
depression, anxiety, and somatic symptoms only
concurrently at T2 suggests that the immediate affective impact of well-being comparisons may have a
more direct and short-term influence on mental
health than a lasting longitudinal effect that cumulates over six months (when regressed with more
trait like predictors). While rumination may also
amplify well-being comparisons or vice versa
(Schlechter & Morina, 2023), as evidenced by their
bidirectional associations, they remain distinct constructs with unique implications for grief. Brooding
rumination, sometimes referred to as ‘moody pondering’ (Treynor, 2003), involves passively focusing
on distress and its causes or consequences without
necessarily engaging in explicit comparative thinking (Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008). In the context
of grief symptoms, brooding rumination may manifest as repetitive cognitions about the loss, its causes,
or self-directed blame. In contrast, well-being comparisons involve evaluating (dis-)similarities
between one’s current well-being and a standard,
such as pre-loss functioning or the perceived wellbeing of others (Morina, 2021). While brooding
rumination may sometimes include comparative
elements (e.g. ‘Why am I struggling more than
others?’; Nolen-Hoeksema, 1991), well-being comparisons are explicitly focused on cognitive evaluations of potential well-being discrepancies.
Brooding rumination perpetuates negative affect by
focusing on the loss, self-blame, or unresolved questions, potentially exacerbating grief reactions and
related symptoms. In contrast, aversive well-being
comparisons may influence grief by accentuating
discrepancies between one’s current state and
desired states, which can amplify feelings of inadequacy and distress and negatively influence coping
efforts. Importantly, these processes might interact,
with aversive comparisons leading to negative
mood and rumination. Conversely, rumination

12

P. SCHLECHTER ET AL.

may intensify the emotional impact of aversive comparisons. To assess this interaction, ecological momentary assessment (EMA) is needed to evaluate the daily
occurrence of brooding rumination and well-being
comparisons, including their potential sequential
order. Additionally, experimental research is necessary
to further elucidate the mechanisms underlying their
influence on grief symptoms.
5.4. Comparative thinking in the context of
other predictors
Our findings indicate that comparative thinking is an
important factor to consider alongside the other predictors examined in this study. In line with prior
work, worry was consistently associated with outcome
variables, highlighting its role in maintaining anticipatory fears and catastrophic thoughts about one’s
capacity to recover from loss (McEvoy et al., 2013).
Rumination demonstrated even broader associations,
significantly predicting grief, PTSD, depression,
anxiety, somatic symptoms, and loneliness. This highlights how repetitive and uncontrollable focus on
unresolved loss can maintain and increase distress
(Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008). While avoidance
showed relatively limited effects compared to other
variables, its positive association with depression and
PTSD at specific time points underscores its role as a
maladaptive coping strategy (Eisma & Stroebe,
2017). In addition, avoidance was broadly assessed
as experiential avoidance and may thus not accurately
capture disorder-specific aspects of avoidance. Childhood adversity emerged as a significant predictor of
PTSD, depression, anxiety, and somatic symptoms
(McLaughlin et al., 2012). However, its influence
diminished or was much smaller in the autoregressive
models, suggesting that its effects may be partially
mediated by more proximal factors.
The absence of consistent effects of comparative
thinking on PTSD symptoms in the regression
models, despite significant bivariate associations,
suggests that its relationship with PTSD may be better
explained through shared variance with other psychological factors, such as rumination or worry. PTSD is
characterized by intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance
behaviour and hyperarousal, which may conceptually
be more strongly related with rumination and worry
(Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008). These constructs
may mediate or overshadow the influence of comparative thinking when considered simultaneously. Importantly, PTSD symptoms in the present study were not
directly related to the loss.
5.5. Serial mediation effects
Our longitudinal mediation models did not yield significant effects. However, cross-sectional models at

Time 2 showed nearly significant indirect effects for
depression, anxiety, and somatic symptoms. This
may correspond with our discussion above concerning
the timeframe of comparative thinking. Effects of
comparison frequency on depression, anxiety, and
somatic symptoms were mediated through comparison discrepancy and comparison affective impact.
These findings suggest that well-being comparisons
may have an indirect influence on mental health outcomes through their cognitive (i.e. assessment of the
comparison discrepancy) and emotional (i.e. the
immediate affective reaction) impact. This is consistent with previous studies on well-being comparison
that repeatedly found this mediation in the context
of various mental health symptoms (Morina &
Schlechter, 2023; Schlechter & Morina, 2023). However, the serial mediation effects were significant at
the α = .05 level and did not meet our preregistered
threshold of α = .01, indicating that these pathways
require further empirical validation, particularly
given that post-hoc power analysis suggested the
study was underpowered to detect these mediation
effects.
5.6. Theoretical contribution
Our study contributes to the theoretical understanding of how aversive well-being comparisons may influence mental health outcomes in the context of
bereavement. Our considerations were based on
gComp (Morina, 2021), which highlights how comparison selection, perceived discrepancies, and affective and behavioural impact shape outcome
variables. Specifically, aversive well-being comparisons not only represent cognitive appraisals of wellbeing but also elicit affective reactions that intensify
grief-related symptoms. The dual process model
emphasizes the need for individuals to balance two
complementary processes when grieving: (1) lossoriented coping, which focuses on the emotional
aspects of the loss, and (2) restoration-oriented coping, which deals with the adaptation to life without
the deceased (Stroebe & Schut, 1999). Aversive wellbeing comparisons may influence both of these coping
processes, and disrupt helpful oscillation as it mostly
reflects loss-oriented coping processes. When individuals frequently engage in aversive well-being comparisons, it might exacerbate the loss-oriented aspect of
grief, as they become preoccupied with what they
have lost, hindering their ability to reorient toward
life outside of bereavement. Negative comparison
affective impact may obstruct the process of restoration-oriented coping. From a cognitive behavioural
perspective (Boelen et al., 2006), frequent engagement
in aversive comparisons may evoke and maintain
depression, anxiety, and grief. Aversive well-being
comparisons may thus fuel maladaptive thinking

patterns and reinforce cognitive distortions that the
comparer’s well-being is permanently diminished.
5.7. Future research
Future research should further disentangle the role of
well-being comparison processes at multiple levels of
analysis, ranging from broader longitudinal trajectories to fine-grained within-person dynamics. In particular, micro-level approaches (e.g. ecological
momentary assessment) are needed to capture the
temporal sequencing and short-term fluctuations of
comparison frequency, discrepancy, and affective
impact in daily life (Schlechter et al., 2025, 2026).
Experimental and intervention studies are also
required to clarify causal mechanisms and determine
whether modifying maladaptive comparison processes
can reduce grief-related distress. Additionally, future
work should examine how well-being comparisons
operate alongside established transdiagnostic processes such as rumination, worry, and avoidance,
and whether they represent partially independent or
interacting mechanisms across different symptom
domains in bereaved individuals.
5.8. Potential clinical implications
Our findings suggest that aversive well-being comparisons contribute to distress in prolonged grief, underscoring their potential importance as a target for
therapeutic intervention. Integrating approaches to
reduce comparison frequency, reframe comparison
discrepancies, or improve coping with the emotional
effects of comparisons could enhance the efficacy of
existing treatments for PGD. This aligns well with cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) interventions, which
has been found effective in treating PGD (LaPlante
et al., 2024) by targeting maladaptive thoughts and
emotions. A targeted treatment focus on aversive
well-being comparisons may help patients balance
loss-oriented and restoration-oriented stressors,
potentially promoting better emotional processing
and grief adjustment. However, these claims require
validation through experimental and clinical research.
5.9. Strengths and limitations
This preregistered study contributes to the literature
by examining the role of aversive well-being comparisons in individuals experiencing loss. It expands upon
previous research by considering the impact of wellbeing comparison processes, including its frequency,
discrepancy, and affective impact, and demonstrating
its unique contribution to mental health outcomes
beyond established risk factors like rumination and
worry. By investigating these factors alongside other
key transdiagnostic risk factors in bereaved

13

individuals, our work provides valuable insights into
the complex cognitive processes that may intensify
grief and contribute to mental health problems.
However, our study has some limitations. One
notable limitation is the dropout rate of 28%. While
mental health variables were not associated with dropouts, unmeasured variables may have contributed to
the drop-out in our study and may thus have influenced
the results. Our study was limited to two time-points,
six months apart. Relevant short-term fluctuations
and within-person person processes thus remain
masked in our study. Although our models tested mediational pathways, causality cannot be established.
Experimental research is needed to address this limitation. Furthermore, we relied on a convenience sample
from Prolific, which restricts the extent to which our
findings can be generalized. This concerns sample
diversity and recruitment. Although Prolific allows
access to a wide range of participants, participants
were self-selected and recruited online, which may
introduce selection biases (e.g. higher digital literacy,
greater willingness to participate in psychological
research). In addition, the sample may not fully capture
the diversity of bereaved populations in terms of cultural background, socioeconomic status, or bereavement context (e.g. cause of death, relationship to the
deceased). Additionally, post-hoc power analyses
suggested that our study may not have had sufficient
statistical power to detect the mediation effects we
hypothesized. This requires caution in interpreting the
mediation findings and underscores the need for larger
samples in future research. Finally, childhood adversity
was assessed retrospectively and may be confounded
with mood-related recall bias (Dunn et al., 2018).

6. Conclusion
Our findings contribute to the growing literature on
cognitive processes involved in bereavement by
emphasizing the role of well-being comparisons in
mental health following the loss of a significant
other. A better understanding of how comparison processes influence mental health during grief may
advance our knowledge of prolonged grief and help
inform interventions aimed at enhancing well-being
among bereaved individuals.

candidate: This cross-sectional study investigated latent classes of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and their associations with impulsivity and mental health among adults in Saudi Arabia. Using an online convenience sample of 379 adults aged 18–65, researchers employed latent class analysis (LCA) to identify patterns of adversity. Participants were categorized into a structural no-ACE reference group and two ACE-exposed classes: limited/mixed ACE and poly-victimisation. The poly-victimisation class, characterized by high probabilities of emotional abuse, physical abuse, and household mental illness, showed significantly higher levels of negative urgency (d = 0.55) and lack of perseverance (d = 0.43) compared to the no-ACE group. Furthermore, this class was associated with a higher prevalence of lifetime psychiatric diagnosis (OR = 6.27) and greater perceived health impact (OR = 12.81). The study concludes that a poly-victimisation pattern is associated with greater emotion-related impulsivity and mental health burden, supporting the use of pattern-level assessments alongside cumulative ACE counts. Key limitations include the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference, the use of self-reported data, and the reliance on a convenience sample and brief, single-item mental health measures.

ABSTRACT

ARTICLE HISTORY

Background: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with later mental-health
difficulties, but simple ACE counts can obscure which adversities co-occur within individuals.
Person-centred modelling can identify groups of people with similar exposure patterns.
Objective: This cross-sectional study identified latent classes of ACEs among adults living in
Saudi Arabia and examined their associations with five facets of UPPS-P impulsive behaviour
and brief mental-health indicators.
Methods: An online convenience sample of 379 adults aged 18–65 years completed the 10item ACE screener, the Arabic Short UPPS-P Impulsive Behaviour Scale, and single-item
measures of lifetime psychiatric diagnosis and perceived health impact. Respondents
reporting no ACEs were retained as a structural no-ACE reference group. Latent class
analysis was conducted among ACE-exposed participants. Model selection considered
information criteria, entropy, average posterior probabilities, class size, and interpretability.
Alternative class specifications were examined in sensitivity analyses. False discovery rate
(FDR) correction was applied to pairwise outcome tests.
Results: Of 379 eligible respondents, 133 (35.1%) reported no ACEs. Among 246 ACE-exposed
respondents, a two-class solution was selected and yielded limited/mixed ACE (n = 140, 36.9%
of the full sample) and poly-victimisation (n = 106, 28.0%) classes. The poly-victimisation class
showed high probabilities of emotional abuse, physical abuse, witnessed domestic violence,
emotional neglect, and household mental illness. Compared with the no-ACE group, the
poly-victimisation class had higher negative urgency (d = 0.55, q < .001), lack of perseverance
(d = 0.43, q = .007), psychiatric diagnosis (42.5% vs 10.5%; OR = 6.27, 95% CI [3.19, 12.31]),
and perceived health impact (77.4% vs 21.1%; OR = 12.81, 95% CI [6.91, 23.75]). Familyconflict interactions were exploratory and not statistically robust.
Conclusions: A poly-victimisation class was associated with greater emotion-related
impulsivity and mental-health burden. The findings support cautious use of pattern-level
ACE assessment alongside ACE counts, while recognising the limitations of cross-sectional
convenience sampling and brief outcome measures.

1. Background
Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) include potentially traumatic or stressful events before age 18, such
as abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction. ACEs
are consistently associated with poorer mental and
physical health in adulthood, and meta-analytic evidence indicates that risk tends to increase as the number of adversities accumulates (Felitti et al., 1998;
Hughes et al., 2017). In Saudi Arabia, prior ACE
research has also reported substantial exposure to
childhood adversity and associations with health,
risk behaviours, and social determinants (AlHemyari
et al., 2022; Almuneef et al., 2014, 2018).
The conventional cumulative ACE score is useful
because it provides a simple burden index. It treats
very different exposure histories as equivalent when
their counts are the same. One person with two
ACEs may report parental separation and household
mental illness, while another may report emotional
abuse and physical abuse. These patterns may differ
in timing, chronicity, relational meaning, and links
with later functioning. A count score gives the same
weight to each item and cannot show which adversities cluster together within the same individuals.
These issues are consistent with calls to move beyond
cumulative ACE totals and examine dimensions or
patterns of adversity (McLaughlin & Sheridan, 2016).
Latent class analysis (LCA) addresses this limitation
by identifying subgroups that share similar itemresponse patterns (Collins & Lanza, 2010; Masyn,
2013). Reviews and empirical comparisons suggest
that ACE classes often distinguish lower-adversity,
household-dysfunction, maltreatment, and poly-victimisation patterns, although the exact number and
content of classes depend on the indicators, sample,
and cultural context (Lanier et al., 2018; Merians
et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024).
Impulsivity is a relevant adult outcome domain
because it cuts across multiple psychiatric and behavioural problems. The UPPS-P model conceptualises
impulsive behaviour as five facets: negative urgency,
positive urgency, sensation seeking, lack of premeditation, and lack of perseverance (Cyders et al., 2014;

Whiteside & Lynam, 2001). Negative and positive
urgency are emotion-driven dimensions, referring to
rash action under negative or positive affect. Early
adversity may be especially relevant to these
emotion-related facets because maltreatment and
family threat can shape stress reactivity, emotion regulation, and inhibitory control, although cross-sectional
survey data cannot test neurobiological mechanisms
directly (Teicher & Samson, 2016). A prior study
linked ACE classes with impulsivity, but evidence
remains limited for how ACE classes relate to specific
UPPS-P facets in Middle Eastern samples (Shin et al.,
2018).
Saudi Arabia is an important context for personcentred ACE research because most LCA-ACE evidence is derived from Western samples. Existing
Saudi studies show that ACEs are not rare, but estimates vary because studies use different instruments,
sampling frames, and adversity definitions (AlHemyari et al., 2022; Almuneef et al., 2014, 2018). Social
norms surrounding family privacy, stigma, and helpseeking may also influence disclosure of ACEs and
psychiatric diagnoses. These factors make it important
to interpret both prevalence and class structure cautiously rather than assuming direct comparability
with Western samples.
The present study used cross-sectional online survey data from adults living in Saudi Arabia. We
aimed to identify ACE classes and examine their
associations with all five UPPS-P impulsivity facets,
lifetime psychiatric diagnosis, and perceived health
impact. We expected that a higher-adversity/poly-victimisation class would show the strongest associations
with emotion-driven impulsivity and mental-health
indicators. We also examined current family conflict
as an exploratory moderator, while recognising that
small cells and cross-sectional measurement limit causal interpretation.

2. Methods
Study design and oversight. This cross-sectional,
questionnaire-based study examined ACE classes

EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTRAUMATOLOGY

and their associations with impulsivity and mentalhealth indicators among adults living in Saudi Arabia.
Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional
Review Board of Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic
University (Project No. 717/2024). All participants
provided electronic informed consent. Reporting follows STROBE guidance for observational studies
(von Elm et al., 2007).
Participants and recruitment. Inclusion criteria
were age 18–65 years, current residence in Saudi Arabia, Arabic literacy, electronic informed consent, and
questionnaire completion. Recruitment used an open
online survey link disseminated between December
2024 and July 2025 through WhatsApp, Telegram,
X/Twitter, Facebook, personal networks, university
channels, and community groups. No incentives or
sociodemographic quotas were used. Because the survey link was open and invitations were redistributed
through multiple channels, the number of people
who viewed the invitation is unknown and a conventional response rate cannot be calculated. The survey
platform recorded 385 submissions. Three respondents did not provide electronic consent and did not
proceed to the questionnaire. Among 382 consenting
respondents, three were older than the prespecified
upper age limit of 65 years and were excluded. The
final analytic sample comprised 379 adults aged 18–
65 years.
Sample size. The target of approximately 385
respondents was set to support descriptive precision
for a large adult population using a 95% confidence
level and an approximate 5% margin of error. For
LCA, this target was also considered adequate for
exploratory binary-indicator class enumeration with
a small number of indicators, provided that
selected classes were not very small. Model selection
therefore prioritised information criteria as well as
class size, posterior classification quality, and
interpretability.
Sociodemographic variables. Participants reported
gender, nationality, broad region of residence in Saudi
Arabia, age group, marital status, education, employment status, family monthly income, and living
arrangement. Following reviewer guidance and current psychotrauma reporting recommendations, gender categories are described as women and men
rather than female and male unless referring to the
original survey response options (Langeland & Olff,
2024).
Adverse childhood experiences. The 10 binary ACE
items assessed physical neglect, parent loss/separation,
household mental illness, household substance abuse,
witnessed domestic violence, household incarceration,
emotional abuse, physical abuse, emotional neglect,
and sexual abuse before age 18. The items correspond
to the standard 10-item ACE domains from the original ACE framework (Felitti et al., 1998). Arabic

3

wording was informed by prior Saudi ACE research
using Arabic ACE-IQ adaptations (Almuneef et al.,
2014; World Health Organization, 2020). The exact
10-item Arabic screener used here should nevertheless
be interpreted as an adapted ACE screener rather than
a standalone instrument with comprehensive psychometric validation in this sample; this limitation is
acknowledged explicitly.
Impulsivity. The Arabic Short UPPS-P Impulsive
Behaviour Scale was used to assess five four-item
facets: negative urgency, positive urgency, sensation
seeking, lack of premeditation, and lack of perseverance (Bteich et al., 2017). Items were scored from 1
to 4 and oriented so that higher scores indicated
greater impulsivity. Internal consistency in the analytic sample was acceptable for negative urgency (α
= .818), positive urgency (α = .704), sensation seeking
(α = .811), and lack of perseverance (α = .816). Lack
of premeditation showed lower internal consistency
(α = .548); findings for this subscale are interpreted
cautiously.
Mental-health indicators. Lifetime psychiatric
diagnosis was assessed with the item: ‘Have you ever
been diagnosed with any psychiatric illness?’ Response
options included ‘No’ and several named diagnoses or
an ‘Other’ option. Responses were dichotomised as
any psychiatric diagnosis versus none. Perceived
health impact was assessed with the item: ‘Do you
believe that these experiences have affected your
health?’ Responses were ‘Not much’, ‘To some extent’,
and ‘A lot’. This variable was dichotomised as Not
much versus Some/A lot because the latter two categories both indicated perceived impact and because
the three-level distribution was sparse for some class
comparisons. These single-item indicators are treated
as brief exploratory outcomes rather than diagnostic
assessments.
Current family conflict. Current family conflict
was assessed with the item: ‘How often does it happen
that people in your family have serious arguments or
fights?’ Response options were Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, and Always. For moderation analyses,
responses were collapsed to low (Never/Rarely), medium (Sometimes), and high (Often/Always) to reduce
sparse cells. This decision was made before interpreting the class-by-conflict comparisons and is reported
because the high-conflict cell in the no-ACE group
remained very small.
Data management and missing data. The online
survey required responses for the analytic items.
Item-level missingness was therefore 0% among consenting respondents who completed the questionnaire. The only exclusions were non-consent and age
outside the prespecified eligibility range. Completecase analyses were used.
Latent class analysis. Because a large proportion of
participants reported no ACEs, respondents with ACE

4

S. A. ALGHAMDI

total = 0 were retained as a structural no-ACE reference group. LCA was then conducted among participants endorsing at least one ACE to identify
heterogeneity among ACE-exposed respondents
rather than allowing the no-ACE subgroup to dominate class formation. Models with one to five ACEexposed classes were estimated for the 10 binary
ACE indicators using maximum likelihood for a
multivariate Bernoulli latent class model with multiple
random starts. Model selection considered AIC, BIC,
sample-size adjusted BIC, entropy, average posterior
probabilities, minimum class size, and substantive
interpretability (Nylund et al., 2007; Nylund-Gibson
& Choi, 2018). Models producing very small classes
were not selected as the primary solution because distal comparisons would be unstable. Sensitivity analyses examining alternative class enumeration
strategies, including a full-sample three-class and
four-class solution, are reported in the Supplementary
Material.
Outcome analyses. Participants were assigned to
the no-ACE reference group or to their modal ACEexposed latent class. Classification quality was assessed
using entropy and average posterior probabilities.
Group differences in continuous UPPS-P facets were
examined with one-way analysis of variance and pairwise Welch tests comparing each ACE-exposed class
with the no-ACE reference group. Binary outcomes
were examined using raw proportions and odds ratios
with 95% confidence intervals. False discovery rate
correction was applied to pairwise tests; q-values
refer to FDR-adjusted p-values. Cumulative ACE
score and class-grouping models were compared
descriptively using adjusted R² for continuous outcomes and McFadden pseudo-R² for binary outcomes.
Family-conflict moderation was examined only as an
exploratory analysis because of small cells.
Software. Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance,
Welch tests, logistic regression, and FDR-adjustment
were conducted in IBM SPSS Statistics version 28.0.
Latent class analysis was performed in R version 4.3
using the poLCA package (Linzer & Lewis, 2011).
All numeric results were independently verified across
the two statistical environments. Figures were prepared in R.

3. Results
Participant flow and sample characteristics. The analytic sample included 379 adults aged 18–65 years.
Respondents came from all five broad geographic
regions coded in the survey, although the sample
was concentrated in the Central Region and should
not be treated as nationally representative. Table 1
summarises sample characteristics by person-centred
group. The mean ACE count was 2.03 (SD = 2.23);
64.9% endorsed at least one ACE, 35.1% endorsed

three or more ACEs, and 24.5% endorsed four or
more ACEs.
Latent class enumeration. Of the 379 eligible participants, 133 (35.1%) reported no ACEs and were
retained as a structural no-ACE reference group. LCA
was then conducted among the 246 ACE-exposed participants. The two-class ACE-exposed model was
selected as the primary model. Although the threeclass model showed slightly lower BIC, it produced
a very small class (n = 13), limiting the stability of outcome comparisons. The selected two-class solution
had acceptable entropy (.808), high average posterior
probabilities (.947 and .944), and no very small
classes. Combined with the no-ACE reference group,
the final person-centred grouping comprised no
ACE (n = 133, 35.1%), limited/mixed ACE (n = 140,
36.9%), and poly-victimisation (n = 106, 28.0%).
Table 2 presents ACE-exposed model fit indices, and
Table 3 presents item-response probabilities. Alternative class enumeration solutions, including a fullsample three-class and four-class solution, are
reported as sensitivity analyses in Supplementary
Tables S1 and S2. The substantive ordering of negative urgency, lack of perseverance, and mental-health
outcomes was preserved across alternative class specifications, indicating that the primary findings did
not depend on the specific class enumeration chosen.
Class interpretation. The limited/mixed ACE
class showed moderate probabilities of emotional
abuse, parent loss/separation, household mental illness, and emotional neglect, but low probabilities
of witnessed domestic violence and physical abuse.
The poly-victimisation class showed very high probabilities of emotional abuse, physical abuse, witnessed domestic violence, emotional neglect, and
household mental illness. Figure 1 displays the
item-response probabilities.
UPPS-P impulsivity facets. Table 4 reports all five
UPPS-P facets. The clearest class differences were
observed for negative urgency and lack of perseverance. Compared with the no-ACE group, the poly-victimisation class had higher negative urgency (mean =
2.56 vs 2.14; d = 0.55, q < .001) and lack of perseverance (mean = 2.14 vs 1.87; d = 0.43, q = .007). The limited/mixed ACE class also showed higher negative
urgency than the no-ACE group (d = 0.32, q = .028).
Positive urgency and sensation seeking were modestly
higher in the poly-victimisation class, but pairwise
comparisons did not survive FDR correction. Lack
of premeditation showed no robust class difference.
Figure 2 summarises the UPPS-P means and 95%
confidence intervals.
Mental-health indicators. Table 5 shows that psychiatric diagnosis and perceived health impact
increased across the person-centred groups. Psychiatric diagnosis was reported by 10.5% of the no-ACE
group, 26.4% of the limited/mixed ACE class, and

4. Discussion
This study identified person-centred ACE groups
among adults living in Saudi Arabia and examined
their associations with multidimensional impulsivity
and brief mental-health indicators. The revised analysis used a structural no-ACE reference group plus
LCA among ACE-exposed respondents. This
approach addressed class-enumeration concerns by
avoiding an unstable full-sample four-class solution
and by preventing the no-ACE group from dominating heterogeneity among exposed participants. The
final grouping identified a limited/mixed ACE class
and a poly-victimisation class, with the latter showing
the highest burden across ACE indicators, emotionrelated impulsivity, psychiatric diagnosis, and perceived health impact.

The class structure is consistent with a broad pattern reported in ACE-LCA studies: many samples
contain a lower-adversity group and a more severe
multi-domain adversity group, while intermediate
classes vary by measurement and sample (Lanier
et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2024). The current results
suggest that in this Saudi online convenience sample,
the key distinction among ACE-exposed respondents was between limited/mixed exposure and a
high-burden poly-victimisation configuration. This
does not mean that household dysfunction or maltreatment-specific classes are absent in the Saudi
population. With the present sample size and indicators, attempts to extract more classes produced
very small groups that would have been unstable
for outcome comparisons (see Supplementary Tables
S1–S2).
The prevalence pattern should be interpreted
cautiously. The mean ACE count in this sample
was 2.03, with 24.5% reporting four or more
ACEs. Prior Saudi ACE studies using broader
ACE-IQ instruments have also reported substantial

design cannot establish whether ACEs preceded the
impulsivity pattern, whether current mental-health
difficulties influenced responses, or whether unmeasured factors contributed to both.
The brief mental-health indicators showed large class
differences, especially for the poly-victimisation class.
These findings should be read as associations with
self-reported diagnosis history and perceived health
impact, not as estimates of current psychiatric disorder.
The high perceived impact in the poly-victimisation
class may reflect subjective recognition of adversityrelated health burden, but it could also reflect current
distress, recall bias, or differences in willingness to attribute health problems to childhood experiences.
The revised comparison with cumulative ACE score
is important. The data did not support the earlier stronger claim that latent classes provided superior explanatory fit. ACE count performed well as an overall severity
measure, especially for mental-health indicators. The
added value of LCA is more modest and more clinically
descriptive: it shows that a sizeable subset of ACEexposed respondents had a pattern marked by
emotional abuse, physical abuse, witnessed domestic
violence, emotional neglect, and household mental illness. For trauma-informed screening, this patternlevel information may help clinicians ask more targeted
follow-up questions than a count score alone, while still
retaining the simplicity of ACE burden.
The family-conflict analysis did not provide consistent evidence of moderation. This does not rule out the
relevance of current family environment; rather, the
present study was not well powered for this interaction
because the no-ACE/high-conflict cell was very small.
Future studies should assess current family functioning
with validated multi-item instruments and recruit larger samples to test whether current conflict amplifies
or buffers associations between ACE classes and adult
outcomes (Repetti et al., 2002).
Cultural and social context requires cautious
interpretation. In Saudi Arabia and other familycentred societies, ACE disclosure may be shaped by
stigma, family privacy, perceived loyalty, and concerns
about social judgement. Psychiatric diagnosis may also
be underreported if respondents have limited access to
diagnosis, avoid mental-health services, or experience
stigma. Conversely, online anonymous surveys may
allow some respondents to disclose experiences they
would not report in interviews. These factors could
affect both prevalence estimates and class formation.
The overrepresentation of respondents from the Central Region and of young, educated, and student participants further limits generalisability. Underrepresented
subgroups might have different ACE patterns, and
rare classes may not have emerged because the sample
was not nationally representative.
Clinical implications should therefore be specific
but cautious. The findings support considering

multi-domain ACE exposure, particularly poly-victimisation, when assessing adults who present with
emotion-driven impulsivity, difficulty sustaining
effort, or mental-health burden. Screening should
not rely solely on a total ACE count; however, pattern-level assessment should be conducted sensitively,
with attention to privacy, stigma, and referral pathways. The results also suggest that services in Saudi
Arabia may benefit from trauma-informed approaches
that integrate emotion regulation and impulse-control
strategies, especially for individuals reporting multiple
forms of childhood maltreatment and household
dysfunction.
Limitations. Several limitations qualify the conclusions. First, the cross-sectional design precludes
temporal or causal inference. Second, ACEs were retrospectively self-reported and may be affected by
recall, reinterpretation, and disclosure bias. Third,
the exact 10-item Arabic ACE screener used here
was adapted from standard ACE items and prior Arabic ACE-IQ use, but it was not validated as a standalone instrument in this sample. Fourth, psychiatric
diagnosis and perceived health impact were singleitem indicators, not structured clinical assessments.
Fifth, current family conflict was assessed using a
single item and the moderation cells were small.
Sixth, the online convenience sample was not nationally representative, overrepresented some sociodemographic groups, and did not allow calculation of a
conventional response rate. Seventh, the lack of premeditation subscale showed low internal consistency
and should be interpreted cautiously. Finally, class solutions depend on the selected indicators and sample;
larger representative Saudi and regional studies are
needed to test whether the present two-class ACEexposed solution replicates. Sensitivity analyses across
alternative class specifications (Supplementary Tables
S1–S2) showed that the substantive ordering of
effects was preserved.
Conclusion. A structural no-ACE reference group
plus ACE-exposed LCA identified limited/mixed
ACE and poly-victimisation classes among adults living in Saudi Arabia. Poly-victimisation was associated
with higher negative urgency, lack of perseverance,
psychiatric diagnosis, and perceived health impact.
The revised findings support using ACE classes as
complementary pattern-level information alongside
cumulative ACE scores, not as causal or temporally
ordered evidence. Future representative studies with
validated Arabic measures and stronger mental-health
assessment are needed before translating these
findings into population-level screening policy.

ABSTRACT

ARTICLE HISTORY

Background: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with later mental-health
difficulties, but simple ACE counts can obscure which adversities co-occur within individuals.
Person-centred modelling can identify groups of people with similar exposure patterns.
Objective: This cross-sectional study identified latent classes of ACEs among adults living in
Saudi Arabia and examined their associations with five facets of UPPS-P impulsive behaviour
and brief mental-health indicators.
Methods: An online convenience sample of 379 adults aged 18–65 years completed the 10item ACE screener, the Arabic Short UPPS-P Impulsive Behaviour Scale, and single-item
measures of lifetime psychiatric diagnosis and perceived health impact. Respondents
reporting no ACEs were retained as a structural no-ACE reference group. Latent class
analysis was conducted among ACE-exposed participants. Model selection considered
information criteria, entropy, average posterior probabilities, class size, and interpretability.
Alternative class specifications were examined in sensitivity analyses. False discovery rate
(FDR) correction was applied to pairwise outcome tests.
Results: Of 379 eligible respondents, 133 (35.1%) reported no ACEs. Among 246 ACE-exposed
respondents, a two-class solution was selected and yielded limited/mixed ACE (n = 140, 36.9%
of the full sample) and poly-victimisation (n = 106, 28.0%) classes. The poly-victimisation class
showed high probabilities of emotional abuse, physical abuse, witnessed domestic violence,
emotional neglect, and household mental illness. Compared with the no-ACE group, the
poly-victimisation class had higher negative urgency (d = 0.55, q < .001), lack of perseverance
(d = 0.43, q = .007), psychiatric diagnosis (42.5% vs 10.5%; OR = 6.27, 95% CI [3.19, 12.31]),
and perceived health impact (77.4% vs 21.1%; OR = 12.81, 95% CI [6.91, 23.75]). Familyconflict interactions were exploratory and not statistically robust.
Conclusions: A poly-victimisation class was associated with greater emotion-related
impulsivity and mental-health burden. The findings support cautious use of pattern-level
ACE assessment alongside ACE counts, while recognising the limitations of cross-sectional
convenience sampling and brief outcome measures.

1. Background
Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) include potentially traumatic or stressful events before age 18, such
as abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction. ACEs
are consistently associated with poorer mental and
physical health in adulthood, and meta-analytic evidence indicates that risk tends to increase as the number of adversities accumulates (Felitti et al., 1998;
Hughes et al., 2017). In Saudi Arabia, prior ACE
research has also reported substantial exposure to
childhood adversity and associations with health,
risk behaviours, and social determinants (AlHemyari
et al., 2022; Almuneef et al., 2014, 2018).
The conventional cumulative ACE score is useful
because it provides a simple burden index. It treats
very different exposure histories as equivalent when
their counts are the same. One person with two
ACEs may report parental separation and household
mental illness, while another may report emotional
abuse and physical abuse. These patterns may differ
in timing, chronicity, relational meaning, and links
with later functioning. A count score gives the same
weight to each item and cannot show which adversities cluster together within the same individuals.
These issues are consistent with calls to move beyond
cumulative ACE totals and examine dimensions or
patterns of adversity (McLaughlin & Sheridan, 2016).
Latent class analysis (LCA) addresses this limitation
by identifying subgroups that share similar itemresponse patterns (Collins & Lanza, 2010; Masyn,
2013). Reviews and empirical comparisons suggest
that ACE classes often distinguish lower-adversity,
household-dysfunction, maltreatment, and poly-victimisation patterns, although the exact number and
content of classes depend on the indicators, sample,
and cultural context (Lanier et al., 2018; Merians
et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024).
Impulsivity is a relevant adult outcome domain
because it cuts across multiple psychiatric and behavioural problems. The UPPS-P model conceptualises
impulsive behaviour as five facets: negative urgency,
positive urgency, sensation seeking, lack of premeditation, and lack of perseverance (Cyders et al., 2014;

Whiteside & Lynam, 2001). Negative and positive
urgency are emotion-driven dimensions, referring to
rash action under negative or positive affect. Early
adversity may be especially relevant to these
emotion-related facets because maltreatment and
family threat can shape stress reactivity, emotion regulation, and inhibitory control, although cross-sectional
survey data cannot test neurobiological mechanisms
directly (Teicher & Samson, 2016). A prior study
linked ACE classes with impulsivity, but evidence
remains limited for how ACE classes relate to specific
UPPS-P facets in Middle Eastern samples (Shin et al.,
2018).
Saudi Arabia is an important context for personcentred ACE research because most LCA-ACE evidence is derived from Western samples. Existing
Saudi studies show that ACEs are not rare, but estimates vary because studies use different instruments,
sampling frames, and adversity definitions (AlHemyari et al., 2022; Almuneef et al., 2014, 2018). Social
norms surrounding family privacy, stigma, and helpseeking may also influence disclosure of ACEs and
psychiatric diagnoses. These factors make it important
to interpret both prevalence and class structure cautiously rather than assuming direct comparability
with Western samples.
The present study used cross-sectional online survey data from adults living in Saudi Arabia. We
aimed to identify ACE classes and examine their
associations with all five UPPS-P impulsivity facets,
lifetime psychiatric diagnosis, and perceived health
impact. We expected that a higher-adversity/poly-victimisation class would show the strongest associations
with emotion-driven impulsivity and mental-health
indicators. We also examined current family conflict
as an exploratory moderator, while recognising that
small cells and cross-sectional measurement limit causal interpretation.

2. Methods
Study design and oversight. This cross-sectional,
questionnaire-based study examined ACE classes

and their associations with impulsivity and mentalhealth indicators among adults living in Saudi Arabia.
Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional
Review Board of Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic
University (Project No. 717/2024). All participants
provided electronic informed consent. Reporting follows STROBE guidance for observational studies
(von Elm et al., 2007).
Participants and recruitment. Inclusion criteria
were age 18–65 years, current residence in Saudi Arabia, Arabic literacy, electronic informed consent, and
questionnaire completion. Recruitment used an open
online survey link disseminated between December
2024 and July 2025 through WhatsApp, Telegram,
X/Twitter, Facebook, personal networks, university
channels, and community groups. No incentives or
sociodemographic quotas were used. Because the survey link was open and invitations were redistributed
through multiple channels, the number of people
who viewed the invitation is unknown and a conventional response rate cannot be calculated. The survey
platform recorded 385 submissions. Three respondents did not provide electronic consent and did not
proceed to the questionnaire. Among 382 consenting
respondents, three were older than the prespecified
upper age limit of 65 years and were excluded. The
final analytic sample comprised 379 adults aged 18–
65 years.
Sample size. The target of approximately 385
respondents was set to support descriptive precision
for a large adult population using a 95% confidence
level and an approximate 5% margin of error. For
LCA, this target was also considered adequate for
exploratory binary-indicator class enumeration with
a small number of indicators, provided that
selected classes were not very small. Model selection
therefore prioritised information criteria as well as
class size, posterior classification quality, and
interpretability.
Sociodemographic variables. Participants reported
gender, nationality, broad region of residence in Saudi
Arabia, age group, marital status, education, employment status, family monthly income, and living
arrangement. Following reviewer guidance and current psychotrauma reporting recommendations, gender categories are described as women and men
rather than female and male unless referring to the
original survey response options (Langeland & Olff,
2024).
Adverse childhood experiences. The 10 binary ACE
items assessed physical neglect, parent loss/separation,
household mental illness, household substance abuse,
witnessed domestic violence, household incarceration,
emotional abuse, physical abuse, emotional neglect,
and sexual abuse before age 18. The items correspond
to the standard 10-item ACE domains from the original ACE framework (Felitti et al., 1998). Arabic

wording was informed by prior Saudi ACE research
using Arabic ACE-IQ adaptations (Almuneef et al.,
2014; World Health Organization, 2020). The exact
10-item Arabic screener used here should nevertheless
be interpreted as an adapted ACE screener rather than
a standalone instrument with comprehensive psychometric validation in this sample; this limitation is
acknowledged explicitly.
Impulsivity. The Arabic Short UPPS-P Impulsive
Behaviour Scale was used to assess five four-item
facets: negative urgency, positive urgency, sensation
seeking, lack of premeditation, and lack of perseverance (Bteich et al., 2017). Items were scored from 1
to 4 and oriented so that higher scores indicated
greater impulsivity. Internal consistency in the analytic sample was acceptable for negative urgency (α
= .818), positive urgency (α = .704), sensation seeking
(α = .811), and lack of perseverance (α = .816). Lack
of premeditation showed lower internal consistency
(α = .548); findings for this subscale are interpreted
cautiously.
Mental-health indicators. Lifetime psychiatric
diagnosis was assessed with the item: ‘Have you ever
been diagnosed with any psychiatric illness?’ Response
options included ‘No’ and several named diagnoses or
an ‘Other’ option. Responses were dichotomised as
any psychiatric diagnosis versus none. Perceived
health impact was assessed with the item: ‘Do you
believe that these experiences have affected your
health?’ Responses were ‘Not much’, ‘To some extent’,
and ‘A lot’. This variable was dichotomised as Not
much versus Some/A lot because the latter two categories both indicated perceived impact and because
the three-level distribution was sparse for some class
comparisons. These single-item indicators are treated
as brief exploratory outcomes rather than diagnostic
assessments.
Current family conflict. Current family conflict
was assessed with the item: ‘How often does it happen
that people in your family have serious arguments or
fights?’ Response options were Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, and Always. For moderation analyses,
responses were collapsed to low (Never/Rarely), medium (Sometimes), and high (Often/Always) to reduce
sparse cells. This decision was made before interpreting the class-by-conflict comparisons and is reported
because the high-conflict cell in the no-ACE group
remained very small.
Data management and missing data. The online
survey required responses for the analytic items.
Item-level missingness was therefore 0% among consenting respondents who completed the questionnaire. The only exclusions were non-consent and age
outside the prespecified eligibility range. Completecase analyses were used.
Latent class analysis. Because a large proportion of
participants reported no ACEs, respondents with ACE

total = 0 were retained as a structural no-ACE reference group. LCA was then conducted among participants endorsing at least one ACE to identify
heterogeneity among ACE-exposed respondents
rather than allowing the no-ACE subgroup to dominate class formation. Models with one to five ACEexposed classes were estimated for the 10 binary
ACE indicators using maximum likelihood for a
multivariate Bernoulli latent class model with multiple
random starts. Model selection considered AIC, BIC,
sample-size adjusted BIC, entropy, average posterior
probabilities, minimum class size, and substantive
interpretability (Nylund et al., 2007; Nylund-Gibson
& Choi, 2018). Models producing very small classes
were not selected as the primary solution because distal comparisons would be unstable. Sensitivity analyses examining alternative class enumeration
strategies, including a full-sample three-class and
four-class solution, are reported in the Supplementary
Material.
Outcome analyses. Participants were assigned to
the no-ACE reference group or to their modal ACEexposed latent class. Classification quality was assessed
using entropy and average posterior probabilities.
Group differences in continuous UPPS-P facets were
examined with one-way analysis of variance and pairwise Welch tests comparing each ACE-exposed class
with the no-ACE reference group. Binary outcomes
were examined using raw proportions and odds ratios
with 95% confidence intervals. False discovery rate
correction was applied to pairwise tests; q-values
refer to FDR-adjusted p-values. Cumulative ACE
score and class-grouping models were compared
descriptively using adjusted R² for continuous outcomes and McFadden pseudo-R² for binary outcomes.
Family-conflict moderation was examined only as an
exploratory analysis because of small cells.
Software. Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance,
Welch tests, logistic regression, and FDR-adjustment
were conducted in IBM SPSS Statistics version 28.0.
Latent class analysis was performed in R version 4.3
using the poLCA package (Linzer & Lewis, 2011).
All numeric results were independently verified across
the two statistical environments. Figures were prepared in R.

3. Results
Participant flow and sample characteristics. The analytic sample included 379 adults aged 18–65 years.
Respondents came from all five broad geographic
regions coded in the survey, although the sample
was concentrated in the Central Region and should
not be treated as nationally representative. Table 1
summarises sample characteristics by person-centred
group. The mean ACE count was 2.03 (SD = 2.23);
64.9% endorsed at least one ACE, 35.1% endorsed

three or more ACEs, and 24.5% endorsed four or
more ACEs.
Latent class enumeration. Of the 379 eligible participants, 133 (35.1%) reported no ACEs and were
retained as a structural no-ACE reference group. LCA
was then conducted among the 246 ACE-exposed participants. The two-class ACE-exposed model was
selected as the primary model. Although the threeclass model showed slightly lower BIC, it produced
a very small class (n = 13), limiting the stability of outcome comparisons. The selected two-class solution
had acceptable entropy (.808), high average posterior
probabilities (.947 and .944), and no very small
classes. Combined with the no-ACE reference group,
the final person-centred grouping comprised no
ACE (n = 133, 35.1%), limited/mixed ACE (n = 140,
36.9%), and poly-victimisation (n = 106, 28.0%).
Table 2 presents ACE-exposed model fit indices, and
Table 3 presents item-response probabilities. Alternative class enumeration solutions, including a fullsample three-class and four-class solution, are
reported as sensitivity analyses in Supplementary
Tables S1 and S2. The substantive ordering of negative urgency, lack of perseverance, and mental-health
outcomes was preserved across alternative class specifications, indicating that the primary findings did
not depend on the specific class enumeration chosen.
Class interpretation. The limited/mixed ACE
class showed moderate probabilities of emotional
abuse, parent loss/separation, household mental illness, and emotional neglect, but low probabilities
of witnessed domestic violence and physical abuse.
The poly-victimisation class showed very high probabilities of emotional abuse, physical abuse, witnessed domestic violence, emotional neglect, and
household mental illness. Figure 1 displays the
item-response probabilities.
UPPS-P impulsivity facets. Table 4 reports all five
UPPS-P facets. The clearest class differences were
observed for negative urgency and lack of perseverance. Compared with the no-ACE group, the poly-victimisation class had higher negative urgency (mean =
2.56 vs 2.14; d = 0.55, q < .001) and lack of perseverance (mean = 2.14 vs 1.87; d = 0.43, q = .007). The limited/mixed ACE class also showed higher negative
urgency than the no-ACE group (d = 0.32, q = .028).
Positive urgency and sensation seeking were modestly
higher in the poly-victimisation class, but pairwise
comparisons did not survive FDR correction. Lack
of premeditation showed no robust class difference.
Figure 2 summarises the UPPS-P means and 95%
confidence intervals.

4. Discussion
This study identified person-centred ACE groups
among adults living in Saudi Arabia and examined
their associations with multidimensional impulsivity
and brief mental-health indicators. The revised analysis used a structural no-ACE reference group plus
LCA among ACE-exposed respondents. This
approach addressed class-enumeration concerns by
avoiding an unstable full-sample four-class solution
and by preventing the no-ACE group from dominating heterogeneity among exposed participants. The
final grouping identified a limited/mixed ACE class
and a poly-victimisation class, with the latter showing
the highest burden across ACE indicators, emotionrelated impulsivity, psychiatric diagnosis, and perceived health impact.

The class structure is consistent with a broad pattern reported in ACE-LCA studies: many samples
contain a lower-adversity group and a more severe
multi-domain adversity group, while intermediate
classes vary by measurement and sample (Lanier
et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2024). The current results
suggest that in this Saudi online convenience sample,
the key distinction among ACE-exposed respondents was between limited/mixed exposure and a
high-burden poly-victimisation configuration. This
does not mean that household dysfunction or maltreatment-specific classes are absent in the Saudi
population. With the present sample size and indicators, attempts to extract more classes produced
very small groups that would have been unstable
for outcome comparisons (see Supplementary Tables
S1–S2).
The prevalence pattern should be interpreted
cautiously. The mean ACE count in this sample
was 2.03, with 24.5% reporting four or more
ACEs. Prior Saudi ACE studies using broader
ACE-IQ instruments have also reported substantial
adversity exposure, including 32% with four or

The impulsivity results were most robust for negative urgency and lack of perseverance. Negative
urgency reflects rash action under negative affect,
and its elevation in ACE-exposed classes is consistent
with the possibility that childhood adversity is linked
with emotion regulation difficulties. Lack of perseverance was elevated mainly in the poly-victimisation
class, suggesting that sustained goal-directed effort
may be particularly affected among respondents

difficulties influenced responses, or whether unmeasured factors contributed to both.
The brief mental-health indicators showed large class
differences, especially for the poly-victimisation class.
These findings should be read as associations with
self-reported diagnosis history and perceived health
impact, not as estimates of current psychiatric disorder.
The high perceived impact in the poly-victimisation
class may reflect subjective recognition of adversityrelated health burden, but it could also reflect current
distress, recall bias, or differences in willingness to attribute health problems to childhood experiences.
The revised comparison with cumulative ACE score
is important. The data did not support the earlier stronger claim that latent classes provided superior explanatory fit. ACE count performed well as an overall severity
measure, especially for mental-health indicators. The
added value of LCA is more modest and more clinically
descriptive: it shows that a sizeable subset of ACEexposed respondents had a pattern marked by
emotional abuse, physical abuse, witnessed domestic
violence, emotional neglect, and household mental illness. For trauma-informed screening, this patternlevel information may help clinicians ask more targeted
follow-up questions than a count score alone, while still
retaining the simplicity of ACE burden.
The family-conflict analysis did not provide consistent evidence of moderation. This does not rule out the
relevance of current family environment; rather, the
present study was not well powered for this interaction
because the no-ACE/high-conflict cell was very small.
Future studies should assess current family functioning
with validated multi-item instruments and recruit larger samples to test whether current conflict amplifies
or buffers associations between ACE classes and adult
outcomes (Repetti et al., 2002).
Cultural and social context requires cautious
interpretation. In Saudi Arabia and other familycentred societies, ACE disclosure may be shaped by
stigma, family privacy, perceived loyalty, and concerns
about social judgement. Psychiatric diagnosis may also
be underreported if respondents have limited access to
diagnosis, avoid mental-health services, or experience
stigma. Conversely, online anonymous surveys may
allow some respondents to disclose experiences they
would not report in interviews. These factors could
affect both prevalence estimates and class formation.
The overrepresentation of respondents from the Central Region and of young, educated, and student participants further limits generalisability. Underrepresented
subgroups might have different ACE patterns, and
rare classes may not have emerged because the sample
was not nationally representative.
Clinical implications should therefore be specific
but cautious. The findings support considering

multi-domain ACE exposure, particularly poly-victimisation, when assessing adults who present with
emotion-driven impulsivity, difficulty sustaining
effort, or mental-health burden. Screening should
not rely solely on a total ACE count; however, pattern-level assessment should be conducted sensitively,
with attention to privacy, stigma, and referral pathways. The results also suggest that services in Saudi
Arabia may benefit from trauma-informed approaches
that integrate emotion regulation and impulse-control
strategies, especially for individuals reporting multiple
forms of childhood maltreatment and household
dysfunction.
Limitations. Several limitations qualify the conclusions. First, the cross-sectional design precludes
temporal or causal inference. Second, ACEs were retrospectively self-reported and may be affected by
recall, reinterpretation, and disclosure bias. Third,
the exact 10-item Arabic ACE screener used here
was adapted from standard ACE items and prior Arabic ACE-IQ use, but it was not validated as a standalone instrument in this sample. Fourth, psychiatric
diagnosis and perceived health impact were singleitem indicators, not structured clinical assessments.
Fifth, current family conflict was assessed using a
single item and the moderation cells were small.
Sixth, the online convenience sample was not nationally representative, overrepresented some sociodemographic groups, and did not allow calculation of a
conventional response rate. Seventh, the lack of premeditation subscale showed low internal consistency
and should be interpreted cautiously. Finally, class solutions depend on the selected indicators and sample;
larger representative Saudi and regional studies are
needed to test whether the present two-class ACEexposed solution replicates. Sensitivity analyses across
alternative class specifications (Supplementary Tables
S1–S2) showed that the substantive ordering of
effects was preserved.
Conclusion. A structural no-ACE reference group
plus ACE-exposed LCA identified limited/mixed
ACE and poly-victimisation classes among adults living in Saudi Arabia. Poly-victimisation was associated
with higher negative urgency, lack of perseverance,
psychiatric diagnosis, and perceived health impact.
The revised findings support using ACE classes as
complementary pattern-level information alongside
cumulative ACE scores, not as causal or temporally
ordered evidence. Future representative studies with
validated Arabic measures and stronger mental-health
assessment are needed before translating these
findings into population-level screening policy.

candidate: This study evaluated a national, three-tiered knowledge mobilization initiative designed to improve support for UK women veterans who have experienced military sexual trauma (MST). Guided by the Knowledge-to-Action framework and co-produced with women veterans, the program aimed to enhance professional knowledge, improve service engagement strategies, and increase clinical capacity for Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT). The methodology employed a mixed-methods approach involving three components: a self-guided online foundational course for 526 individuals, a live online workshop for 363 professionals, and a truncated CPT training for 98 clinicians across 34 organizations. Quantitative analysis of the third course showed that clinician self-efficacy in delivering CPT significantly increased at a three-month follow-up ($p < .001, r = 0.915$), with a mean confidence increase of 1.00 (SE = 0.12). Qualitative findings highlighted themes regarding clinician confidence and systemic barriers to CPT delivery. The study concluded that the program successfully addressed knowledge gaps and demonstrated that co-produced knowledge mobilization can translate research into real-world impact. Limitations included low participation from Scotland, a potentially insufficient three-month follow-up period for assessing long-term systemic change, and the use of true-or-false quizzes for knowledge consolidation.

ABSTRACT

ARTICLE HISTORY

Background: Military sexual trauma (MST) disproportionately impacts women veterans
globally. UK research highlights that these in-service experiences may contribute to unique
mental and physical health needs. Yet, service providers are often perceived to be unaware
of and unable to meet these needs.
Objective: To evaluate a national training programme that synthesised evidence to support UK
women veterans. Situated within a wider knowledge mobilization (KMb) initiative and guided
by the Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework, a three-part programme was developed for
different professional audiences to enhance understanding of and support for women
veterans.
Method: Co-produced and grounded in KMb theory. Course 1 aimed to enhance knowledge of
women veterans’ health needs. Course 2 targeted healthcare professionals and veteran
specialist providers, exploring evidence-based considerations for promoting service
engagement. Course 3 aimed to increase UK clinical capacity in the best-evidenced
treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder associated with MST in women veterans,
through training mental health professionals in cognitive processing therapy (CPT). Mixedmethods data were collected from all programme attendees. CPT attendees completed preand 3-month post-training measures; quantitative data were analysed using a Wilcoxon
signed-rank test and qualitative data using manifest content analysis.
Results: Course 1 was completed by 526 individuals, 363 completed Course 2, and 98
completed Course 3. Course 3 attendees were split across two cohorts (n = 57; n = 41).
Compared with pre-training, 3-month post-training self-efficacy in delivering CPT across
cohort one increased significantly (p < .001, r = 0.915). Content analysis identified three
themes: (1) Clinician confidence delivering CPT; (2) Clinicians’ perceptions of CPT; and (3)
CPT in a service system.
Conclusions: The education programme addressed gaps in UK service provider knowledge
and increased CPT clinical capacity. The wider KMb initiative demonstrates how research can
be translated into impact for military populations and highlights the value of co-produced
KMb approaches.

1. Background
Military sexual trauma (MST) is a continuum of violence from sexual harassment and bullying to sexual
assault, perpetrated by serving personnel on other service members during military service (Herriott et al.
2024). Although there is currently no universally
accepted definition of MST, it has been found to disproportionately impact women across military health
research globally (Buyse et al., 2023; Moreau et al.,
2021; Mota et al., 2023). A US meta-analysis found
that 38.4% of serving and formerly serving women
reported having experienced MST, over nine times
higher than that reported by men (3.9%) (Wilson,
2018). While both men and women report experiencing MST, the higher number of serving men means
that absolute numbers may be comparable, although
underreporting remains a prevailing issue for all
(Ministry of Defence, 2019, 2021). MST has been
associated with a plethora of negative health outcomes, including physical pain (Shapiro et al., 2023),
gastrointestinal problems (Pulverman & Creech,
2021), and symptoms of anxiety and depression (MacDermid et al., 2025). In women veterans specifically,
MST has been identified as a potentially leading contributor to military-service linked post-traumatic
stress disorder (PTSD) (Campbell & Murphy, 2023;
Surís et al., 2004).
Despite the commonalities evidenced across different militaries, the world’s armed forces are not homogeneous. Therefore, it is necessary to understand the
impacts of MST within specific national veteran populations (Godier-McBard et al., 2021). In the UK, a
veteran is defined someone who has completed at
least one full day in the armed forces and is no longer
serving (Burdett et al., 2012). UK veteran health
research has predominantly focused on the male
veteran majority, although there are estimated to be
over 250,000 women veterans, representing approximately 13% of the total veteran population (National

Records of Scotland, 2024; Office for National Statistics, 2021). With a target to reach 30% inflow of
women to the military by 2030, the number of
women veterans in future years is expected to increase,
alongside the need to better understand and support
this group through and beyond military service (Ministry of Defence, 2022). With international evidence
indicating that MST is likely to be a significant contributor to poor mental health in women veterans, there
is a need to build evidence-based interventions and
support provision for UK women who have experienced MST.

1.1. Moving from research to action
Evidence-based practice integrates research, clinical
expertise, and contextual understanding of patient
groups to optimize outcomes through robust, consistent, and cost-effective care (Cook et al., 2017). This
requires the transfer of research findings into practice,
variously referred to as knowledge transfer,
implementation science, and knowledge exchange, to
name a few. There are myriad extant models to
describe this process of ‘closing the gap’ between
research and its real-world operationalization and
implementation (Davies et al., 2015; Strifler et al.,
2018). Current knowledge mobilization (KMb) (the
authors’ preferred term) models emphasize a non-linear set of stages that embed research evidence into
practice within healthcare and societal ‘systems’ (Durrant et al., 2024).
KMb approaches are unstandardized and iterative
in nature, although core functions include ‘dissemination and engagement of academic research beyond
that made possible by traditional forms of scholarly
communication’ (Phipps, 2011) and capacity building,
which serves to augment the capability of organizations to achieve and sustain longer term objectives
(Bate et al., 2004). Co-production and co-design are

EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTRAUMATOLOGY

also commonly used to bridge the knowledge gap,
enhance acceptability among policy makers, increase
relevance to target populations, and improve the likelihood of successful implementation within service
systems (Grindell et al., 2022).
The most widely used KMb model is Graham and
colleagues’ Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework
(Field et al., 2014; Graham et al., 2006), which divides
the process into two linked concepts (Figure 1). The
first concept – knowledge creation – is concerned
with tailoring and refining information to be of increasing utility. This encompasses three stages: gathering
knowledge from primary research (‘knowledge
inquiry’); interpretation of primary research through
syntheses such as systematic reviews (‘knowledge synthesis’); and finally, presenting this synthesized knowledge in accessible, audience-appropriate formats to
promote evidence-based decision making (‘knowledge
tools and products’). The second concept – the action
cycle – details the activities required to implementation

3

this knowledge. This is split into seven stages: identify a
problem that needs addressing, and identify, review,
and select the knowledge or research relevant to the
problem; adapt the identified knowledge to the local
context; assess barriers to using the knowledge; select,
tailor, and implement interventions to promote the
use of knowledge; monitor knowledge use; evaluate
the outcomes of using the knowledge; and sustain
ongoing knowledge use. Although the KTA framework
describes two concepts and constituent stages, the
boundaries between each are seen as fluid, and action
phases need not be sequential or discrete.
This paper examines how the KTA framework was
applied to a series of interlinked projects focusing on
improving support for UK women veterans who
have experienced MST. It first outlines in brief the
knowledge creation stage, before detailing the application of the action cycle in designing, implementing,
and assessing interventions to help address the impact
of MST through KMb.
