1.1.1. Knowledge inquiry: building the evidence
base around MST
A cohort of 750 UK women veterans was recruited in
the largest study to date exploring their experiences
during military service and their current health
profile; for full methodology, see Hendrikx, Williamson, et al. (2021). The study identified a high prevalence of common mental health disorders (CMDs)
(28.6%) and probable PTSD (10.8%) in the cohort.
In addition, 23% reported having experienced sexual
harassment, 23% emotional bullying, and 5% sexual
abuse (Hendrikx, Williamson, & Murphy, 2021),
figures broadly comparable to other countries
(Wilson, 2018). Significant associations were found
between reporting a high number of adverse childhood experiences and experiencing MST (Williamson
et al., 2022). Crucially, MST was found to be significantly associated with increased odds of reporting
probable PTSD as a veteran (Hendrikx, Williamson,
& Murphy, 2021). Furthermore, using a checklist of
in-service challenging experiences co-produced with
women veterans and subject-matter experts, 42.7%
of the cohort reported that sexist assumptions were
made about them during their service and 40.1% felt
that they had to be better than their male colleagues
to receive the same recognition at work. These in-service challenges were also significantly associated with
an increased risk of reporting poor mental and physical health as a veteran (Baumann et al., 2022).
Additional analysis explored the impact of past
gender-based discrimination, such as forced discharge
for pregnancy and experiences of the so-called ‘gay
ban’ (Biscoe et al., 2024). These studies cumulatively
established an evidence base, which indicated that
UK women veterans experienced idiosyncratic, gender-based challenges during their military service
that were different from those of their male counterparts, and which were likely to contribute to poor
mental health as a veteran. MST specifically was
reported as a significant contributor. Accordingly,
the need to focus on MST as significant potential inservice adversity with long-term health implications
for UK women veterans was indicated.
1.1.2. Knowledge synthesis: exploring women
veterans’ needs and experiences
Further exploration of MST and resultant PTSD in UK
women veterans was conducted. In line with the KTA
framework, research questions were formulated
specifically relating to how support services could be
improved for women veterans. These focused on
what evidence-based treatments work and where systemic improvements could be made. A systematic
review of treatments specifically for PTSD related to
MST in women veterans found that cognitive processing therapy (CPT) was the best-evidenced current
treatment (Campbell, Biscoe, et al., 2024). CPT is

also a reccomended trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy under the National Institute for Health
and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines (NICE, 2018).
Furthermore, a subcohort of UK women veterans
from the first study with scores indicative of probable
PTSD was invited to take part in semi-structured
interviews exploring their experiences of accessing
psychological healthcare. Qualitative analysis showed
that women veterans reported facing similar barriers
to men veterans, such as stigma around help-seeking
(Randles & Finnegan, 2022), but that these were
exacerbated as the result of their minority status
(Campbell et al., 2025; Campbell, Perry, et al., 2024).
Additional salient barriers and facilitators included a
perceived lack of professional knowledge and awareness about women veterans’ needs and experiences,
the invalidation of specific service traumatic experiences such as MST, and gender discrimination in the
design, provision, and focus of veteran-specific services, which were viewed as catering for the male
majority (Campbell et al., 2025).
1.1.3. Knowledge tools and products: evidencebased recommendations for action
Drawing on the findings from the previous stages, core
recommendations were co-produced with expert stakeholders (veteran experts, healthcare professionals,
and women veterans with lived experience) to guide
future improvements in support for UK women veterans, and specifically those who had experienced MST
(Campbell & Murphy, 2023). Policy experts were
also engaged to ensure that recommendations were
applicable in the policy domain. These recommendations included:
.

.

.

Increase healthcare professionals’ awareness of
women veterans, their military service experiences,
and mental healthcare needs.
Address specific barriers to engagement for women
veterans within services, potentially through
bespoke service design, access, and treatment
pathways.
Ensure that the best evidence-based treatment is
available for women veterans who have experienced
MST.

1.1.4. The action cycle: the current study
The current study, guided by the KTA framework,
aimed to address each of the three evidence-based recommendations by mobilizing knowledge to improve
access to, and provision of, evidenced treatment and
support for UK women veterans who have experienced MST.
A three-tiered education and training programme
was developed as part of this action cycle. Course 1
aimed to enhance general knowledge about women

EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTRAUMATOLOGY

veterans’ mental health needs, and was aimed at anyone who may have professional contact with women
veterans. Course 2 targeted healthcare professionals
and veteran specialist providers, and included evidence-based considerations for promoting service
engagement. Since women veterans often seek support
for mental health difficulties from non-veteranspecific services, engaging these groups was prioritized
(Campbell & Murphy, 2023; Hooks et al., 2023). In
line with KMb theory, to sustain the longer-term
objective of the programme and ensure that best-evidenced support is available to women veterans in the
UK, Course 3 aimed to increase UK clinical capacity
in the best-evidenced treatment for PTSD associated
with MST in women veterans by providing fully
funded training places, for appropriately qualified
mental health professionals, in CPT (Campbell, Biscoe, et al., 2024).

2. Method
2.1. Overview
The KTA framework’s action cycle was used as a guide
(Figure 1) throughout the KMb process. The three evidence-based recommendations for action were
reframed as problems against which the evidence
base could be mobilized to provide a solution. In
response, an online three-tiered education and training programme was conceived, with each course
responding to one problem, and aimed at a specific
professional end-user group. These courses
comprised:
(1) an introductory course designed to raise basic
awareness of woman veterans’ needs and experiences, aimed at anybody who had professional
contact with women veterans
(2) an advanced course designed to explore how services can be adapted to be more accessible, welcoming, and appropriate to women veterans,
aimed at those working in veteran-specific services and healthcare providers
(3) training in CPT to increase UK clinical capacity in
the best-evidenced treatment for PTSD related to
MST in women veterans, for mental health professionals who work with women veterans.
To reduce barriers to access, the programme was
made freely available via an online open access website
(https://veterans.training).
2.2. Co-production stakeholder group
The programme content and structure were co-produced with a stakeholder group comprised of
women veterans, currently serving military personnel,

5

and experts including clinical, academic, and support
practitioners. The group included 12 policy and practice partners from the UK (n = 7), Australia (n = 2),
Canada (n = 2), and New Zealand (n = 1). The stakeholder group was asked to anonymously prioritize
topics for inclusion in the introductory and advanced
courses, as well as providing recommendations on
delivery modality (e.g. self-directed versus live seminar learning) and terminology preferences (e.g. the
acceptability of the term ‘MST’). Stakeholders also
completed a semi-structured questionnaire following
course testing, with feedback on usability, acceptability, design, and content.

2.3. Course content
2.3.1. Course 1: Introduction to women veterans’
experiences and needs
Course 1 was a 10 min, online, self-guided, foundational knowledge course. It explored the unique
experiences of UK women veterans, challenges faced
during military service, global conceptualizations of
MST, and issues related to women veteran’s mental
health and healthcare. Each topic included a brief
true-or-false quiz to consolidate learning. Four trueor-false questions were asked following each topic,
resulting in a total of 12 questions across Course
1. True-or-false quizzes were chosen because this
method of consolidation provides a frictionless
method of engaging participants across learning
materials (Uner et al., 2022), compatible with the
WordPress content management system used to host
the online education programme. Courses 2 and 3
were both advertised on completion, and all attendees
confirmed their consent to be contacted and provided
informed consent for their data to be used under the
privacy policy.
2.3.2. Course 2: Advanced understanding of
women veterans – how services can better meet
their needs
Course 2 was a 2 h live online workshop, facilitated by
members of the project team (DD and GMC), focusing on addressing barriers to engagement with support services among women veterans by enhancing
knowledge among veteran specialist providers and
developers (e.g. veteran charities) and non-specialist
healthcare providers (e.g. family doctors). The workshop contextualized and summarized the evidence
base, explored women veterans’ experiences accessing
healthcare services, and presented evidence-based
considerations for promoting service engagement.
During workshops, attendees were encouraged to
engage in discussions on the material covered and
share their own professional experiences of working
in the sector.

6

D. DRYDEN ET AL.

2.3.3. Course 3: Advanced understanding of
women veterans plus cognitive processing
therapy (CPT) training
Course 3 consisted of a truncated, 1 h long version of
Course 2 plus foundational CPT training, delivered
online over 2 days to appropriately qualified professionals working with veterans. Course material
included a series of training videos and written content, developed and delivered by two clinical experts
in CPT. Training covered the theory underlying
CPT, session-by-session review of the CPT protocol
with examples specific to MST, common challenges
to implementation, and strategies to overcome challenges, such as clinical adherence and managing
comorbidities (Resick et al., 2024).
2.4. Dissemination
The programme was disseminated using a multi-pathway outreach strategy. This included targeted promotion via social media platforms, network
dissemination from the stakeholder group, and direct
contact with relevant organizations, including UK military charities, healthcare professional bodies, and
veteran-focused employers. Prospective audiences
were identified based on their professional relevance
to the programme’s objectives; outreach was conducted
primarily through e-mail. Prospective audiences were
guided to the website. All users were requested to complete Course 1 and then register their subsequent interest in Course 2 or Course 3. Those who indicated an
interest in Course 2 were invited to attend by e-mail.
Appropriately qualified mental health professionals
who registered their interest in Course 3 were invited
to attend the CPT training.
2.5. Data collection and analysis
Qualitative measures of participant demographics,
location, and occupational details were recorded at
sign-up for all courses. A total of 681 individuals
signed up to Course 1, of whom 526 completed the
full course and provided response data, representing
an attrition rate of 22.76%.
For Course 2, 0.55% demographic data were
recorded as ‘unknown’ owing to participants attending the live online sessions anonymously. Missing
demographic data were also recorded for Course 3
(5%), again categorized as ‘unknown’. Qualitative
and quantitative analyses were conducted using available data only. Attendees’ qualitative feedback was collected at the end of all courses via semi-structured
online questionnaires, assessing the appropriateness
of each course content and ongoing applicability to
attendees’ professional role (Appendix A).
Qualitative feedback from the post-training survey
in Course 3 additionally focused on factors influencing

CPT implementation. Responses were analysed using
a manifest content analysis framework, chosen for its
flexibility as a deductive or inductive analytical
approach and its suitability for use with open-ended
questionnaire data (Bengtsson, 2016). A manifest
approach was used to explore clinicians’ surface-level
perspectives in response to the questions asked; manifest content analysis is concerned with ‘What has been
said?’ and during data analysis stays close to the text,
often using the participants’ words to describe what
is visible to the researcher (Berg, 2002). Response
data were read for familiarization, and meaning
units were extracted, condensed, and coded inductively, whereby the coding list was created during
data analysis. A code list was created, and frequently
occurring codes or related codes were organized into
subthemes, which were organized into main themes.
Categorization modifications were made subject to
peer consultation (DD and GMC). The resulting
themes and subthemes were discussed among the
research team for refinement before consensus was
reached (Table 2).
In addition, self-efficacy in delivering CPT for trainees on Course 3 was assessed pre-training and
3 months post-training, using a modified item from
the therapist’s self-efficacy measure by Pace et al.
(2021). Responses were collected via an online semistructured questionnaire. Trainees were asked ‘How
confident are you currently delivering CPT?’
Responses were scored on a four-point scale: Not at
all confident (1), A little confident (2), Quite confident
(3), Very confident (4). Quantitative data were analysed using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, whereas
qualitative data were analysed using manifest content
analysis (Bengtsson, 2016). Descriptive statistics were
reported for all demographic and outcome measures
as appropriate, and across time-points. Analysis was
performed using IBM SPSS 29.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk,
NY, USA).

3. Results
3.1. Course 1: Introduction to women veterans’
experiences and needs
A total of 526 professionals completed Course 1.
Attendees represented a range of service organizations
and sectors, almost one-third had served in the military (30.03%), most worked with armed forces veterans or for an organization working with veterans
(96.76%), and 192 attendees (36.50%) were registered
mental health professionals. The majority (79.28%)
were from England; numbers across Wales (7.98%)
and Northern Ireland (2.85%) were representative of
the UK population, although attendance from Scotland was lower than anticipated (8.37%). Mean quiz
percentage correctness showed a progressive increase

EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTRAUMATOLOGY

across the three quizzes (Quiz 1: 76.7%; Quiz 2: 81.9%;
Quiz 3: 92.3%).
After completion, 92.39% indicated that they would
recommend the course to a colleague and 92.20% indicated that they found it useful and informative. Openended response options for further thoughts and feedback suggested that the course was generally well
received: ‘I have worked with female veterans and
have found this research to be very relevant to each
case. This course has given me more insight into
what female veterans face during service and just
how much they can be impacted. A very enlightening
course’; ‘I think everyone who has any contact with
women veterans should have access to this very informative course’.
3.2. Course 2: Advanced understanding of
women veterans – how services can better meet
their needs
The 2 h workshop was delivered 14 times, with a total
of 363 professionals attending, 238 (65.56%) of whom
had previously completed Course 1. The intended target audience of veteran specialist providers and nonspecialist healthcare providers was reached, with
82.92% of live session attendees representing these
occupational groups. As with Course 1, most attendees
were based in the UK (90.35%), with limited numbers
from Scotland (2.20%, n = 8). One webinar delivered
to a Canadian cohort accounted for 8.82% (n = 32)
attendees from outside the UK.
A small number of attendees (14.2%, n = 46) completed the voluntary feedback at the end of the live
workshop. When asked whether they found the
workshop useful and whether they were likely to
apply the knowledge from the workshop in their professional work, the majority agreed (88.10% and
88.09%, respectively). All respondents agreed that
the strategies and considerations for engaging and
supporting women veterans presented were feasible
and practical within their organization or practice,
and 90.47% indicated that they would recommend
the course to a colleague. Open-ended response
options for further thoughts and feedback indicated
that the course was generally well received: ‘The discussion was interesting especially because there were
people from a variety of backgrounds and hearing
other points of view and knowledge shared was
rewarding’; ‘This workshop gave me a better understanding of the needs and experiences of women
veterans, which has improved my understanding of
what we may need to do to meet the needs of our
female veterans’.
Course 2 materials were made available as a selfguided course in response to requests from attendees
of the live sessions for continued access to the
resources (Table 1).

3.3. Course 3: Advanced understanding of
women veterans plus cognitive processing
therapy (CPT) training – quantitative results
Two cohorts of clinicians were trained, resulting in a
total of 98 UK clinicians working across 34 organizations providing UK clinical services trained in CPT
(Table 1).
A total of 57 clinicians completed the first CPT
training. Most were female (87.72%, n = 50) and had
over 5 years’ experience working with PTSD
(71.93%, n = 47). Half had at least one woman veteran
currently on their caseload (50%, n = 29) and six clinicians held supervisory or lead roles within their service. Pre-training, 10.53% (n = 6) had used CPT over
the previous 3 months, although none had used it to
treat PTSD related to MST in women veterans.
Cohort 1 clinicians were followed up 3 months
after training; 68.4% (n = 39) responded to the survey,
but reasons were not specified for those who did not
complete the measures. Seventeen clinicians reported
using CPT after training, five of whom indicated
using CPT to treat PTSD related to MST in women
veterans. Of the clinicians who had not used CPT (n
= 22), most described not having the opportunity to
implement CPT with their current caseload as the
reason for this (n = 14) (see Table 2 for further details).
A Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated that clinician self-reported confidence was significantly higher
3 months post-training (Md = 3.00, n = 39) compared
to pre-training (Md = 2.00, n = 39, z = −4.756, p
< .001), with a large effect size (r = 0.915). The mean
increase in confidence was 1.00 (SE = 0.12). None
reported a decrease, 12 reported no change, and 27
reported increased confidence.
Owing to the high demand for CPT places, a second
cohort of clinicians was trained to further increase
capacity. Cohort 2 included 41 clinicians; most were
female (73.17%, n = 30) and had over 5 years’ experience working with PTSD (56.09%, n = 23). Over
one-third had at least one woman veteran currently
on their caseload (39.02%, n = 16), and over half of
clinicians (51.22%, n = 21) held supervisory or lead
roles within their service. Pre-training, 19.51% (n =
8) had used CPT over the previous 3 months, although
only one had used it to treat PTSD related to MST in
women veterans. For cohort 2, the eligibility criteria
were extended to include clinicians who work with
veterans of all genders, (not exclusively women veterans) to further increase UK clinical capacity.

Clinicians’ perceptions of CPT varied. These coalesced

3.4.3. Theme 3: CPT in a service system
Clinicians discussed using CPT at the service system
level. Two subthemes were identified: (1) lack of
resources and opportunities to use CPT; and (2)
embedding CPT into a service system.

3.4.2.1. Subtheme 1: Clinicians’ perception of CPT as
suitable for their patients. Clinicians who had not had
an opportunity to implement CPT in the 3 months
post-training discussed their intention to use CPT
and perceived the modality as suitable for future use.
One participant described CPT as a ‘Really good
approach which I hope to use as soon as an opportunity arises’ (P13).
Clinicians who had the opportunity to use CPT in
the 3 months post-training discussed the benefits
and challenges of the therapy in practice, particularly
with veteran groups. Clinicians valued CPT for its
effectiveness with shame and guilt: ‘When working
with guilt and shame-based memories, I really like
working with CPT’ (P9) and ‘Although CPT requires
more prep than other trauma-focused protocols, I
really enjoy using the model’ (P10). Positive patient
outcomes were discussed, including improved patient
outcome scores and patients getting along well with
the therapeutic process.
3.4.2.2. Subtheme 2: Clinicians’ perception of CPT as
not suitable for their patients. Patient-centred challenges to implementing CPT were discussed, including logistical challenges; for example, ‘they are not
always able to commit to sessions on a regular
basis’ (P27), and the need for patients to have a certain level of written ability to engage with the worksheets. Other reasons clinicians reported not using
CPT included the perception that it was not suited
to individuals on their caseload, who were then allocated to alternative treatment modalities. One clinician perceived that their patients’ needs were
‘Better addressed with a more elective modality’
(P38), although the modality in question was not
stated.

3.4.3.1. Subtheme 1: Lack of resources and opportunities to use CPT. Clinicians identified service system-level barriers as the reason they were unable to
implement CPT post-training. Resource constraints
hindering CPT delivery included a lack of access to
the latest manuals: ‘We still do not have access to
the manuals to aid practice and consolidate learning’
(P20), whereas others reported not having the opportunity to implement CPT with their current caseload.
For example, patients who may have benefited from
CPT were ‘already on a treatment plan with other
treatment methods’ (P33). Furthermore, some clinicians in lead roles reported having a limited caseload
and reduced patient contact, as their responsibilities
shifted their focus from direct CPT delivery to clinical
supervision and support: ‘[I have] not worked with a
veteran in this time as I have a limited caseload due
to leadership responsibilities’ (P24).
3.4.3.2. Subtheme 2: Embedding CPT into a system.
Some clinicians described a ripple effect of the training, leading to wider team development discussions
and service system growth in some cases. Knowledge
sharing and advocacy for CPT within services was
reported; clinicians discussed promoting and disseminating information about CPT during supervision and
training, and among professional networks: ‘I will
shortly be delivering teaching to trainee clinical psychologists about working with military veterans in
which I will include information about CPT’ (P35).
Further organizational investment in training and service developments included colleagues undertaking
CPT training to build service pathways; one clinician
wrote, ‘I have seen an increase in referrals for CPT
and the lead psychologist has since completed training
herself and is looking at getting funding for the other
psychologists in the team to get trained in it’ (P32).
Clinicians highlighted the value of ongoing training,
with both new – ‘The training was amazing I would

4. Discussion
This paper outlines the three-tiered online education
and training programme developed to enhance professional knowledge and improve service support for
UK women veterans, specifically those who have
experienced MST. Guided by KMb theory, which
uses research evidence to inform real-world impact,
the programme formed part of a wider KMb initiative
and was operationalized in line with the KTA framework (Field et al., 2014; Graham et al., 2006). A
mixed-methods evaluation of attendee feedback across
all three courses indicated that the programme successfully enhanced professional knowledge. The
courses were well received, 98 clinicians were trained
in CPT, and the evidence-based service adaptations
and considerations proposed in Course 2 were perceived to be practical, relevant, and implementable
by those who completed the feedback survey. Positive
feedback on Course 2 prompted the research team to
convert the live sessions into self-guided materials,
which remain available online alongside Course 1, to
support sustained knowledge use and growing participation beyond the end of the current project.
4.1. KMb frameworks and questions of impact
The KTA framework provided an effective scaffold
throughout the project, supporting the interrogation
and operationalization of each stage, while maintaining a clear focus on outcomes. The framework linked
the early research evidence on UK women veterans
through to the education programme. This process
involved translating evidence into targeted problems
and subsequent solutions while moving from knowledge creation to the action cycle. Stakeholder co-production also ensured that the programme was adapted
and implemented in a manner appropriate to the context. However, notable limitations remain.
Phipps et al. (2016) criticise the KTA framework
because it does not explicitly define the end goal of
the KMb process. They argue that KMb is concerned
with sharing knowledge to ultimately support meaningful change and create impact beyond the mere creation of interventions. In their conceptualization,
impact can include social, economic, and health
benefits, and media and public awareness, as well as
addressing specific vulnerabilities. Nonetheless, assessing and measuring what constitutes impact raises several issues. For example, the current study can be
viewed as a patient-mediated intervention, as it aims

to improve veteran health outcomes indirectly by
changing the knowledge and behaviour of health professionals (Stacey & Hill, 2013). However, interventions such as training and clinical capacity building
cannot be viewed in isolation outside the context(s)
in which they are ultimately delivered and actioned.
The professionals who engaged with the education
programme worked across different organizations,
structures, and contexts; therefore, ongoing monitoring of whether new knowledge was embedded in
their daily practice is challenging.
Rutter et al. (2017) argue that rather than concentrating on whether an intervention fixes a problem,
the focus should be on whether and how an intervention contributes to reshaping wider systems in a desirable manner. This more holistic approach promotes a
move towards continual KMb that ‘develops’ rather
than ‘builds’ capacity and knowledge by engaging participants at different levels: as individuals, groups, and
organizations (Kislov et al., 2014). Viewed through
this lens, although participant numbers from Scotland
were comparatively low, at less than 10% of attendees
across Course 1 (n = 42) and Course 2 (n = 7), these
attendees were predominantly engaged in policy and
service design roles at a time when services across
the nation were under review and redesign. As such,
the impact of the educational programme may be
greater than the numbers indicate, and the longerterm impact of the education programme in a Scottish
context may yet be realized. The inclusion of international participants may also result in farther-reaching impact, once knowledge has been translated to
their specific national contexts. However, assessing
this requires in-depth, longitudinal follow-up.
Finally, the KTA framework underplays the role of
so-called ‘knowledge brokers’, whose role is to promote the mobilization of evidence (Davies et al.,
2015). In the current study, the research team acted
as an initial broker, advocating for and demonstrating
evidence-based practice, facilitating the building of
professional networks through the live workshops,
and recruiting participants. Notably, the decision to
continue to make Course 1 and an adapted self-guided
Course 2 freely available beyond the stipulated end of
the project was made in response to requests from participants who were developing their own KMb projects and wanted to use the materials as signposts,
thus assuming the role of brokers.
However, comparatively few participants came
from outside veteran-specific support organizations,
potentially limiting the project’s wider impact. While
outreach efforts were made, engagement from veteran
employers, for example, remained limited. This highlights a continuing gap in engagement and remains a
priority area for future initiatives. Although successful
knowledge brokering may have common features irrespective of context (Phipps et al., 2017), moving

EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTRAUMATOLOGY

beyond one’s own disciplinary boundaries into unfamiliar domains such as political or social policy can
be challenging (MacKillop et al., 2020). Doing so
requires clear guidance in the form of operationalizable KMb frameworks, potentially including more
overt benchmarking of project impact.
4.2. Implementing and promoting change: CPT
clinical capacity building
CPT is a gold-standard treatment, and the structured
protocol requires the use of many clinical skills
throughout therapy (usually 12 sessions) (Resick
et al., 2024). Cohort 1 clinicians who completed CPT
training reported significantly higher self-efficacy in
delivering CPT 3 months post-training compared to
pre-training. Five clinicians had applied CPT to treat
PTSD related to MST in women veterans during this
period. Although modest, these numbers reflect the
early stages of implementation within clinical practice.
CPT was also used more broadly across clinicians’ varied caseloads, including with male veterans and other
blue-light service populations, demonstrating wider
clinical impacts.
Notably, the ‘events in systems’ approach to KMb
acknowledges that change requires not just the intervention itself, but also an appreciation that the context
in which it is delivered may aid or hinder impact (Skivington et al., 2021). This approach includes wider,
interlinked questions around acceptability, implementational considerations, cost-effectiveness, and scalability. Importantly, positive impact is viewed as
obtaining information that will be useful to aid
decision making and subsequent, future work. In
line with this perspective, the current study collected
qualitative data exploring clinicians’ experiences
using CPT, to generate context-sensitive insights
into barriers, facilitators, and implementation considerations beyond intervention effectiveness.
Clinicians acknowledged the effectiveness of CPT
for addressing feelings of shame and guilt (LoSavio
et al., 2023; Resick et al., 2002). Service system-level
barriers to implementation included limited opportunities to use CPT and resource limitations. However, those who had not yet had the chance to use
CPT expressed their intention to do so in the future,
underscoring the importance of longer-term evaluation of evidence-based therapeutic implementation
service systems. For individuals who had not encountered service system-level barriers, clinicians’ confidence and perception of CPT, factors that are
known to shape implementation (Damschroder
et al., 2009; LoSavio et al., 2019), impacted its use.
Ongoing training and supervision were described as
essential. This aligns with work by Pace et al.
(2021), who found that post-training consultation
and ongoing support improved clinicians’ self-

11

efficacy in delivering CPT, which was significantly
associated with implementation.
Attendees reported actively disseminating CPT
knowledge within their organization, which in some
cases led to service system developments and the
accommodation of CPT in clinical pathways. Six
attendees held clinical lead roles, which limited their
opportunities to directly implement CPT owing to
smaller caseloads and competing responsibilities, but
also enabled them to support other clinicians in delivering CPT. Notably, the second cohort of clinicians
trained included a higher number of individuals in
supervisory or lead roles. Training individuals in leadership positions has been shown to promote treatment fidelity (the degree of adherence to and
competence in delivering a protocol) (Godley et al.,
2011). The provision of such training in this study
may therefore be considered strategically valuable for
increasing service capacity, addressing barriers to
implementation (e.g. clinician confidence), and facilitating the organizational adoption of evidence-based
interventions.
4.3. Implications for future work
Captured within the feedback from attendees on the
education programme was a desire for the experiences
of men to be included as part of the project. In
response, a factsheet on MST was developed and
included on the website. It provides an overview of
MST in relation to men and women veterans in the
UK. Although women veterans may be at higher risk
of experiencing MST, owing to the greater number
of serving men in the military absolute numbers of
those who have experienced such incidents may be
comparable (Ministry of Defence, 2025). Underreporting of MST remains an issue irrespective of gender, and future research should look towards
strengthening the evidence base on men’s experiences,
with the aim of improving support for all veterans who
have experienced MST.
The authors do not claim that the current project
resolves all issues. Rather, they view it as a step in
the right direction, whereby the process of evaluating
and learning from equivocal findings to stimulate
further research can positively generate momentum
towards progress (Skivington et al., 2021). The education programme represents a meaningful step
towards improving service provision for UK women
veterans affected by MST. However, ensuring
improved access to effective, evidence-based psychological care for women veterans who have experienced
MST undoubtedly extends beyond the scope of a
single educational and clinical capacity-building intervention. Achieving this goal requires broad, multifaceted adaptive change across interrelated service systems, encompassing policy makers as well as actors

from the public, private, and third sectors (Rutter
et al., 2017).
4.4. Strengths and limitations
A key strength of this study is that co-production with
women veterans was central to the project, to ensure
that the research processes and outputs were informed
by lived experience, particularly given the limited evidence base outside the US context. The stakeholder
group played a crucial role in informing the education
programme and ensuring its relevance to the target
population. Although evidence and action from international partners can be transferable, care was taken to
adapt the programme’s content to the UK context.
The inclusion of both UK and international stakeholders represents a key strength of the programme;
however, future similar initiatives should continue to
ensure that appropriate contextual adaptations are
made.
The choice to include true-or-false quizzes to
consolidate online learning materials in Course 1
represents a limitation, as evidence suggests that
alternative methods such as multiple choice may
yield better learning outcomes (Hildenbrand &
Wiley, 2025). However, true-or-false options
were selected to support user engagement and minimize the time required to complete the online
course materials. Future similar programmes
may wish to consider alternative consolidation
approaches that more effectively balance efficiency
with retention.
The iterative nature of this work and the responsiveness to participant feedback have strengthened
the relevance and utility of the education programme.
Consistent with the KTA framework, this adaptive
approach supported the development of a self-guided
version of Course 2, and the expansion of available
places on CPT training courses for UK clinicians. Eligibility criteria for the second cohort of CPT trainees
was broadened to include clinicians working with
veterans of any gender, further increasing UK clinical
capacity in CPT. The inclusion of the factsheet, alongside the extension of training to clinicians working
with veterans of all genders, reflects a recognition
that MST can be experienced by any member of the
armed forces, irrespective of age, rank, or gender,
thus broadening the scope of the programme to
enhance awareness for all individuals who may have
experienced MST.
Evidence suggests that implementing new training
into existing services takes time, and embedding new
knowledge or treatment modalities such as CPT
within a service system, can take 6–12 months or
longer, suggesting that the 3 month follow-up period
may be insufficient to assess the long-term impacts

on clinical practice or to observe broader servicewide or policy-level changes (Cook et al., 2020; Wiltsey Stirman et al., 2017). Future research should
explore the impact of such programmes longitudinally
to capture sustained impacts.
More widely, the authors are sensitive to the view
that, because the majority of participants were from
clinical or support settings, the project could be considered translational research manifesting as continual
professional development, rather than KMb, which
aims to cast a wider net of influence (Graham et al.,
2006). Nonetheless, the efforts to include nonveteran-specific audiences, albeit limited in number,
as well as different courses targeting specific groups,
can be viewed positively.

5. Conclusion
This paper describes a co-produced KMb initiative
that successfully operationalized the principles of the
KTA framework to enhance professional understanding of and increase support for UK women veterans.
The online education programme addressed an
important knowledge gap. To date, 684 individuals,
primarily professionals working with veterans in the
UK, have engaged with the programme, and numbers
continue to increase across Courses 1 and 2, which
remain available online to sustain knowledge use.
Course 3 increased clinical capacity for CPT delivery
in the UK, and barriers and facilitators to CPT
implementation discussed 3 months post-training
aligned with existing literature on clinicians’ perceptions of the modality and the importance of ongoing
supervision and training when embedding evidencebased therapies in service systems. Ultimately, this
work represents a model for translating research into
practice and highlights the potential for structured
KMb approaches to drive systemic and policy-level
change in veteran care. The initiative shows that
meaningful impact can be achieved in the short term
while simultaneously laying the foundations for sustained, multi-sector progress to better support
women veterans in the future.

candidate: This paper describes a three-part online education and training program designed to enhance professional knowledge and improve support for UK women veterans who have experienced military sexual trauma (MST). Guided by knowledge mobilization (KMb) theory and the Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework, the program aimed to address gaps in service provider understanding and increase clinical capacity for evidence-based treatments, particularly cognitive processing therapy (CPT). The study involved 684 participants, including healthcare professionals, veteran specialists, and policy makers, who engaged with three courses: an introductory course on women veterans’ experiences, an advanced course on service adaptations, and a CPT training course. Mixed-methods data were collected, with quantitative analysis showing a significant increase in self-efficacy in delivering CPT among participants three months post-training (p < .001, r = 0.915). Qualitative feedback highlighted clinicians’ confidence in CPT, perceptions of its suitability for different patient groups, and challenges in implementation due to resource limitations and lack of training. The study found that the program successfully enhanced professional knowledge and supported the development of evidence-based practices, though limitations include the need for ongoing monitoring of long-term impact and broader engagement beyond veteran-specific organizations. The initiative demonstrates how research can be translated into real-world impact for military populations, emphasizing the value of co-produced KMb approaches.

ABSTRACT

ARTICLE HISTORY

Background: Military sexual trauma (MST) disproportionately impacts women veterans
globally. UK research highlights that these in-service experiences may contribute to unique
mental and physical health needs. Yet, service providers are often perceived to be unaware
of and unable to meet these needs.
Objective: To evaluate a national training programme that synthesised evidence to support UK
women veterans. Situated within a wider knowledge mobilization (KMb) initiative and guided
by the Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework, a three-part programme was developed for
different professional audiences to enhance understanding of and support for women
veterans.
Method: Co-produced and grounded in KMb theory. Course 1 aimed to enhance knowledge of
women veterans’ health needs. Course 2 targeted healthcare professionals and veteran
specialist providers, exploring evidence-based considerations for promoting service
engagement. Course 3 aimed to increase UK clinical capacity in the best-evidenced
treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder associated with MST in women veterans,
through training mental health professionals in cognitive processing therapy (CPT). Mixedmethods data were collected from all programme attendees. CPT attendees completed preand 3-month post-training measures; quantitative data were analysed using a Wilcoxon
signed-rank test and qualitative data using manifest content analysis.
Results: Course 1 was completed by 526 individuals, 363 completed Course 2, and 98
completed Course 3. Course 3 attendees were split across two cohorts (n = 57; n = 41).
Compared with pre-training, 3-month post-training self-efficacy in delivering CPT across
cohort one increased significantly (p < .001, r = 0.915). Content analysis identified three
themes: (1) Clinician confidence delivering CPT; (2) Clinicians’ perceptions of CPT; and (3)
CPT in a service system.
Conclusions: The education programme addressed gaps in UK service provider knowledge
and increased CPT clinical capacity. The wider KMb initiative demonstrates how research can
be translated into impact for military populations and highlights the value of co-produced
KMb approaches.

1. Background
Military sexual trauma (MST) is a continuum of violence from sexual harassment and bullying to sexual
assault, perpetrated by serving personnel on other service members during military service (Herriott et al.
2024). Although there is currently no universally
accepted definition of MST, it has been found to disproportionately impact women across military health
research globally (Buyse et al., 2023; Moreau et al.,
2021; Mota et al., 2023). A US meta-analysis found
that 38.4% of serving and formerly serving women
reported having experienced MST, over nine times
higher than that reported by men (3.9%) (Wilson,
2018). While both men and women report experiencing MST, the higher number of serving men means
that absolute numbers may be comparable, although
underreporting remains a prevailing issue for all
(Ministry of Defence, 2019, 2021). MST has been
associated with a plethora of negative health outcomes, including physical pain (Shapiro et al., 2023),
gastrointestinal problems (Pulverman & Creech,
2021), and symptoms of anxiety and depression (MacDermid et al., 2025). In women veterans specifically,
MST has been identified as a potentially leading contributor to military-service linked post-traumatic
stress disorder (PTSD) (Campbell & Murphy, 2023;
Surís et al., 2004).
Despite the commonalities evidenced across different militaries, the world’s armed forces are not homogeneous. Therefore, it is necessary to understand the
impacts of MST within specific national veteran populations (Godier-McBard et al., 2021). In the UK, a
veteran is defined someone who has completed at
least one full day in the armed forces and is no longer
serving (Burdett et al., 2012). UK veteran health
research has predominantly focused on the male
veteran majority, although there are estimated to be
over 250,000 women veterans, representing approximately 13% of the total veteran population (National

Records of Scotland, 2024; Office for National Statistics, 2021). With a target to reach 30% inflow of
women to the military by 2030, the number of
women veterans in future years is expected to increase,
alongside the need to better understand and support
this group through and beyond military service (Ministry of Defence, 2022). With international evidence
indicating that MST is likely to be a significant contributor to poor mental health in women veterans, there
is a need to build evidence-based interventions and
support provision for UK women who have experienced MST.

1.1. Moving from research to action
Evidence-based practice integrates research, clinical
expertise, and contextual understanding of patient
groups to optimize outcomes through robust, consistent, and cost-effective care (Cook et al., 2017). This
requires the transfer of research findings into practice,
variously referred to as knowledge transfer,
implementation science, and knowledge exchange, to
name a few. There are myriad extant models to
describe this process of ‘closing the gap’ between
research and its real-world operationalization and
implementation (Davies et al., 2015; Strifler et al.,
2018). Current knowledge mobilization (KMb) (the
authors’ preferred term) models emphasize a non-linear set of stages that embed research evidence into
practice within healthcare and societal ‘systems’ (Durrant et al., 2024).
KMb approaches are unstandardized and iterative
in nature, although core functions include ‘dissemination and engagement of academic research beyond
that made possible by traditional forms of scholarly
communication’ (Phipps, 2011) and capacity building,
which serves to augment the capability of organizations to achieve and sustain longer term objectives
(Bate et al., 2004). Co-production and co-design are

EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTRAUMATOLOGY

also commonly used to bridge the knowledge gap,
enhance acceptability among policy makers, increase
relevance to target populations, and improve the likelihood of successful implementation within service
systems (Grindell et al., 2022).
The most widely used KMb model is Graham and
colleagues’ Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework
(Field et al., 2014; Graham et al., 2006), which divides
the process into two linked concepts (Figure 1). The
first concept – knowledge creation – is concerned
with tailoring and refining information to be of increasing utility. This encompasses three stages: gathering
knowledge from primary research (‘knowledge
inquiry’); interpretation of primary research through
syntheses such as systematic reviews (‘knowledge synthesis’); and finally, presenting this synthesized knowledge in accessible, audience-appropriate formats to
promote evidence-based decision making (‘knowledge
tools and products’). The second concept – the action
cycle – details the activities required to implementation

3

this knowledge. This is split into seven stages: identify a
problem that needs addressing, and identify, review,
and select the knowledge or research relevant to the
problem; adapt the identified knowledge to the local
context; assess barriers to using the knowledge; select,
tailor, and implement interventions to promote the
use of knowledge; monitor knowledge use; evaluate
the outcomes of using the knowledge; and sustain
ongoing knowledge use. Although the KTA framework
describes two concepts and constituent stages, the
boundaries between each are seen as fluid, and action
phases need not be sequential or discrete.
This paper examines how the KTA framework was
applied to a series of interlinked projects focusing on
improving support for UK women veterans who
have experienced MST. It first outlines in brief the
knowledge creation stage, before detailing the application of the action cycle in designing, implementing,
and assessing interventions to help address the impact
of MST through KMb.

Figure 1. Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework stages and action taken.

4

D. DRYDEN ET AL.

1.1.1. Knowledge inquiry: building the evidence
base around MST
A cohort of 750 UK women veterans was recruited in
the largest study to date exploring their experiences
during military service and their current health
profile; for full methodology, see Hendrikx, Williamson, et al. (2021). The study identified a high prevalence of common mental health disorders (CMDs)
(28.6%) and probable PTSD (10.8%) in the cohort.
In addition, 23% reported having experienced sexual
harassment, 23% emotional bullying, and 5% sexual
abuse (Hendrikx, Williamson, & Murphy, 2021),
figures broadly comparable to other countries
(Wilson, 2018). Significant associations were found
between reporting a high number of adverse childhood experiences and experiencing MST (Williamson
et al., 2022). Crucially, MST was found to be significantly associated with increased odds of reporting
probable PTSD as a veteran (Hendrikx, Williamson,
& Murphy, 2021). Furthermore, using a checklist of
in-service challenging experiences co-produced with
women veterans and subject-matter experts, 42.7%
of the cohort reported that sexist assumptions were
made about them during their service and 40.1% felt
that they had to be better than their male colleagues
to receive the same recognition at work. These in-service challenges were also significantly associated with
an increased risk of reporting poor mental and physical health as a veteran (Baumann et al., 2022).
Additional analysis explored the impact of past
gender-based discrimination, such as forced discharge
for pregnancy and experiences of the so-called ‘gay
ban’ (Biscoe et al., 2024). These studies cumulatively
established an evidence base, which indicated that
UK women veterans experienced idiosyncratic, gender-based challenges during their military service
that were different from those of their male counterparts, and which were likely to contribute to poor
mental health as a veteran. MST specifically was
reported as a significant contributor. Accordingly,
the need to focus on MST as significant potential inservice adversity with long-term health implications
for UK women veterans was indicated.
1.1.2. Knowledge synthesis: exploring women
veterans’ needs and experiences
Further exploration of MST and resultant PTSD in UK
women veterans was conducted. In line with the KTA
framework, research questions were formulated
specifically relating to how support services could be
improved for women veterans. These focused on
what evidence-based treatments work and where systemic improvements could be made. A systematic
review of treatments specifically for PTSD related to
MST in women veterans found that cognitive processing therapy (CPT) was the best-evidenced current
treatment (Campbell, Biscoe, et al., 2024). CPT is

also a reccomended trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy under the National Institute for Health
and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines (NICE, 2018).
Furthermore, a subcohort of UK women veterans
from the first study with scores indicative of probable
PTSD was invited to take part in semi-structured
interviews exploring their experiences of accessing
psychological healthcare. Qualitative analysis showed
that women veterans reported facing similar barriers
to men veterans, such as stigma around help-seeking
(Randles & Finnegan, 2022), but that these were
exacerbated as the result of their minority status
(Campbell et al., 2025; Campbell, Perry, et al., 2024).
Additional salient barriers and facilitators included a
perceived lack of professional knowledge and awareness about women veterans’ needs and experiences,
the invalidation of specific service traumatic experiences such as MST, and gender discrimination in the
design, provision, and focus of veteran-specific services, which were viewed as catering for the male
majority (Campbell et al., 2025).
1.1.3. Knowledge tools and products: evidencebased recommendations for action
Drawing on the findings from the previous stages, core
recommendations were co-produced with expert stakeholders (veteran experts, healthcare professionals,
and women veterans with lived experience) to guide
future improvements in support for UK women veterans, and specifically those who had experienced MST
(Campbell & Murphy, 2023). Policy experts were
also engaged to ensure that recommendations were
applicable in the policy domain. These recommendations included:
.

.

.

Increase healthcare professionals’ awareness of
women veterans, their military service experiences,
and mental healthcare needs.
Address specific barriers to engagement for women
veterans within services, potentially through
bespoke service design, access, and treatment
pathways.
Ensure that the best evidence-based treatment is
available for women veterans who have experienced
MST.

1.1.4. The action cycle: the current study
The current study, guided by the KTA framework,
aimed to address each of the three evidence-based recommendations by mobilizing knowledge to improve
access to, and provision of, evidenced treatment and
support for UK women veterans who have experienced MST.
A three-tiered education and training programme
was developed as part of this action cycle. Course 1
aimed to enhance general knowledge about women

EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTRAUMATOLOGY

veterans’ mental health needs, and was aimed at anyone who may have professional contact with women
veterans. Course 2 targeted healthcare professionals
and veteran specialist providers, and included evidence-based considerations for promoting service
engagement. Since women veterans often seek support
for mental health difficulties from non-veteranspecific services, engaging these groups was prioritized
(Campbell & Murphy, 2023; Hooks et al., 2023). In
line with KMb theory, to sustain the longer-term
objective of the programme and ensure that best-evidenced support is available to women veterans in the
UK, Course 3 aimed to increase UK clinical capacity
in the best-evidenced treatment for PTSD associated
with MST in women veterans by providing fully
funded training places, for appropriately qualified
mental health professionals, in CPT (Campbell, Biscoe, et al., 2024).

2. Method
2.1. Overview
The KTA framework’s action cycle was used as a guide
(Figure 1) throughout the KMb process. The three evidence-based recommendations for action were
reframed as problems against which the evidence
base could be mobilized to provide a solution. In
response, an online three-tiered education and training programme was conceived, with each course
responding to one problem, and aimed at a specific
professional end-user group. These courses
comprised:
(1) an introductory course designed to raise basic
awareness of woman veterans’ needs and experiences, aimed at anybody who had professional
contact with women veterans
(2) an advanced course designed to explore how services can be adapted to be more accessible, welcoming, and appropriate to women veterans,
aimed at those working in veteran-specific services and healthcare providers
(3) training in CPT to increase UK clinical capacity in
the best-evidenced treatment for PTSD related to
MST in women veterans, for mental health professionals who work with women veterans.
To reduce barriers to access, the programme was
made freely available via an online open access website
(https://veterans.training).
2.2. Co-production stakeholder group
The programme content and structure were co-produced with a stakeholder group comprised of
women veterans, currently serving military personnel,

5

and experts including clinical, academic, and support
practitioners. The group included 12 policy and practice partners from the UK (n = 7), Australia (n = 2),
Canada (n = 2), and New Zealand (n = 1). The stakeholder group was asked to anonymously prioritize
topics for inclusion in the introductory and advanced
courses, as well as providing recommendations on
delivery modality (e.g. self-directed versus live seminar learning) and terminology preferences (e.g. the
acceptability of the term ‘MST’). Stakeholders also
completed a semi-structured questionnaire following
course testing, with feedback on usability, acceptability, design, and content.

2.3. Course content
2.3.1. Course 1: Introduction to women veterans’
experiences and needs
Course 1 was a 10 min, online, self-guided, foundational knowledge course. It explored the unique
experiences of UK women veterans, challenges faced
during military service, global conceptualizations of
MST, and issues related to women veteran’s mental
health and healthcare. Each topic included a brief
true-or-false quiz to consolidate learning. Four trueor-false questions were asked following each topic,
resulting in a total of 12 questions across Course
1. True-or-false quizzes were chosen because this
method of consolidation provides a frictionless
method of engaging participants across learning
materials (Uner et al., 2022), compatible with the
WordPress content management system used to host
the online education programme. Courses 2 and 3
were both advertised on completion, and all attendees
confirmed their consent to be contacted and provided
informed consent for their data to be used under the
privacy policy.
2.3.2. Course 2: Advanced understanding of
women veterans – how services can better meet
their needs
Course 2 was a 2 h live online workshop, facilitated by
members of the project team (DD and GMC), focusing on addressing barriers to engagement with support services among women veterans by enhancing
knowledge among veteran specialist providers and
developers (e.g. veteran charities) and non-specialist
healthcare providers (e.g. family doctors). The workshop contextualized and summarized the evidence
base, explored women veterans’ experiences accessing
healthcare services, and presented evidence-based
considerations for promoting service engagement.
During workshops, attendees were encouraged to
engage in discussions on the material covered and
share their own professional experiences of working
in the sector.

6

D. DRYDEN ET AL.

2.3.3. Course 3: Advanced understanding of
women veterans plus cognitive processing
therapy (CPT) training
Course 3 consisted of a truncated, 1 h long version of
Course 2 plus foundational CPT training, delivered
online over 2 days to appropriately qualified professionals working with veterans. Course material
included a series of training videos and written content, developed and delivered by two clinical experts
in CPT. Training covered the theory underlying
CPT, session-by-session review of the CPT protocol
with examples specific to MST, common challenges
to implementation, and strategies to overcome challenges, such as clinical adherence and managing
comorbidities (Resick et al., 2024).
2.4. Dissemination
The programme was disseminated using a multi-pathway outreach strategy. This included targeted promotion via social media platforms, network
dissemination from the stakeholder group, and direct
contact with relevant organizations, including UK military charities, healthcare professional bodies, and
veteran-focused employers. Prospective audiences
were identified based on their professional relevance
to the programme’s objectives; outreach was conducted
primarily through e-mail. Prospective audiences were
guided to the website. All users were requested to complete Course 1 and then register their subsequent interest in Course 2 or Course 3. Those who indicated an
interest in Course 2 were invited to attend by e-mail.
Appropriately qualified mental health professionals
who registered their interest in Course 3 were invited
to attend the CPT training.
2.5. Data collection and analysis
Qualitative measures of participant demographics,
location, and occupational details were recorded at
sign-up for all courses. A total of 681 individuals
signed up to Course 1, of whom 526 completed the
full course and provided response data, representing
an attrition rate of 22.76%.
For Course 2, 0.55% demographic data were
recorded as ‘unknown’ owing to participants attending the live online sessions anonymously. Missing
demographic data were also recorded for Course 3
(5%), again categorized as ‘unknown’. Qualitative
and quantitative analyses were conducted using available data only. Attendees’ qualitative feedback was collected at the end of all courses via semi-structured
online questionnaires, assessing the appropriateness
of each course content and ongoing applicability to
attendees’ professional role (Appendix A).
Qualitative feedback from the post-training survey
in Course 3 additionally focused on factors influencing

CPT implementation. Responses were analysed using
a manifest content analysis framework, chosen for its
flexibility as a deductive or inductive analytical
approach and its suitability for use with open-ended
questionnaire data (Bengtsson, 2016). A manifest
approach was used to explore clinicians’ surface-level
perspectives in response to the questions asked; manifest content analysis is concerned with ‘What has been
said?’ and during data analysis stays close to the text,
often using the participants’ words to describe what
is visible to the researcher (Berg, 2002). Response
data were read for familiarization, and meaning
units were extracted, condensed, and coded inductively, whereby the coding list was created during
data analysis. A code list was created, and frequently
occurring codes or related codes were organized into
subthemes, which were organized into main themes.
Categorization modifications were made subject to
peer consultation (DD and GMC). The resulting
themes and subthemes were discussed among the
research team for refinement before consensus was
reached (Table 2).
In addition, self-efficacy in delivering CPT for trainees on Course 3 was assessed pre-training and
3 months post-training, using a modified item from
the therapist’s self-efficacy measure by Pace et al.
(2021). Responses were collected via an online semistructured questionnaire. Trainees were asked ‘How
confident are you currently delivering CPT?’
Responses were scored on a four-point scale: Not at
all confident (1), A little confident (2), Quite confident
(3), Very confident (4). Quantitative data were analysed using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, whereas
qualitative data were analysed using manifest content
analysis (Bengtsson, 2016). Descriptive statistics were
reported for all demographic and outcome measures
as appropriate, and across time-points. Analysis was
performed using IBM SPSS 29.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk,
NY, USA).

3. Results
3.1. Course 1: Introduction to women veterans’
experiences and needs
A total of 526 professionals completed Course 1.
Attendees represented a range of service organizations
and sectors, almost one-third had served in the military (30.03%), most worked with armed forces veterans or for an organization working with veterans
(96.76%), and 192 attendees (36.50%) were registered
mental health professionals. The majority (79.28%)
were from England; numbers across Wales (7.98%)
and Northern Ireland (2.85%) were representative of
the UK population, although attendance from Scotland was lower than anticipated (8.37%). Mean quiz
percentage correctness showed a progressive increase

After completion, 92.39% indicated that they would

3.2. Course 2: Advanced understanding of
women veterans – how services can better meet
their needs
The 2 h workshop was delivered 14 times, with a total
of 363 professionals attending, 238 (65.56%) of whom
had previously completed Course 1. The intended target audience of veteran specialist providers and nonspecialist healthcare providers was reached, with
82.92% of live session attendees representing these
occupational groups. As with Course 1, most attendees
were based in the UK (90.35%), with limited numbers
from Scotland (2.20%, n = 8). One webinar delivered
to a Canadian cohort accounted for 8.82% (n = 32)
attendees from outside the UK.
A small number of attendees (14.2%, n = 46) completed the voluntary feedback at the end of the live
workshop. When asked whether they found the
workshop useful and whether they were likely to
apply the knowledge from the workshop in their professional work, the majority agreed (88.10% and
88.09%, respectively). All respondents agreed that
the strategies and considerations for engaging and
supporting women veterans presented were feasible
and practical within their organization or practice,
and 90.47% indicated that they would recommend
the course to a colleague. Open-ended response
options for further thoughts and feedback indicated
that the course was generally well received: ‘The discussion was interesting especially because there were
people from a variety of backgrounds and hearing
other points of view and knowledge shared was
rewarding’; ‘This workshop gave me a better understanding of the needs and experiences of women
veterans, which has improved my understanding of
what we may need to do to meet the needs of our
female veterans’.
Course 2 materials were made available as a selfguided course in response to requests from attendees
of the live sessions for continued access to the
resources (Table 1).

3.3. Course 3: Advanced understanding of
women veterans plus cognitive processing
therapy (CPT) training – quantitative results
Two cohorts of clinicians were trained, resulting in a
total of 98 UK clinicians working across 34 organizations providing UK clinical services trained in CPT
(Table 1).
A total of 57 clinicians completed the first CPT
training. Most were female (87.72%, n = 50) and had
over 5 years’ experience working with PTSD
(71.93%, n = 47). Half had at least one woman veteran
currently on their caseload (50%, n = 29) and six clinicians held supervisory or lead roles within their service. Pre-training, 10.53% (n = 6) had used CPT over
the previous 3 months, although none had used it to
treat PTSD related to MST in women veterans.
Cohort 1 clinicians were followed up 3 months
after training; 68.4% (n = 39) responded to the survey,
but reasons were not specified for those who did not
complete the measures. Seventeen clinicians reported
using CPT after training, five of whom indicated
using CPT to treat PTSD related to MST in women
veterans. Of the clinicians who had not used CPT (n
= 22), most described not having the opportunity to
implement CPT with their current caseload as the
reason for this (n = 14) (see Table 2 for further details).
A Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated that clinician self-reported confidence was significantly higher
3 months post-training (Md = 3.00, n = 39) compared
to pre-training (Md = 2.00, n = 39, z = −4.756, p
< .001), with a large effect size (r = 0.915). The mean
increase in confidence was 1.00 (SE = 0.12). None
reported a decrease, 12 reported no change, and 27
reported increased confidence.
Owing to the high demand for CPT places, a second
cohort of clinicians was trained to further increase
capacity. Cohort 2 included 41 clinicians; most were
female (73.17%, n = 30) and had over 5 years’ experience working with PTSD (56.09%, n = 23). Over
one-third had at least one woman veteran currently
on their caseload (39.02%, n = 16), and over half of
clinicians (51.22%, n = 21) held supervisory or lead
roles within their service. Pre-training, 19.51% (n =
8) had used CPT over the previous 3 months, although
only one had used it to treat PTSD related to MST in
women veterans. For cohort 2, the eligibility criteria
were extended to include clinicians who work with
veterans of all genders, (not exclusively women veterans) to further increase UK clinical capacity.

3.4.2. Theme 2: Clinicians’ perceptions of CPT
Clinicians’ perceptions of CPT varied. These coalesced

CPT as suitable for their patients; (2) clinicians’ perception of CPT as not suitable for their patients; and

3.4.3. Theme 3: CPT in a service system
Clinicians discussed using CPT at the service system
level. Two subthemes were identified: (1) lack of
resources and opportunities to use CPT; and (2)
embedding CPT into a service system.

3.4.2.1. Subtheme 1: Clinicians’ perception of CPT as
suitable for their patients. Clinicians who had not had
an opportunity to implement CPT in the 3 months
post-training discussed their intention to use CPT
and perceived the modality as suitable for future use.
One participant described CPT as a ‘Really good
approach which I hope to use as soon as an opportunity arises’ (P13).
Clinicians who had the opportunity to use CPT in
the 3 months post-training discussed the benefits
and challenges of the therapy in practice, particularly
with veteran groups. Clinicians valued CPT for its
effectiveness with shame and guilt: ‘When working
with guilt and shame-based memories, I really like
working with CPT’ (P9) and ‘Although CPT requires
more prep than other trauma-focused protocols, I
really enjoy using the model’ (P10). Positive patient
outcomes were discussed, including improved patient
outcome scores and patients getting along well with
the therapeutic process.
3.4.2.2. Subtheme 2: Clinicians’ perception of CPT as
not suitable for their patients. Patient-centred challenges to implementing CPT were discussed, including logistical challenges; for example, ‘they are not
always able to commit to sessions on a regular
basis’ (P27), and the need for patients to have a certain level of written ability to engage with the worksheets. Other reasons clinicians reported not using
CPT included the perception that it was not suited
to individuals on their caseload, who were then allocated to alternative treatment modalities. One clinician perceived that their patients’ needs were
‘Better addressed with a more elective modality’
(P38), although the modality in question was not
stated.

3.4.3.1. Subtheme 1: Lack of resources and opportunities to use CPT. Clinicians identified service system-level barriers as the reason they were unable to
implement CPT post-training. Resource constraints
hindering CPT delivery included a lack of access to
the latest manuals: ‘We still do not have access to
the manuals to aid practice and consolidate learning’
(P20), whereas others reported not having the opportunity to implement CPT with their current caseload.
For example, patients who may have benefited from
CPT were ‘already on a treatment plan with other
treatment methods’ (P33). Furthermore, some clinicians in lead roles reported having a limited caseload
and reduced patient contact, as their responsibilities
shifted their focus from direct CPT delivery to clinical
supervision and support: ‘[I have] not worked with a
veteran in this time as I have a limited caseload due
to leadership responsibilities’ (P24).
3.4.3.2. Subtheme 2: Embedding CPT into a system.
Some clinicians described a ripple effect of the training, leading to wider team development discussions
and service system growth in some cases. Knowledge
sharing and advocacy for CPT within services was
reported; clinicians discussed promoting and disseminating information about CPT during supervision and
training, and among professional networks: ‘I will
shortly be delivering teaching to trainee clinical psychologists about working with military veterans in
which I will include information about CPT’ (P35).
Further organizational investment in training and service developments included colleagues undertaking
CPT training to build service pathways; one clinician
wrote, ‘I have seen an increase in referrals for CPT
and the lead psychologist has since completed training
herself and is looking at getting funding for the other
psychologists in the team to get trained in it’ (P32).
Clinicians highlighted the value of ongoing training,
with both new – ‘The training was amazing I would
