state, particularly with respect to H3K27me3 methylation, differ markedly between females and males,
indicating a strong influence on the immune-reactive tumor phenotype.
Taken together, the findings from our study indicate that NK cell-related immune responses against
PDAC are stronger in females than in males in both in vitro and in vivo mouse models. Initial differences
in NK cell cytotoxicity appear to be primarily driven by epigenetic mechanisms that operate independently
of sex hormones.

Discussion
It is generally known that PDAC incidence and survival are worse for men than for women and that
women are able to mount a stronger immune response than men.13,37 NK cells are key mediators of
antitumor immunity and are known to exhibit sex-specific differences;14,68 however, whether this extends
to PDAC, potentially contributing to divergent PDAC pathologies between the sexes, has remained
unclear. This study focused on determining whether biological sex influences NK cell-mediated immunity
against pancreatic cancer in vitro and in vivo.
In this study, we used the mouse cell line Panc02 as a PDAC model. Although Panc02 was originally
described as male,57 karyotyping and RNA-seq revealed no Y-chromosomal features, indicating the loss of
sex-specific properties. Loss of the Y chromosome is a frequent event in human PDAC and in multiple
PDAC cell lines.69 In addition, Panc02 displays SMAD4 deficiency, which is described as a PDAC
hallmark,70 and expresses mild inflammatory features.57 Therefore, it represents a sex-neutral target
suitable for studying NK cell function in PDAC. The Panc02 cells not only proved to be a good model
in vitro but also in vivo. We established a syngeneic allograft mouse model by injecting Panc02 cells
subcutaneously into the right leg of male and female BL6 mice. The histological structure of the allograft
tumors was remarkably similar to that of human PDAC, as it included a complex tumor stroma infiltrated
with immune cells (e.g., TAMs, CAFs, and T and NK cells). A major advantage of the allograft model in
comparison with genetically engineered cancer models is the identical origin of the tumor cells, which is
consistent across age, sex, and individual properties of the mice. The context of studying sex-dependent
differences, therefore, allows maximal focus on infiltrating immune cells and the sex of the host. In
addition, in genetically engineered mouse models, tumors do not occur at exactly the same time in all
animals, and often progress before the immune system of the host is fully developed. With the allograft
model, we could ensure a uniform starting point for all animals, ensuring that each had a fully mature
immune system. This approach allowed us to isolate and focus solely on the sex-based differences, free
from any time-dependent biases. Future studies should involve an orthotopic injection of Panc02 cells into
the pancreas of male and female mice, as this could allow investigations into the impact of tumorigenesis
on the exocrine pancreatic function.71
In order to study sex-dependent differences in NK cell function, we isolated primary NK cells from male
and female BL6 mice to be used in subsequent killing assays. The primary NK cells were phenotypically
naïve after isolation, but transcriptomic analysis revealed subtle intrinsic sex-dependent differences in gene
regulation. We found that male NK cells expressed lower levels of H3K27me3-regulated genes, a difference
likely driven by reduced UTX activity. UTX was shown to influence NK cell cytotoxicity in a sexdependent manner.25 As an X-linked gene that escapes inactivation, UTX is expressed at higher levels
in females,25 facilitating the removal of repressive H3K27me3 and supporting sex-specific gene regulation.
The H3K27me3 pathway is known to regulate the activity of various immune cells in the context of
cancer.72 In addition, downregulated cytokine response signatures and upregulation of an IL-4/IL-10
program could be observed, suggesting a more immunosuppressive baseline in male NK cells.73 Our
findings are consistent with previous reports that describe an enhanced intrinsic cytotoxic capacity in
female NK cells.14,25
During cultures with and without Panc02 cells, we showed that IL-2 alone was capable of activating NK
cells. In turn, Panc02 cells dampened this activation, which was reflected in diminished surface densities of
the activating receptors NCR1 and NKG2D. Tumor cells employ various strategies to escape NK cellmediated responses; among these, the shedding of ligands to impair NKG2D-mediated activation is a wellcharacterized mechanism of immune evasion.74 NK cell maturation was evident in the killing assays, with
female NK cells displaying a slightly more advanced differentiation state in co-culture. Furthermore,

female NK cells respond more strongly to Panc02, and the enhanced immune response is driven
predominantly by tumor contact.54,73 In contrast, male NK cells are largely IL-2-driven and less responsive
to tumor cell-derived cues. These results were validated with another PDAC cell line (KPC3595), albeit the
differences were pronounced to a lesser extent because of its lower suitability as a killing target. Functional
killing assays with Panc02 cells revealed that female NK cells are able to kill more tumor cells, resulting in
slower tumor cell proliferation and higher tumor cell death over time. Importantly, the enhanced killing
capacity of female NK cells was independent of sex hormones. We observed slight initial differences in
hormone responses between freshly isolated male and female NK cells, which subsided after cultivation in
the absence of sex hormones. Notably, the differences in killing efficacy persisted, suggesting that systemic
hormonal signals may influence NK cells under physiological conditions but not after isolation in our
setting. Importantly, these findings were consistent across both primary NK cells and NK cell line-based
models using NK-92, supporting the conclusion that the observed enhanced cytotoxicity of female NK
cells can be attributed to stable epigenetic programs rather than hormonal influences.
The observed sex differences in vitro correlate with findings from the in vivo allograft setting,
reinforcing the relevance of NK cell-tumor interactions. Female tumors grow more slowly, which is
correlated with a higher NK cell infiltration. In line with these findings, previous studies have
demonstrated that the NK cell infiltration of tumors from PDAC patients is positively correlated
with survival.30,40 A decrease in peripheral NK cells was evident in female allografts, which was most
likely caused by enhanced NK cell migration to the tumor site. Following up from here, multiplex
spatial immunofluorescence staining and RNA-seq revealed differences in the overall tumor composition between males and females. Male tumors display a dense, compact architecture, including stiff
and tumor-promoting stroma, increased basal-like properties, and increased proliferative properties.
The male TME is characterized by the infiltration of immune-suppressive cell types, and NK cells are
characterized by reduced infiltration, activation, and cytotoxic function. In contrast, female tumors
showed a looser architecture, with less basal-like properties and reduced proliferation, leading to an
overall immune-permissive stroma with stronger immune response programs and infiltration of proinflammatory immune cells. The infiltrating NK cells were strongly activated and displayed high
cytotoxic activity. It is reasonable to assume that the loose, pro-inflammatory tumor structure in
female mice favors and facilitates NK cell infiltration, as well as other immune cells of the TME. In this
context, intrinsic differences in NK cell function collaborate with an environment conducive to NK
cells, leading to enhanced NK cell immunity in females in vivo. It must be said that, despite NK cells
constitute only a small fraction of the TME, they present some of the largest sex differences in terms of
their immigration and activation among infiltrating immune cells. In addition, their strong sexdependent regulation might be far more relevant in the context of naturally arising tumors than in
the high-dose allograft injection model, as they are crucial for the control of single transformed cells
and metastases.2 The data from this study support the conclusion that NK cells provide a sex-specific
contribution to anti-tumor immunity in concert with the TME and other immune cells. Nevertheless,
future NK cell-depletion studies will be needed to definitively delineate their causal role. Beyond this,
the greater pro-inflammatory TME of female mice, together with enhanced PD-L1 expression on
tumor cells, suggests a greater responsiveness of female allograft tumors to ICB, which was further
supported by the GSEA data. This suggests that sex contributes to the prognostic outcome of immune
therapies but likely acts in concert with additional influencing factors.64 Future studies should
therefore prioritize the analysis of clinical data from male and female patients undergoing immunotherapies in order to determine whether sex-specific differences are reflected in patient outcomes.
Large-scale pan-cancer bulk transcriptomic studies of human tumors have provided important insights
into sex-associated immune differences and offer a useful foundation for translational research.36 However,
bulk analyses can mask sex-specific effects within individual immune cell populations. Future studies
combining single-cell and spatial transcriptomic approaches may therefore be needed to more precisely
define sex-specific immune programs in the tumor microenvironment. Such analyses could help clarify
whether female PDAC patients differentially benefit from immune-based combination therapies when
stratified by sex-associated immune features, as suggested by mouse data.
Although we proved that initial sex-dependent differences in NK cell cytotoxicity are independent
of sex hormones in vitro, they must be considered in the in vivo setting. We did not monitor the

E. ARLT ET AL.

estrous cycle in female mice in order to assess general sex differences under standard laboratory
conditions. Additionally, including females at various cycle stages reflects natural biological variability. It is worth noting that hormone levels in females can vary more extensively across different life
stages than during the normal estrous cycle, and the variability introduced by the estrous cycle stage in
female mice is generally not greater than the variability observed among males.75 Nevertheless,
hormones may influence tumor architecture in vivo. In allograft tumors, we observed slightly
increased AR and ER responses in males. It should be noted that both estrogen and androgen response
gene sets include numerous genes involved in cell proliferation. Considering our data showing that
male tumors grow faster, this may therefore reflect, at least in part, variations in tumor proliferation
rates rather than direct effects of sex hormones. Nevertheless, future studies should involve allograft
models using gonadectomized mice to elucidate whether the observed differences in tumor composition persist independently of sex hormones.
Together, our study offers relevant insights into the sex-dependent regulation of NK cells in PDAC.
These findings indicate that the combination of initial enhanced NK cell function and NK cell-beneficial
tumor architecture in females results in superior NK cell-mediated tumor control in patients with PDAC.
This occurs within the context of a proinflammatory TME with enhanced immune cell infiltration,
potentially explaining the associations between female sex and reduced PDAC incidence and mortality.
Although hormones might play a role in in vivo, the observed in vitro differences in NK cell cytotoxicity
are most likely attributable to intrinsic (epigenetic) mechanisms. The definitive role of NK cells in our
in vivo setting remains to be elucidated, as further experiments, such as NK cell depletion experiments or
the use of NK cell-deficient mice, are needed to clarify this point. Although the mouse data reveal clear
patterns, the extent to which these findings apply to the much more heterogeneous human system still
needs to be determined. Sex-based disparities warrant increased consideration in clinical practice and
underscore the importance of considering biological sex as a variable in future research and targeted
therapy.

candidate: This study investigates the influence of biological sex on natural killer (NK) cell-mediated immunity against pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Using in vitro and in vivo models, the researchers found that female-derived NK cells exhibit superior cytotoxic activity and immune activation compared to male-derived NK cells. These findings were corroborated in a syngeneic allograft PDAC model, where female mice showed enhanced NK cell function and distinct tumor microenvironment (TME) characteristics that supported stronger NK cell activity. The study highlights that host sex significantly shapes the TME composition and architecture, with female tumors displaying a more immune-permissive environment and reduced proliferation. Female NK cells showed increased expression of genes associated with immune response and cytotoxicity, such as granzyme B, and exhibited enhanced antitumor activity independent of sex hormones. However, the study does not establish causality or clinical outcomes, and the observed associations are not definitive. Limitations include the use of a single cell line and the lack of direct clinical validation. The findings suggest that sex differences in NK cell function may differentially impact tumor control in PDAC, emphasizing the importance of considering sex as a biological variable in preclinical research.

ABSTRACT

ARTICLE HISTORY

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) ranks among the most aggressive malignancies and exhibits a higher prevalence and poorer prognosis in male patients. While both
the importance of natural killer (NK) cells in anti-tumor immunity and sex differences in
NK cell function are well established, the interplay between biological sex and NK cellmediated responses in PDAC has not been systematically addressed. Here, we provide
novel insights revealing that both the intrinsic cytotoxic capacity of NK cells and the
tumor microenvironment differ between sexes and jointly modulate anti-tumor immunity in PDAC. Using in vitro assays with primary NK cells from male and female mice, we
found that female-derived NK cells exhibit consistently superior cytotoxic activity and
immune activation. Importantly, these findings were reflected and even amplified
in vivo. In a syngeneic allograft PDAC model, female mice displayed enhanced NK
cell function, and female tumors exhibited distinct structural characteristics supporting
stronger NK cell activity. Notably, this occurred despite the use of the same cell line in
both sexes, indicating that host sex significantly shapes the composition and architecture of the tumor microenvironment. Our results provide new evidence that sex
differences in NK cell-mediated immunity, within the broader immune and stromal
landscape, may differentially impact tumor control in male and female PDAC hosts. This
study therefore underscores the importance of considering sex as a biological variable
in the preclinical evaluation of pancreatic cancer therapies.

E. ARLT ET AL.

Introduction
Natural killer (NK) cells are granular innate lymphocytes that represent an efficient endogenous firstline defense against cancer. They can identify virus-infected and malignant cells without prior
antigen exposure, distinguishing them from cytotoxic T cells.1 Upon degeneration of an individual
cell, it is recognized by NK cells and subsequently eliminated prior to further proliferation.
Nevertheless, NK cells can infiltrate the tumor microenvironment (TME) of solid cancers as well
as tumor-infiltrated lymph nodes or metastases, therefore playing an important role in preventing
tumor growth and spread.2,3 When activated, NK cells can perform two different killing approaches:
the release of lytic granules containing perforin and granzyme, or inducing death receptor-mediated
apoptosis via the expression of Fas ligand or TRAIL.4 In addition, NK cells are major producers of
IFN-γ, as well as other cytokines like TNF-α and GM-CSF, that attract and activate other immune
cells.5 The NK cell activity is determined by the balance of inhibitory and activating receptors on the
surface, which in turn are affected by activating and inhibitory signals.6 NK cells can recognize
whether a potential target cell exhibits a ligand profile associated with oncogenic transformation.7
One of the strongest NK cell activators is the lack of MHC class I-specific receptors on a target cell.8
Also, NK cells recognize stress-induced ligands.9 In addition to surface molecules, soluble components of the TME impact the NK cell function.10 The joint activating and inhibitory signals determine
whether a target cell is killed.7
Women in general tend to experience better outcomes than men when affected by conditions such
as infectious diseases, sepsis, trauma, or injury.11,12 However, this is accompanied by a markedly
higher prevalence of autoimmune diseases among women compared to men.13 Sex differences in NK
cell function have already been described previously. The general consensus is that female NK cells
might be more functional than male NK cells.14 Prior studies have proposed hormonal regulation as
well as epigenetic differences as reasons for that. For instance, estrogens in general are known to
exhibit immunoenhancing effects.15 Previous research suggests that estrogens’ impact is dosedependent,16 and their effect on NK cells may vary depending on the NK cell phenotype.14 On the
other hand, testosterone exhibits mainly immunosuppressive effects on NK cells.14,17 However, the
inhibitory impact is not fully unraveled, but might involve the upregulation of PD-L1.14 In line with
this, medical castration in healthy men has been proven to increase circulating numbers of NK cells.18
Sex hormones exert their effects not only through classical receptors such as ESR (estrogen receptor)

ONCOIMMUNOLOGY

3

and AR (androgen receptor) but also via alternative pathways, involving various GPRs or ZIP9.19,20
Additionally, testosterone can be converted intracellularly to DHT (dihydrotestosterone), further
interacting with distinct pathways, and even ESRs.21,22
Epigenetic mechanisms influencing NK cell activity involve an increasing array of genes and
microRNAs, which are partially X-linked. Naturally existing variations within these genetic elements
can explain sex-based disparities in immune system characteristics.13,23 Additionally, as females have two
X chromosomes, one of them is randomly silenced during X chromosome inactivation to avoid double
dosage of proteins in females.23 However, some genes can escape X-inactivation and are expressed from
both chromosomes.24 This results in elevated levels of functional immune proteins in females, potentially
leading to a better immune function.23 Recently, the X-linked histone demethylase UTX (Kdm6a) was
identified to escape X inactivation and shape gene expression, leading to enhanced NK cell responsiveness
and function in females.25
With over 400,000 deaths per year, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest
tumor entities worldwide.26 The incidence and mortality are increasing, and PDAC is predicted to be the
second-leading cause of cancer-related death by 2030.27 The pathophysiology and progression of PDAC
are strongly affected by the TME.28 NK cells in the peripheral blood and in the tissue of PDAC patients
exhibit a reduced cytotoxic function and a regulatory, IL-10-producing phenotype.29 Patients with high
NK cell infiltration in the tumor demonstrated improved survival, compared with those with low NK cell
infiltration.30 TME-infiltrating NK cells display downregulated activating receptors caused by immune
evasion factors produced by tumor cells, e.g., tumor-derived lactate and expression of IGHG1.31,32
Furthermore, tumor cells consume important nutrients, such as vitamin B6, which NK cells need as a
critical energy source to exhibit proper function.30 As there are various approaches to increasing the NK
cell antitumor activity by immunotherapy, more fundamental research promises major advances in the
treatment of PDAC.7
The biological sex plays a crucial role in multiple tumor entities, like melanoma, lung cancer, and
bladder cancer,33‐36 and is also known to highly influence PDAC pathology. Men have higher incidence
and mortality rates, poorer prognoses, shorter survival times after diagnosis, and poorer therapy outcomes.37‐39 Since the early development of PDAC is closely related to the TME, it is conceivable that sexspecific differences in the NK cell immune response play a crucial role in the development and progression
of pancreatic cancer.28,40 In line with this, stronger innate immune responses have been described in
female PDAC patients.41
The present study aims to answer the question of whether biological sex influences the NK cellmediated immunity against PDAC and can, therefore, at least partially explain the divergent clinical
outcomes. We systematically investigated sex-dependent differences in NK cell-mediated antitumor
responses in PDAC. Using complementary in vitro and in vivo approaches, we assessed functional,
transcriptional, and phenotypic differences between male and female NK cells and their impact on tumor
control. In addition, we applied high-dimensional, multiplex immunofluorescence-based analyses in
combination with RNA-sequencing of syngeneic PDAC allografts to characterize sex-specific differences
in tumor growth, immune infiltration, cellular activity, epigenetic regulation, and stromal composition.
Together, this integrative approach was designed to elucidate how biological sex shapes NK cell function
toward PDAC cells in vitro and influences PDAC growth in vivo in concert with other components of
the TME.

Materials and methods
Cells and culture conditions
Primary NK cells were isolated from the mouse spleen and utilized immediately for experiments after
isolation owing to their limited ex vivo lifespan. For co-culture experiments, the culture medium of the
target cell line was used.
Stable GFP-transfected mouse Panc02 cells (GenTarget Inc.) were cultivated in RPMI supplemented
with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. To select GFP-positive cells, 3 µg/ml puromycin was added
to the cell culture flask.

4

E. ARLT ET AL.

The mouse KPC3595 cell line42 was kindly provided by Ivonne Regel, Institute of Tumor Immunology,
Medical Faculty of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg. It was cultivated in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin-streptomycin.
Human NK-92 cells (ATCC) were cultivated in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillinstreptomycin, 1 U/µl IL-2, 0.1 ng/ml estradiol, 5 ng/ml testosterone (Thermo Fisher), or no hormones.
The human SU.86.86 cell line (ATCC) was cultivated in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS and 1%
penicillin–streptomycin. They were stably transduced with GFP to allow for cell identification in co-culture
experiments using lentiviral transduction as previously described.43 In brief, HEK293T cells (3.5 × 106) were
transfected using Lipofectamine 3000 with the packaging plasmids psPax2, pMD2.G, and the pLVX-GFP
lentiviral expression vector.43 Virus titers were determined 48 hours post-infection by flow cytometry using a
MACSQuantX Analyzer (Miltenyi Biotec). Transduction was performed at 5 MOI, and stably transduced cells
were sorted for purity of >95% using a BD FACS Melody.
Animal housing and Allograft model
Healthy male and female C57BL/6JRj mice (Janvier Labs) at 12 weeks of age were used. They underwent a
two-week acclimatization before entering the experiments. Mice for cell isolation and in vitro assays were
euthanized at the Institute of Anatomy in Halle (n = 18/sex), while the allograft mouse study was
conducted at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf. For tumor induction, 2 × 106 Panc02 cells
in 100 µl of PBS were injected subcutaneously into the right leg (n = 5/sex); controls received only PBS (n =
3/sex). All procedures were performed under light anesthesia with 9% (v/v) desflurane (Baxter) in 30/10%
(v/v) oxygen/air, and the mice were continuously warmed at 37 °C. The mice were monitored three times
weekly for well-being and tumor growth via calipers, which were calculated by assuming a tri-axial
ellipsoid with diameters a, b, and c using the formula V = π/6 × a × b × c. All the mice were euthanized as
soon as any of the tumors reached 300 mm³ (four weeks). Tumours were collected and measured, and all
organs were examined for metastases or abnormalities. Blood was sampled retroorbitally before tumor
injection, and at 1, 2, and 4 weeks after injection, blood NK cells were analyzed by flow cytometry.44
Euthanasia occurred in the morning during the light period by cervical dislocation.
NK cell isolation
Primary NK cells were isolated from the mouse spleen. Positive isolation was performed to obtain a pure
NK cell suspension. The spleens were dissociated using the gentleMACS Dissociator (Miltenyi Biotec). The
suspension was filtered, and after erythrocyte-lysis, stained with NK1.1 and CD3 antibodies (Miltenyi
Biotec) as well as with DAPI live/dead staining and sorted by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)
(BD FACS Aria II, BD Biosciences) for DAPI⁻NK1.1+CD3⁻ cells.
Negative isolation was used to obtain unlabeled primary NK cells via magnetic-associated cell sorting
(MACS) with an NK cell isolation kit (Miltenyi Biotec). Spleens were dissociated with a gentleMACS
Dissociator (Miltenyi Biotec) and filtered, and non-NK cells were depleted by column separation, yielding
an NK cell-enriched population. Isolation success was checked by flow cytometry. Based on the NK cell
yields from each mouse, cell suspensions were prepared for use in killing assays.
NK cell killing assays
Killing assays were conducted by co-culturing primary negatively isolated NK cells with Panc02 and
KPC3595 cells, as well as NK-92 cells with SU.86.86 cells. Target cells (4500/cm2) were seeded in a well
plate by FACS (BD FACS Melody, BD Biosciences) to ensure highly accurate cell numbers and, if
applicable, GFP-positivity rates close to 100%. NK cells were added 24 hours post-seeding at 5:1 and
10:1 effector:target (E:T) ratio, and incubated for 24 h. An NK cell-only control was used to determine
target cell-independent effects. The target cell only served as a growth control. All conditions were
supplemented with 1 U/µl IL-2. NK input controls were analyzed to assess culture-dependent effects.
Effector-focused killing assays were analyzed by flow cytometry and RNA sequencing. For target-focused
killing assays, time-lapse imaging was carried out in an Incucyte S3 device (Sartorius) for 64 h using phase

of target viability were performed on phase contrast and GFP fluorescence using Incucyte S3 GUI 2022B
rev2 software and the AI health module to determine the GFP intensities, the percentage of dead cells, and
the number of living cells. The AI health classifications were validated by the addition of PI on termination
of the experiment, confirming the percentage of dead cells.

To determine the sex of the Panc02 cells, multicolor fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) was
performed.45 Whole chromosome paints (wcps) for all 21 murine autosomes were obtained from the
21XMouse commercial kit (MetaSystems), as well as custom wcps for the X and Y chromosomes, which
were generated in-house via glass-needle-based chromosome microdissection.46 The chromosomal
workup and FISH procedures, including denaturation, overnight hybridization, and washing procedures,
were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. At least 30 metaphases were documented
and analyzed for each probe set on a Zeiss Axioplan microscope equipped with ISIS software
(MetaSystems).
Flow cytometry
Flow cytometry was performed to control the success of the negative NK cell isolation, with isolated NK
cells before and after co-culture, with peripheral blood from allografted mice, and with NK-92 cells before
and after co-culture. In the framework of primary NK cell isolation, NK cells were stained with CD45,
NK1.1, CD3, and PI for live/dead discrimination. Surface staining of primary mouse NK cells and allograft
blood samples included CD45, NK1.1, CD3, NCR1, NKG2D, CD11b, CD27, and PI.44 Surface staining of
human NK-92 cells included Fc receptor block (Miltenyi Biotec), CD45, NKp30, NKp44, NKp46, NKG2D,
NKG2A, and DAPI. Intracellular staining was exclusively performed with primary mouse NK cell cultures
and included NK1.1, CD3, granzyme A and B, and a fixable live/dead stain. For this purpose, an Inside
Stain Kit (Miltenyi Biotec) was used. Fluorescence minus one (FMO) controls were conducted for each
antibody for which the fluorescence signal was not clearly separable into positive and negative signals or
was poorly detectable. All antibodies are summarized in Supplementary Table T1.
The samples were analyzed via MACS Quant 16 (Miltenyi Biotec). The flow cytometry results were
analyzed using FlowJo™ v10.10 Software (BD Life Sciences). Target cells were excluded by scatter, GFP
fluorescence, and lack of CD45. Mouse primary NK cells were identified as CD45+CD3-NK1.1+, NK-92
cells as CD45+, and MFI values were assessed for every antibody.

RNA from positively sorted NK cells was extracted using Dynabeads™ Oligo(dT)25 RNA isolation kit
(Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The quality of the RNA was
assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis. Reverse transcription was performed with the Reverse
Transcription System (Promega).
Total RNA from cell experiments or allograft tumors was isolated by TriZOL® (Thermo Fisher
Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.47 For allograft tumors, the tissue was dispersed
using an Ultra Turrax (IKA®). RNA integrity was determined with an RNA Pico kit using a Bioanalyzer
2100 (Agilent Technologies). Samples with RIN values between 8.5 and 10 were considered. The isolated
RNA served as a template for RNA sequencing.
Real-time RT-PCR
RT-PCR was performed on a qTower3G thermocycler (Analytik Jena), using primer sets listed in
Supplementary Table T1 and the iQ SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad). The PCR products were size
separated by agarose gel electrophoresis.

RNA sequencing and differential gene expression
For library preparation, total RNA from cell culture (100 ng) or allograft samples (500 ng) was used. PolyA
enrichment was performed using oligo dT beads, followed by strand-specific library construction with the
Stranded mRNA Prep kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.48 Paired-end sequencing was
carried out on a NextSeq 1000 instrument (Illumina) with a P2 flow cell and a P200 cartridge (Illumina).
Low-quality reads and sequencing adapters were trimmed using Cutadapt (V4.4).49 Reads were aligned
to the murine genome (UCSC GRCm39) using HiSat2 (V2.2.1).50 FeatureCounts (V2.0.6)51 were used to
summarize the gene-mapped reads. Ensembl (GRCm39.113) was used for annotation. Differential gene
expression was determined by DeSeq2 (Galaxy V2.11.40.8+galaxy0) using the Galaxy-EU project (V25.0).
Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)
Log2 fold-changes in gene expression and their respective adjusted p-values (DESeq2) were used for gene ranking
before GSEA was conducted52,53using the GSEA software (V4.3.2) and MSigDB (V2025.1Mm). Hallmarks, M2
chemical and genetic perturbations (M2cgp), M2 – canonical pathways Reactome and Biocarta, M7 – immunology gene set collections, NK cell sets by Cui et al. 54, and the UTX-KO gene set were analyzed. The UTX-KO gene
set reflects the intersection of Kdm6a-KO, Kdm6a-Chip data, and cut&seq data according to Cheng et al. 25 The
detailed composition of this gene set is provided in Supplementary Table T2.
Histological staining, imaging, and analysis
All tumors were partially fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Carl Roth GmbH), embedded in paraffin, and
sectioned at 5 µm. After deparaffinization, the sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (Carl
Roth GmbH) to assess the tumor structure, and NK1.1 immunohistochemistry was performed to identify
infiltrating NK cells. Antigen retrieval was performed with citrate buffer (Zytomed Systems), followed by
different blocking steps. The sections were incubated overnight with the primary antibody (Cell Signaling),
then with a secondary antibody (Biozol), visualized with DAB (Vector Laboratories), and counterstained
with Haemalaun (Carl Roth GmbH). The slides were scanned using the Panoramic Scan II (3D HISTECH
Ltd.) and analyzed via QuPath (V0.3.2),55 the tumor area was quantified, NK cells were annotated, and NK
cell infiltration per area was calculated. The antibodies are listed in Supplementary Table T1.
Multiplex immunofluorescence imaging and cyclic staining (MICS)
High-dimensional multiplex immunofluorescence imaging was performed using the MACSima™ Imaging
Platform (Miltenyi Biotec). FFPE tumor samples were processed as described above. Antigen retrieval was
carried out by heat-induced epitope retrieval in Tris buffer (pH 9). Imaging was performed in five
independent runs, each including two samples processed in parallel (one female and one male).
Antibodies directly conjugated to fluorophores were applied sequentially over 12 imaging cycles, with
fluorescence signal removal achieved by bleaching for 6 min between cycles. A complete list of antibodies
and corresponding fluorophores is provided in Supplementary Table T1.
Prior to analysis, the images were pre-processed to exclude background fluorescence and residual
signals from previous staining cycles. Image analysis, including cell segmentation, classification, gating,
and TME subtyping, was performed using MACSima IQ View software (definitions provided in
Supplementary Table T3). The mean fluorescence intensities were thresholded for all marker channels
before scaled inverse hyperbolic sine transformation with a factor of 5.
Statistical analysis, bias control, and quality assurance
Unless stated otherwise, the visualization and statistical evaluation of the data were performed with
GraphPad Prism (V10.4.2). Statistical tests and n-counts are indicated in the figure legends. The p-values
are indicated in the graphs if they are smaller than 0.1 (90% confidence interval). The data are presented as
median with individual values or standard error.

Results
As sex-dependent differences have been reported for the incidence and mortality of PDAC (Figure 1),39 as
well as NK cell function, we aimed to elucidate the role of biological sex in NK cell-mediated immunity
against PDAC-derived cell lines in vivo and in vitro.
Appropriate sex characterization of effector and target cells allows for unbiased sex-specific NK
cell killing assays
To investigate potential sex-dependent differences in the interaction of NK cells with pancreatic cancer
cells, we established a murine killing assay. For use as effector cells, we isolated primary NK cells from the

spleens of male and female mice via negative isolation (Figure 2A). The isolated NK cells displayed purities
around 85%–100% (Supplementary Figure S1), and their sex was confirmed via RNA-seq. As expected, we
detected clear differences in the expression of X and Y chromosomal genes between male and female NK
cells. Kdm5d and Uty were exclusively expressed in male NK cells, while Kdm5c and Kdm6a (UTX) were
predominantly detected in female NK cells (Figure 2B). These Kdm5/6 genes encode histone demethylases
involved in epigenetic regulation, and notably, Kdm5c and Kdm6a are known to escape X-chromosome
inactivation.25
As target cell line and PDAC model, we utilized the murine Panc02 cell line stably labeled with GFP,
enabling rapid identification of tumor cells via downstream analyses. It is derived from chemically induced
PDAC in a male C57BL/6 mouse.57 As our study focused on sex-dependent interactions, we verified the sex
chromosome status of Panc02 cells via mFISH and RNA-seq. mFISH identified hyperploidy of the Panc02 cells
without any detection of the Y chromosome and a reduced number of X chromosomes (Figure 2C).
Consistently, transcriptomic profiling revealed a significant reduction but not absence in Y-linked gene
expression compared to freshly isolated male NK cells, along with low expression levels of X-linked genes
(Supplementary Figure S2). In addition, the data were translated to the human genome,45 which revealed
notable similarities in chromosomal aberrations in Panc02 cells compared to human PDAC, with 16 of 25
regions (64%) being affected (Supplementary Table T4).58 Therefore, the Panc02 cell line is a suitable PDAC
model and was considered sex-neutral for the purposes of our study.
Naïve NK cells from males and females show a similar phenotype with subtle differences in
cytokine response and histone methylation signatures
To elucidate the initial differences between male and female NK cells, we analyzed the phenotypes of
freshly isolated NK cells via flow cytometry and RNA-seq. We found that freshly isolated NK cells
displayed a naïve, non-activated phenotype, characterized by low expression of the maturity markers
CD11b and CD27, and the activation markers NCR1 and NKG2D, as well as a low intracellular content of
granzymes A and B (Figure 2D). We detected no significant differences between male and female NK cells
(Figure 2D). In line with this, RNA-seq showed comparable expression levels of NK cell activationassociated transcripts in both sexes and minimal detection of markers for other immune cell lineages,
confirming the isolation success (Figure 2E). The expression of Ar and Esr1 did not differ markedly
between freshly isolated male and female NK cells (Figure 2F, upper panel). Notably, Esr2 was not
expressed in primary mouse NK cells (Figure 2F, upper panel). The expression of Ar and Esr1 was
confirmed with RT-PCR in positively isolated NK cells (Supplementary Figure S3). The expression of their
respective response genes differed only marginally between males and females (Figure 2F, lower panel).
Interestingly, we identified sex-dependent differences in the cytokine response and histone methylation
signatures. In line with previous reports25 and in agreement with the absence of Kdm6a in male NK cells
(Figure 2B), Kdm6a-regulated genes were lower in male than in female NK cells (Figure 2G, upper panel).
This includes genes linked to the repressive H3K27me3 histone mark,56 which were expressed at lower
levels in freshly isolated male NK cells compared to females (Figure 2G, lower panel). Although male and
female NK cells showed similar baseline phenotypes (Figure 2D, E), IL-1A- and IL-1B-associated response
genes were significantly upregulated in male NK cells, whereas response signatures for IFN-α, IL-12, and
IL-15, which essentially enhance NK cell activity in a Kdm6a-dependent manner, were significantly
downregulated (Figure 2H and Supplementary Table T5).25,54 These findings are consistent with previous
reports showing reduced IL-12 and IL-15 responsiveness in males.25 This finding indicates that female NK
cells are epigenetically primed for enhanced killing capacity.

Female NK cells display enhanced immune responses and cytotoxic capacity in co-culture with
Panc02
To further examine sex-dependent differences in NK cell-tumor cell interactions, we examined the RNAseq data from the killing assays. To distinguish NK cells from Panc02 tumor cells in co-cultures, we
derived marker genes from the respective mono-cultures that clearly segregated the two populations
(Supplementary Figure S4A). We detected a significant reduction in the number of tumor cells and,
correspondingly, a relative enhancement of NK cells in female co-cultures (Figure 4A). Among the genes
whose expression was most highly upregulated in female co-cultures, a variety of interferon-stimulated
genes (ISGs), indicating an enhanced immune response were identified (Figure 4A). This phenomenon
was conserved in another PDAC cell line (KPC3595), although immune responses were less prominent in
these cells, likely due to the additional alteration of IL-10 response genes suggested to act as immune
suppressors (Supplementary Figure S4B). Consistently, GSEA revealed enrichment of hallmark immuneresponse gene sets in female co-cultures of both cell lines (Figure 4B and Supplementary Figure S4C),
while proliferative programs such as MYC and E2F targets exhibited reduced normalized enrichment
scores (NES) (Figure 4B and Supplementary Tables T6+T7). This pattern was corroborated by Reactome,
Biocarta, and Gene Ontology Biological Process (GOBP) analyses, which indicated decreased proliferation
and enhanced immune activity (Figure 4C+D, Supplementary Figure S4D+E, and Supplementary
Tables T7–T9).
Our analyses suggest that male and female NK cells are activated by different mechanisms.
Pathways such as the Reactome: Immunoregulatory interactions between lymphoid and a nonlymphoid cell, Biocarta NKT pathway, and NK cell pathway were enriched exclusively in female cocultures (Figure 4B+C, and Supplementary Figure S4D+E). In contrast, no sex-dependent enrichment
of immune-related gene sets was observed in mono-cultures or freshly isolated NK cells (Figure 4B+C,
and Supplementary Figure S4D+E). In female co-cultures, expression, interaction, and signaling of
DAP12 (Tyrobp) were among the most prominently upregulated reactome pathway sets (Figure 4C
and Supplementary Table T7). DAP12 is an ITAM-containing adaptor that pairs with NK cell
receptors such as NKG2D (Klrk1) to modulate downstream signaling.60 Recent studies have shown
that CARs containing NKG2D and DAP12 domains reduce cytokine production but enhance tumor
cell killing, highlighting the importance of this receptor in NK cell cytotoxicity.61 Consistent with this,
distinct response gene sets were enriched in female versus male co-cultures (Figure 4C and
Supplementary Table T7). Female-enriched response gene sets were exclusively observed in cocultures, indicating induction by target-cell contact (Figure 4D and Supplementary Table T10). In
male cultures, upregulated pathways associated with the cytokine response were likely induced by IL2, as these programs were elevated in both mono- and co-cultures (Figure 4D and Supplementary
Table T11).
In conclusion, female NK cells display contact-dependent activation mediated predominantly by the IL1α/β- and IFN-β-associated response pathways in co-culture with two independent cell lines, while males
show IL-2-dependent activation. These results clearly indicate differential anti-tumor immune responses in
our study.

In order to investigate the potential effect of sex hormones on NK cell cytotoxicity, we performed
co-culture experiments using the human NK-92 cell line and the PDAC cell line SU.86.86.63 NK-92
cells were stimulated for at least one week with physiological concentrations of estradiol and
testosterone, after which their cytotoxic efficacy against SU.86.86 cells was assessed. This approach
mirrors our experiments with primary NK cells, which were exposed to hormones until isolation, but
were not subjected to hormonal influence during the actual killing assay. Although we detected initial
differences in NK cell activity following hormone stimulation, these effects dissipated within 24 hours
in the presence of SU.86.86 and in the absence of hormones (Supplementary Figure S6A) and had no
impact on the cytotoxic efficacy (Supplementary Figure S6B). This finding is in line with the findings
from primary NK cell co-cultures, where we observed an initially higher androgen response in freshly
isolated male NK cells, which subsided in co-culture with Panc02 cells, while estrogen responses

Slower growth of female allograft tumors is associated with higher NK cell infiltration
To examine the interaction of NK cells with pancreatic cancer cells in vivo, an allograft mouse model was
established. For that purpose, Panc02 cells were injected into the right leg of male and female mice
(Figure 6A). Multiple blood samples were collected during tumor development and analyzed via flow
cytometry. A decrease in peripheral NK cells was evident in allograft females. No significant differences in
quantity, activity, or maturation were observed between the groups (Supplementary Figure S7).
The tumor growth was quantified three times per week. We measured faster tumor growth in males
than in females (average doubling time: 20.8 d in males vs. 37.4 d in females; final volume: 196.0 vs. 67.6
mm³, Figure 6B). Histological H.E. staining of the tumors revealed a homogeneous tumor composition of
Panc02 cells with individual infiltration into different subcutaneous tissues (Supplementary Figure
S8A–D). Immunohistochemistry of NK1.1 revealed infiltration of NK cells into the tumor tissues,
especially at the tumor margin (Figure 6C1, Supplementary Figure S8E). We detected more NK cells
infiltrating female tumors than male tumors (Figure 6C1+2). In line with these findings, we observed more
NK cell-associated transcripts and fewer tumor cell-associated transcripts in females compared to males
(Figure 6C3). Furthermore, tumor size is negatively correlated with NK cell infiltration, underscoring the
connection between greater NK cell presence in females and reduced tumor burden. (Figure 6D). Our
findings suggest that reduced Panc02 tumor growth in females in our study is at least partly associated with
the NK cell function.

Female and male allograft tumors differ in their anti-tumor immune programs and their TME
composition
To investigate sex-dependent differences in allograft tumors in greater detail, we combined RNA sequencing with high-dimensional multiplex imaging and cyclic staining (MICS) on the MACSima platform and
analyzed more than 260,000 single cells based on functional gating strategies. By integrating differential
gene expression analysis and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) with a MICS panel of 18 markers for
tumor, immune, and stromal cells, we were able to characterize the molecular profiles and spatial
organization of these tumors at the protein level, which is especially important in cancers with highly
reactive stroma, such as PDAC (Figure 7A).
Although both male and female tumors are derived from the same PDAC cell line, their architecture
and microenvironment differ markedly. Male tumors have a dense, compact structure with a higher
abundance of immune-suppressive cell types and a stiffer stroma. In contrast, female tumors featured a
looser connective tissue and increased infiltration by immune cells that are involved in anti-tumor
responses (Figure 7B). Marker-based cell type profiling of the RNA-seq data revealed that female tumors
contained greater proportions of NK cells, MDSC-like cells, T cells, non-M2 tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), endothelial cells, and inflammatory cancer-associated fibroblasts (iCAFs) (Figure 7C).
Correspondingly, female tumors contained fewer tumor cells, myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs), neutrophils, and M2-like TAMs compared to male tumors. This composition was confirmed by spatial MICS
quantification, which showed non-M2 TAMs as the most prominent immune cell type in female tumors.
In males, neutrophils and myCAFs were predominant (Figure 7D). Overall, myCAFs and iCAFs together
accounted for 23% of intratumoral cells, while M2-like TAMs made up 18% of intratumoral cells, closely
mirroring the cellular landscape of human PDAC with highly reactive stroma and predominant M2-TAM
infiltration.
At the transcriptional level, female tumors exhibited significant enrichment of interferon response and
allograft rejection gene sets, highlighting increased immune activation. In contrast, male tumors presented
upregulated proliferation pathways, including E2F and MYC targets, the G2M checkpoint, and mTORC1
signaling (Figure 7E, Supplementary Table T12). These differences were consistent with co-culture
experiments, as the same hallmark and response gene sets were upregulated in vitro and in vivo
(Figure 4B, Supplementary Figure S9A, B).54 Increased proliferative activity in male tumors was also
supported by increased Ki67 expression (Figure 7F). The heightened immune activation in female tumors
was further evidenced by an enrichment of NK cell response genes and markers of cytotoxic activity, such
as elevated granzyme B expression in infiltrating T and NK cells (Figure 7G). Thereby, enhanced NK cell
response gene sets in the allograft mirrored the findings from the co-culture setting (Supplementary
Figure 9B, Supplementary Table T13).54 Consistently, MHC-I and PD-L1 expression was globally higher in
female tumors and their immune compartments, reflecting stronger immune engagement (Figure 7H).
Notably, the analyses revealed that neutrophils and MDSC-like cells in female tumors presented higher
MHC-I to PD-L1 ratios, while the same cells in male tumors tended to express more PD-L1, implying
more pronounced immune suppression in males (Figure 7H). CD44 expression also followed a sexdependent pattern: it was increased in NK cells in female tumors but was associated with proliferative and
immune-evasive tumor cell populations in males (Figure 7I). Differential expression analyses of genes with
effector functions further supported these observations; for example, females upregulated CXCL11 and
IGFBP6, while males showed higher levels of Cxcl2, Cd24a, and Alpl, which was consistent with enhanced
neutrophil recruitment, macrophage evasion, and greater extracellular matrix stiffness (Figure 7J).
Fibroblast distribution also differed by sex. In males, SMA⁺ myCAFs were abundant and associated
with dense, poorly vascularized tumors, while in females, myCAFs were mainly found around CD31+
vessels, and most tumor-infiltrating fibroblasts consisted of iCAFs embedded in a looser, immunepermissive collagen matrix (Figure 7K).
Minor yet consistent alterations in androgen and estrogen response programs were observed in the
tumor tissues, potentially contributing to differences in tumor growth and immune regulation and
exceeding those observed in mono- and co-culture settings (Figure 7L, Supplementary Figure S6C).
Beyond immune and stromal programs, female tumors consistently exhibited globally reduced levels of
H3K27me3, especially in tumor, T, and NK cells, along with decreased SUZ12 expression and reduced

Overall, these results show that female tumors are less proliferative and more immunologically active,
characterized by an NK cell-enriched, immune-permissive stroma driven by a combination of epigenetic
and, to a certain extent, hormone-dependent cues. In contrast, male tumors are more proliferative,
aggressive, and immunosuppressive, underscoring sex as a key factor in tumor biology and therapy
response (Figure 8). Although NK cells made up only a small fraction of the tumor microenvironment,
they showed some of the most pronounced sex-specific differences. Both their function and epigenetic

state, particularly with respect to H3K27me3 methylation, differ markedly between females and males,
indicating a strong influence on the immune-reactive tumor phenotype.
Taken together, the findings from our study indicate that NK cell-related immune responses against
PDAC are stronger in females than in males in both in vitro and in vivo mouse models. Initial differences
in NK cell cytotoxicity appear to be primarily driven by epigenetic mechanisms that operate independently
of sex hormones.

Discussion
It is generally known that PDAC incidence and survival are worse for men than for women and that
women are able to mount a stronger immune response than men.13,37 NK cells are key mediators of
antitumor immunity and are known to exhibit sex-specific differences;14,68 however, whether this extends
to PDAC, potentially contributing to divergent PDAC pathologies between the sexes, has remained
unclear. This study focused on determining whether biological sex influences NK cell-mediated immunity
against pancreatic cancer in vitro and in vivo.
In this study, we used the mouse cell line Panc02 as a PDAC model. Although Panc02 was originally
described as male,57 karyotyping and RNA-seq revealed no Y-chromosomal features, indicating the loss of
sex-specific properties. Loss of the Y chromosome is a frequent event in human PDAC and in multiple
PDAC cell lines.69 In addition, Panc02 displays SMAD4 deficiency, which is described as a PDAC
hallmark,70 and expresses mild inflammatory features.57 Therefore, it represents a sex-neutral target
suitable for studying NK cell function in PDAC. The Panc02 cells not only proved to be a good model
in vitro but also in vivo. We established a syngeneic allograft mouse model by injecting Panc02 cells
subcutaneously into the right leg of male and female BL6 mice. The histological structure of the allograft
tumors was remarkably similar to that of human PDAC, as it included a complex tumor stroma infiltrated
with immune cells (e.g., TAMs, CAFs, and T and NK cells). A major advantage of the allograft model in
comparison with genetically engineered cancer models is the identical origin of the tumor cells, which is
consistent across age, sex, and individual properties of the mice. The context of studying sex-dependent
differences, therefore, allows maximal focus on infiltrating immune cells and the sex of the host. In
addition, in genetically engineered mouse models, tumors do not occur at exactly the same time in all
animals, and often progress before the immune system of the host is fully developed. With the allograft
model, we could ensure a uniform starting point for all animals, ensuring that each had a fully mature
immune system. This approach allowed us to isolate and focus solely on the sex-based differences, free
from any time-dependent biases. Future studies should involve an orthotopic injection of Panc02 cells into
the pancreas of male and female mice, as this could allow investigations into the impact of tumorigenesis
on the exocrine pancreatic function.71
In order to study sex-dependent differences in NK cell function, we isolated primary NK cells from male
and female BL6 mice to be used in subsequent killing assays. The primary NK cells were phenotypically
naïve after isolation, but transcriptomic analysis revealed subtle intrinsic sex-dependent differences in gene
regulation. We found that male NK cells expressed lower levels of H3K27me3-regulated genes, a difference
likely driven by reduced UTX activity. UTX was shown to influence NK cell cytotoxicity in a sexdependent manner.25 As an X-linked gene that escapes inactivation, UTX is expressed at higher levels
in females,25 facilitating the removal of repressive H3K27me3 and supporting sex-specific gene regulation.
The H3K27me3 pathway is known to regulate the activity of various immune cells in the context of
cancer.72 In addition, downregulated cytokine response signatures and upregulation of an IL-4/IL-10
program could be observed, suggesting a more immunosuppressive baseline in male NK cells.73 Our
findings are consistent with previous reports that describe an enhanced intrinsic cytotoxic capacity in
female NK cells.14,25
During cultures with and without Panc02 cells, we showed that IL-2 alone was capable of activating NK
cells. In turn, Panc02 cells dampened this activation, which was reflected in diminished surface densities of
the activating receptors NCR1 and NKG2D. Tumor cells employ various strategies to escape NK cellmediated responses; among these, the shedding of ligands to impair NKG2D-mediated activation is a wellcharacterized mechanism of immune evasion.74 NK cell maturation was evident in the killing assays, with
female NK cells displaying a slightly more advanced differentiation state in co-culture. Furthermore,

female NK cells respond more strongly to Panc02, and the enhanced immune response is driven
predominantly by tumor contact.54,73 In contrast, male NK cells are largely IL-2-driven and less responsive
to tumor cell-derived cues. These results were validated with another PDAC cell line (KPC3595), albeit the
differences were pronounced to a lesser extent because of its lower suitability as a killing target. Functional
killing assays with Panc02 cells revealed that female NK cells are able to kill more tumor cells, resulting in
slower tumor cell proliferation and higher tumor cell death over time. Importantly, the enhanced killing
capacity of female NK cells was independent of sex hormones. We observed slight initial differences in
hormone responses between freshly isolated male and female NK cells, which subsided after cultivation in
the absence of sex hormones. Notably, the differences in killing efficacy persisted, suggesting that systemic
hormonal signals may influence NK cells under physiological conditions but not after isolation in our
setting. Importantly, these findings were consistent across both primary NK cells and NK cell line-based
models using NK-92, supporting the conclusion that the observed enhanced cytotoxicity of female NK
cells can be attributed to stable epigenetic programs rather than hormonal influences.
The observed sex differences in vitro correlate with findings from the in vivo allograft setting,
reinforcing the relevance of NK cell-tumor interactions. Female tumors grow more slowly, which is
correlated with a higher NK cell infiltration. In line with these findings, previous studies have
demonstrated that the NK cell infiltration of tumors from PDAC patients is positively correlated
with survival.30,40 A decrease in peripheral NK cells was evident in female allografts, which was most
likely caused by enhanced NK cell migration to the tumor site. Following up from here, multiplex
spatial immunofluorescence staining and RNA-seq revealed differences in the overall tumor composition between males and females. Male tumors display a dense, compact architecture, including stiff
and tumor-promoting stroma, increased basal-like properties, and increased proliferative properties.
The male TME is characterized by the infiltration of immune-suppressive cell types, and NK cells are
characterized by reduced infiltration, activation, and cytotoxic function. In contrast, female tumors
showed a looser architecture, with less basal-like properties and reduced proliferation, leading to an
overall immune-permissive stroma with stronger immune response programs and infiltration of proinflammatory immune cells. The infiltrating NK cells were strongly activated and displayed high
cytotoxic activity. It is reasonable to assume that the loose, pro-inflammatory tumor structure in
female mice favors and facilitates NK cell infiltration, as well as other immune cells of the TME. In this
context, intrinsic differences in NK cell function collaborate with an environment conducive to NK
cells, leading to enhanced NK cell immunity in females in vivo. It must be said that, despite NK cells
constitute only a small fraction of the TME, they present some of the largest sex differences in terms of
their immigration and activation among infiltrating immune cells. In addition, their strong sexdependent regulation might be far more relevant in the context of naturally arising tumors than in
the high-dose allograft injection model, as they are crucial for the control of single transformed cells
and metastases.2 The data from this study support the conclusion that NK cells provide a sex-specific
contribution to anti-tumor immunity in concert with the TME and other immune cells. Nevertheless,
future NK cell-depletion studies will be needed to definitively delineate their causal role. Beyond this,
the greater pro-inflammatory TME of female mice, together with enhanced PD-L1 expression on
tumor cells, suggests a greater responsiveness of female allograft tumors to ICB, which was further
supported by the GSEA data. This suggests that sex contributes to the prognostic outcome of immune
therapies but likely acts in concert with additional influencing factors.64 Future studies should
therefore prioritize the analysis of clinical data from male and female patients undergoing immunotherapies in order to determine whether sex-specific differences are reflected in patient outcomes.
Large-scale pan-cancer bulk transcriptomic studies of human tumors have provided important insights
into sex-associated immune differences and offer a useful foundation for translational research.36 However,
bulk analyses can mask sex-specific effects within individual immune cell populations. Future studies
combining single-cell and spatial transcriptomic approaches may therefore be needed to more precisely
define sex-specific immune programs in the tumor microenvironment. Such analyses could help clarify
whether female PDAC patients differentially benefit from immune-based combination therapies when
stratified by sex-associated immune features, as suggested by mouse data.
Although we proved that initial sex-dependent differences in NK cell cytotoxicity are independent
of sex hormones in vitro, they must be considered in the in vivo setting. We did not monitor the

estrous cycle in female mice in order to assess general sex differences under standard laboratory
conditions. Additionally, including females at various cycle stages reflects natural biological variability. It is worth noting that hormone levels in females can vary more extensively across different life
stages than during the normal estrous cycle, and the variability introduced by the estrous cycle stage in
female mice is generally not greater than the variability observed among males.75 Nevertheless,
hormones may influence tumor architecture in vivo. In allograft tumors, we observed slightly
increased AR and ER responses in males. It should be noted that both estrogen and androgen response
gene sets include numerous genes involved in cell proliferation. Considering our data showing that
male tumors grow faster, this may therefore reflect, at least in part, variations in tumor proliferation
rates rather than direct effects of sex hormones. Nevertheless, future studies should involve allograft
models using gonadectomized mice to elucidate whether the observed differences in tumor composition persist independently of sex hormones.
Together, our study offers relevant insights into the sex-dependent regulation of NK cells in PDAC.
These findings indicate that the combination of initial enhanced NK cell function and NK cell-beneficial
tumor architecture in females results in superior NK cell-mediated tumor control in patients with PDAC.
This occurs within the context of a proinflammatory TME with enhanced immune cell infiltration,
potentially explaining the associations between female sex and reduced PDAC incidence and mortality.
Although hormones might play a role in in vivo, the observed in vitro differences in NK cell cytotoxicity
are most likely attributable to intrinsic (epigenetic) mechanisms. The definitive role of NK cells in our
in vivo setting remains to be elucidated, as further experiments, such as NK cell depletion experiments or
the use of NK cell-deficient mice, are needed to clarify this point. Although the mouse data reveal clear
patterns, the extent to which these findings apply to the much more heterogeneous human system still
needs to be determined. Sex-based disparities warrant increased consideration in clinical practice and
underscore the importance of considering biological sex as a variable in future research and targeted
therapy.

candidate: This study investigated the mechanisms underlying ulcerative colitis (UC) and associated hepatobiliary complications, specifically focusing on the gut–liver axis and hepatic lipid metabolism. Researchers utilized mouse models (C57BL/6J and 129/Sv) and human metabolomic/transcriptomic datasets to evaluate the roles of pristimerin (PSM), the commensal *Lactobacillus johnsonii*, and the LXRα–SCD1 signaling pathway. Results demonstrated that DSS-induced colitis increased saturated free fatty acids and saturated lysophospholipids while decreasing unsaturated species. PSM and *L. johnsonii* culture supernatant (Ljsup) significantly reduced the Disease Activity Index (DAI) and systemic inflammatory markers, reversing these lipid trends. Specifically, Ljsup activated the hepatic LXRα–SCD1 axis, increasing anti-inflammatory lipid species like LPC20:2 and LPC20:3. Conversely, corticosterone (CORT) exacerbated UC and liver injury by downregulating LXRα signaling, an effect mitigated by the LXRα antagonist SR9243. Human data corroborated these findings, showing that elevated ratios of specific lysophospholipids and ceramides correlated with higher clinical activity scores. The study concludes that hepatic lipid dysregulation, driven by impaired LXRα–SCD1 signaling, contributes to UC comorbidity. Limitations include the use of animal models, a lack of human clinical trials, and potential sex-related hormonal influences.

against ulcerative colitis and concomitant liver injury through remodeling
hepatic lipid metabolism via LXRα–SCD1 axis

ABSTRACT

ARTICLE HISTORY

Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a systemic disease that can involve multiple organs, and hepatobiliary diseases in UC patients are frequently observed. However, the pathogenesis
of UC and its associated hepatobiliary complications remains elusive, and limited therapeutic options are available. This study revealed that disrupted hepatic lipid metabolism
plays a pivotal role in driving the progression of UC and its extraintestinal hepatobiliary
manifestations. Mechanistically, colitis-elevated circulating endogenous corticosterone
(CORT) mediates the downregulation of hepatic LXRα–SCD1 signaling, resulting in diminished monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA), reduced unsaturated lysophospholipids, and the
accumulation of alkyl lysophospholipids, ceramide and hexosylceramide. These alterations
contribute to liver lipotoxicity and, in turn, exacerbate colitis. A similar lipid profile is
observed in UC patients. Importantly, pristimerin, a natural compound structurally similar
to the star molecule celastrol, has been demonstrated to alleviate UC and concomitant liver
injury by remodeling hepatic lipid metabolism in a microbiota-dependent manner. The
gut commensal Lactobacillus johnsonii mediates the effects of PSM by activating hepatic
LXRα–SCD1 signaling and increasing the potential anti-inflammation lipid species LPC20:2
and LPC20:3. This investigation suggests a novel therapeutic strategy for UC and associated
liver injury based on the L. johnsonii-hepatic LXRα–SCD1 axis. This study also opens new
avenues for mechanistic exploration of systemic diseases and therapeutic strategies of
multi-organ comorbidity.

Introduction
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic relapsing and remitting inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterized by abdominal pain, diarrhea, rectal bleeding and weight loss. As the incidence and prevalence of UC
are increasing globally, its pathogenesis and therapy remain key areas of research interest.1 Currently, there
is no curative therapy for UC. The treatment goal is to control inflammation and alleviate symptoms.
Medications include the front-line therapy 5-amino-salicylates (5-ASA), while second-line therapies are
corticosteroids, immunomodulators and biologics.2,3 However, owing to the limited efficacy and side
effects of existing treatments, the exploration of novel, effective and safe treatment strategies continue to
attract growing interest.4
UC is a systemic disease that can involve multiple organs. Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) are
frequently observed, typically involving the joints, eyes, hepatobiliary tract and skin,5 which may eventually lead to severe complications and impair patients' prognosis.6 Hepatobiliary manifestations are
disorders that affect the hepatobiliary system, including primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), hepatic fibrosis, cholangiocarcinoma, and cholelithiasis, etc.7 In
recent years, biologics such as anti-TNF (infliximab, IFX), anti-integrin α4β7 (vedolizumab, VDZ) and
anti-interleukin12/23 (ustekinumab, UST) agents have been frequently employed for UC-associated
NAFLD.8,9 Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) has been used for concomitant UC and PSC.10 Owing to the
lack of rigorous “evidence-based” data supporting the efficacy and various adverse effects, these therapeutic
approaches should be carefully considered until further research specifically clarifies their roles in
managing the hepatobiliary complications of UC patients.9,11
Given that numerous clinical needs in the management of UC and its hepatobiliary complications
remain unmet, it is imperative to identify promising therapeutic targets and develop multi-organ strategies
for these comorbidities. However, the etiology and pathogenesis of UC and associated hepatobiliary
disease remain unclear. One extensively studied underlying mechanism is based on the gut‒liver axis.
Specifically, liver injury in UC has been described as a direct consequence of a sustained, extended
inflammatory response triggered by gut bacterial and viral endotoxins, such as bile acid (BA), lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and lactoferrin.12-14 Perturbation of gut‒liver crosstalk in various liver diseases has
been demonstrated by clinical evidence.15 Likewise, as the interaction between the gut and liver is

GUT MICROBES

3

bidirectional, liver secretions also play crucial roles in intestinal homeostasis. Consequently, disruption of
hepatic homeostasis and metabolism aggravates intestinal inflammation.16-18
Lipid metabolic disorders are very common in UC patients, particularly substantial shifts in phospholipid and sphingolipid metabolism.19,20 Overall, hepatic lipid metabolism, including lipogenesis, reverse
cholesterol transport, and lipid oxidation mediated by LXRα-dependent pathways, is disrupted in DSSinduced colitis.21 Stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 (SCD1) is a downstream target gene of LXRα and a key
enzyme for mono-unsaturated fatty acid (MUFA) synthesis. SCD1 deficiency induced the production of
ceramide, which is the central lipid building block of sphingolipids.22 Inhibition of SCD1 dramatically
exacerbated colonic inflammation in colitis mice.17 We therefore speculated that hepatic de novo lipid
synthesis mediated by LXRα–SCD1 signaling pathway may play a crucial role in the progression of UC and
associated liver injury. In addition, UC patients with depression have been reported to exhibit abnormal
cortisol levels, which can lead to metabolic dysregulation.23 In rodent models, increased corticosterone
(CORT) drives the progression of NAFLD.24 Downregulation of LXRα caused by CORT induction has
been observed in liver of juvenile chickens.25 Taken together, we hypothesized that CORT may exert an
effect on hepatic LXRα–SCD1 signaling in mice with UC and concomitant liver steatosis.
Natural compounds have been a major source for drug discovery.1,26 Interestingly, some natural
compounds, such as cryptotanshinone and celastrol, can ameliorate colitis by modulating host lipid
metabolism and the gut microbiota.27,28 Pristimerin (PSM, Figure 1a) is a pentacyclic triterpene isolated
from the herbal plant Tripterygium wilfordii Hook. f. It is a natural compound structurally similar to the
star molecule celastrol and also possesses various pharmacological activities. A recent study revealed that it
exerts anti-colitis activity by modulating the gut microbiota balance and host lipid metabolism.29 However,
it remains unclear what is the pivotal microbe it targets and the specific mechanisms by which it regulates
lipid metabolism.
In this study, we demonstrated that PSM attenuates DSS-induced experimental UC and associated liver
injury in a gut microbiota-dependent manner. The gut commensal L. johnsonii mediates the protective
effects of PSM against this comorbidity by remodeling hepatic lipid metabolism via activation of the
LXRα‒SCD1 signaling pathway. This finding indicates an underlying mechanism involving the microbiota‒liver‒gut axis in the pharmacological activity of PSM and paves the way for exploring L. johnsonii as
a novel multi-organ therapeutic target for UC and concomitant hepatic diseases.

Materials and methods
Mouse experiments
All animal protocols were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of West China Hospital,
Sichuan University (Approval ID: 20220226032). Male C57BL/6J mice (6–8 weeks old) were purchased
from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). 6–8 weeks-old male 129/Sv wild-type mice (WT) and
129/Sv Pparα-null mice were used to evaluate the function of PPARα. The method for creating Pparα-null
mice have been described previously.30 Mice were groups-housed in individually ventilated cages under a
standard 12 h light/dark cycle with a relative humidity of 40%–60% at a constant temperature of 22 °C. All
the mice had ad libitum access to food and water during the experiments. Colitis was induced by the
addition of drinking water containing 3.0% (w/v) DSS for 7 d.
Animal experiment 1: PSM alleviated UC and associated liver injury study. Male C57BL/6J mice were
randomly divided into four groups (n=6): (1) CTRL, (2) DSS, (3) DSS+PSM (MCE, cat#1258-84-0), and
(4) PSM. Regular sterilized water was given to CTRL and PSM groups, and 3% (w/v) DSS water was
administered to DSS and DSS+PSM groups. Based on the previous literature and our preliminary
experiment,31,32 a dosage of 0.5 mg/kg of PSM was selected. Over the duration of 7 d, mice in
DSS + PSM and PSM groups were treated with PSM (0.5 mg/kg) by intraperitoneally injection (i.p.
injection) once every 2 d, 4 doses in total. The CTRL and DSS groups were concurrently administered
vehicle (1% DMSO + 2% Tween-80 sterilized water) by i.p. injection.
Animal experiment 2: ABX treatment depleted the gut microbiota study. Male C57BL/6J mice were
randomly assigned to three groups (n = 6): (1) CTRL, (2) PSM, and (3) ABX+PSM. Over the three weeks
duration, regular sterilized water was given to the CTRL and PSM groups, and the mice in the ABX+PSM

Untargeted metabolomics and lipidomics
Metabolomics and Lipidomics analyses were performed at the Advanced Mass Spectrometry Center of
West China Hospital. LC-MS-grade acetonitrile, methanol, isopropanol, and formic acid were obtained
from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA), and ammonium acetate was purchased from Macklin
(Shanghai, China). The internal standard chlorpropamide was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (Missouri,
USA), and LPC12:0 was bought from Avanti Polar Lipids (Alabaster, AL).
Metabolomics analysis was performed on mice serum and liver samples. Sample preparations were carried out
as described previously.1 UHPLC-MS analysis was performed using a Vanquish UHPLC-Q-Exactive plus MS
system (Thermo Fisher, USA). Chromatographic separation was carried out with an ACQUTY UPLC HSS T3
column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.8 µm). Mobile phase A was 0.1% formic acid (FA) in water, and mobile phase B was
0.1% FA in acetonitrile (ACN). The flow rate was 0.3 mL/min, with a linear gradient ranging from 2% to 98%
ACN over a 17 min run. MS/MS spectra were collected in both positive and negative ion modes and was operated
in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) model at m/z 60 to 900. The acquired raw data were processed with MSDAIL ver.4.38, and SIMCA-P 13.0 (Umetrics, NJ) was used for PCA and OPLS-DA analysis. Targeted analysis
was carried out by integrating the peak area of each metabolite using Xcalibur. The list of altered typical
metabolites in the serum and liver were present in Tables S1 and S2.
Lipidomic analysis was performed on mice liver samples. Approximately 20 mg of liver tissue was homogenized with a cold methanol/chloroform (1:1) solution containing 5 µM LPC12:0 as an internal standard. Each
sample underwent vortexing for 30 s and then centrifuged at 1,2000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. The lower organic
layer was transferred and dried under vacuum. The residue was resuspended in 25 µL of chloroform/methanol
(1:1) solution, followed by diluting with 200 µL of isopropanol (IPA)/ACN/H2O (2:1:1). All samples were
analyzed using Vanquish UHPLC-Q Exactive plus MS system equipped with an Acquity UPLC CSH C18
column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 µm). For UHPLC, mobile phase A was ACN:H₂O (60:40) with 10 mM ammonium
acetate and 0.1% FA, and mobile phase B was IPA: ACN (90:10) with 10 mM ammonium acetate and 0.1% FA.
Elution gradient is as follows: 0–2.0 min, 40% B; 2.0–2.1 min, 40%–43%B; 2.1%–12.0min, 43%–50%B;
12.0–12.1 min, 50%–54%B; 12.1–18.0 min, 54%–70%B; 18.0–18.1 min, 70%–99%B; 18.1–20.0 min, 99%–40%B.
The flow rate was 0.4 mL/min and the injection volume was 5 µL.
The raw files were processed for lipid annotation, peak extraction and peak alignments using MS-DIAL
software (V.4.38). The set of parameters was described as a reference.33 All the identified lipids were
confirmed by matching their MS/MS spectral fragmentations against the in-built library of MS DIAL.
PCA, orthogonal projection to latent structures discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA), and VIP scoring were
conducted using MetaboAnalyst 4.0. Significance thresholds were set as fold-change > 2 and adjusted
p < 0.05 (FDR-corrected). The list of altered typical lipid metabolites was present in Table S3.

16S rRNA gene sequencing and data analysis
Total microbial genomic DNA was extracted from the stool samples using the TianGen stool DNA
extraction kit (Beijing, China). The bacterial 16S rRNA (V3–V4 regions) was amplified using universal
primers 338F/806R and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform. In brief, the raw sequencing data were
processed with QIIME 2. Taxonomy was assigned using RDP classifier and annotated with the Silvav138
reference database. Alpha diversity analysis was based on one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc
test. Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) plot was used to visualize beta diversity differences based on
unweighted UniFrac distances. Kruskal–Wallis and post-hoc Dunn's tests were used for differentially
enriched bacteria taxa analysis. The difference of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes at the phylum level was
assessed using student's t-test and Mann–Whitney nonparametric test. Bioinformatic analysis was performed and visualized on the online platform of the Majorbio Cloud Platform (Shanghai, China).

PSM alleviates DSS-induced experimental UC in mice
In the present study, 3% (w/v) DSS treated mice were used as a model of severe colitis with comorbid liver
injury.34 To investigate the protective effects of PSM, it was given to mice i.p. once every two days. A
